title: Use reports of the 33 instruments and their AI-literacy mapping

framework.citation: OECD / European Union (2026), Empowering learners for the age of AI: An AI literacy framework for primary and secondary education, OECD Publishing, Paris, https://doi.org/10.1787/65cd27d4-en
framework.wording: The 19 competence statements, 57 Learner Expectations and 57 "In the Classroom" examples are read verbatim from docs/ailit/learner_expectations.tsv and docs/ailit/classroom_scenarios.tsv, with their pages; the build checks that every quote in the reports is identical.

categories.a: 100 % hit: the scenario contains the activity of the framework's classroom example for that competence and level.
categories.b: Mutatis mutandis: a modification, named in the entry, brings the scenario to the level of the classroom example.
categories.beyond: Where the scenarios go beyond every classroom example of the framework; one paragraph per instrument.
categories.non_fits: The competences the instrument's scenarios do not reach, named by the report.

competences.title: Recognise AI’s role and influence in different contexts.
Describe how AI systems perform tasks using language that addresses and clarifies common misconceptions.
Evaluate whether AI outputs should be accepted, revised or rejected.
Examine how predictive AI systems provide recommendations that can inform or limit perspectives.
Compare how AI systems consume energy and natural resources.
Explain how AI could be used to amplify societal biases.
Analyse how well the use of an AI system aligns with ethical principles and human values.
Use AI systems to explore new perspectives and approaches that build upon original ideas.
Visualise, prototype and combine ideas using different types of AI systems.
Direct generative AI systems to elicit feedback, refine results and support reflection.
Analyse how AI can safeguard or violate content authenticity and intellectual property.
Decide whether to use AI systems based on the nature of the task.
Choose an appropriate AI approach for a task by comparing how different AI systems operate and what they are best suited to do.
Decompose a problem to determine when and how AI systems should be used to automate or augment tasks.
Monitor and evaluate AI use throughout a problem-solving process.
Investigate how an AI system is intended to work, whom it is designed for and what its limitations are.
Evaluate AI systems using defined criteria, expected outcomes, test cases and user feedback.
Design AI systems with attention to how data sources, selection and information flow influence behaviour and outputs.
Improve AI systems to address and promote human well-being and societal benefit.

expectations.Engage 1|Basic: Learners can identify where different types of AI are present in their everyday lives.
expectations.Engage 1|Intermediate: Learners share examples of how AI systems have influenced their own choices and experiences at home, in school or online.
expectations.Engage 1|Advanced: Learners can analyse how AI systems may shape individuals’ beliefs and behaviours as consumers, learners, workers and citizens.
expectations.Engage 2|Basic: Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding.
expectations.Engage 2|Intermediate: Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works.
expectations.Engage 2|Advanced: Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding.
expectations.Engage 3|Basic: Learners understand why AI-generated outputs should be verified and recognise how they can verify the content themselves.
expectations.Engage 3|Intermediate: Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations.
expectations.Engage 3|Advanced: Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them.
expectations.Engage 4|Basic: Learners know that AI can use data about a user to provide recommendations or predictions for them.
expectations.Engage 4|Intermediate: Learners consider when AI-generated recommendations might be helpful to them or when they may seem too narrow and too general.
expectations.Engage 4|Advanced: Learners weigh the benefits and drawbacks of AI systems using data to shape access to information and consider how this might influence worldviews, ideas or behaviours.
expectations.Engage 5|Basic: Learners recognise that computers and AI systems require resources to function.
expectations.Engage 5|Intermediate: Learners describe different ways that AI impacts the environment (e.g. hardware production, data centre development, water use, energy intensity).
expectations.Engage 5|Advanced: Learners analyse how individual choices along with different design, deployment or business decisions can affect AI’s overall energy and resource use.
expectations.Engage 6|Basic: Learners understand that biases can exist in the data used to train AI and can be perpetuated when humans design, develop and use AI systems.
expectations.Engage 6|Intermediate: Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups.
expectations.Engage 6|Advanced: Learners analyse how individuals, companies or institutions may build and deploy AI systems to serve particular interests and how these systems might shape opportunities, representations or public perceptions.
expectations.Engage 7|Basic: Learners recognise that ethical AI use depends on a number of factors that include AI system design, development and a user’s own intentions.
expectations.Engage 7|Intermediate: Learners identify when AI use may have unintended impacts or implications that are different from a user’s immediate goals.
expectations.Engage 7|Advanced: Learners evaluate the use of AI according to multiple ethical principles, considering trade-offs and who may benefit or be harmed.
expectations.Create 1|Basic: Learners explore how different AI tools can expand their thinking or spark new ideas.
expectations.Create 1|Intermediate: Learners compare AI-generated suggestions to their own ideas during a brainstorming process.
expectations.Create 1|Advanced: Learners purposefully integrate AI-generated outputs with their own ideas to develop comprehensive solutions and creative approaches.
expectations.Create 2|Basic: Learners use AI to generate an image, story or model to represent an idea.
expectations.Create 2|Intermediate: Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs.
expectations.Create 2|Advanced: Learners select and integrate outputs from multiple AI systems to develop, refine or present a final product.
expectations.Create 3|Basic: Learners know how to prompt AI systems to generate accurate feedback and helpful responses to an idea.
expectations.Create 3|Intermediate: Learners refine their work through iterative exchanges with AI, comparing those outputs to their own ideas to determine what serves their goals.
expectations.Create 3|Advanced: Learners critically evaluate how AI-generated feedback shapes their own ideas, then reflect on how they would like to use AI in their creative process.
expectations.Create 4|Basic: Learners know that AI-generated content may reuse or copy work protected by intellectual property or copyright laws and recognise implications for the humans who created the original work.
expectations.Create 4|Intermediate: Learners consider when attribution, permission or avoidance of AI is appropriate for a creative task and apply these choices in their own work.
expectations.Create 4|Advanced: Learners assess the ethical implications of AI-generated outputs for creative work, distinguish inspiration from replication in their outputs, and justify how their use of AI maintains authenticity and respects other creators.
expectations.Manage 1|Basic: Learners identify a variety of AI systems and the tasks they are designed to support.
expectations.Manage 1|Intermediate: Learners use what they know about AI to determine whether AI is an appropriate digital tool for a specific task.
expectations.Manage 1|Advanced: Learners determine whether AI is the right digital tool for a specific task by comparing the task’s complexity and need for human judgement with the ethical implications of AI use.
expectations.Manage 2|Basic: Learners recognise that some types of AI systems can be programmed with specific rules to accomplish tasks, while others can learn patterns from data.
expectations.Manage 2|Intermediate: Learners identify the benefits and drawbacks of using a rules-based approach and a machine learning approach to solve a problem.
expectations.Manage 2|Advanced: Learners evaluate when AI is an effective approach for a task by considering factors such as context, data availability and quality, efficiency, transparency, desired outcomes and potential impacts.
expectations.Manage 3|Basic: Learners identify the type of problem at hand and consider whether AI might help solve it.
expectations.Manage 3|Intermediate: Learners break a problem into component parts and consider ways AI might help with specific steps.
expectations.Manage 3|Advanced: Learners deliberately assign tasks within a multi-step process based on appropriate human strengths and relevant AI capabilities.
expectations.Manage 4|Basic: Learners recognise that they should make decisions about AI use that support accountability, learning and fairness.
expectations.Manage 4|Intermediate: Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves.
expectations.Manage 4|Advanced: Learners establish checkpoints based on human and AI roles, monitor progress against success criteria and adjust roles accordingly.
expectations.Shape 1|Basic: Learners identify what different AI systems are designed to do.
expectations.Shape 1|Intermediate: Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool.
expectations.Shape 1|Advanced: Learners assess the strengths and limitations of an AI tool by considering its purpose, intended users, constraints and potential impacts.
expectations.Shape 2|Basic: Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task.
expectations.Shape 2|Intermediate: Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests.
expectations.Shape 2|Advanced: Learners design their own evaluation criteria for an AI system, compare performance across different inputs and users and use it to propose improvements.
expectations.Shape 3|Basic: Learners identify examples of data that might be used to train AI systems.
expectations.Shape 3|Intermediate: Learners compare the importance of data selection and collection methods in cases when AI is used to make decisions that affect others.
expectations.Shape 3|Advanced: Learners evaluate how specific properties of a dataset (e.g. size, features, biases) affect the performance and impact of an AI model.
expectations.Shape 4|Basic: Learners recognise that AI systems can be designed or adjusted to better support individuals, communities and the environment.
expectations.Shape 4|Intermediate: Learners propose specific design changes to improve an AI system for themselves and others.
expectations.Shape 4|Advanced: Learners design and justify improvements to an AI system based on technical constraints, ethical considerations and user needs.

classroom.Engage 1|Basic: Learners play “AI or Not” with their teacher. Given examples, such as smart home devices, social media or apps, they can categorise each based on whether it uses AI.
classroom.Engage 1|Intermediate: Learners compare examples of “for you” landing pages on social media platforms and reflect on how and why they are influenced by what appears.
classroom.Engage 1|Advanced: Learners explore screenshots from AI chatbots and apps to identify when it may be designed to persuade, rather than inform. With a teacher, they discuss how features like “streak” counts, character names or overly-agreeable responses might be engineered to increase engagement.
classroom.Engage 2|Basic: As their teacher introduces common phrases used to describe AI use (e.g. “AI thinks,” “AI understands,”), learners identify which ones are misleading and why. Learners develop better descriptions using technically accurate and age-appropriate language, then reflect on how language shapes their understanding of what AI can or cannot do.
classroom.Engage 2|Intermediate: Learners identify a common AI myth among peers (e.g. “AI understands like humans” or “AI is always correct”). They create an artefact, such as a poster, short video or podcast to address the misconception by explaining how AI works.
classroom.Engage 2|Advanced: Learners review different types of AI tools and compare design choices that make the systems appear human-like, friendly or intelligent. In small groups, learners practise explaining how the tools produce outputs, focussing on programmed processes rather than human qualities. As a class, they share and refine their explanations and reflect on how different design features affect understanding and trust in AI systems.
classroom.Engage 3|Basic: Learners review an AI-powered tool’s solution to a maths problem and accompanying explanation, then compare the AI-generated content to the process that their teacher has introduced to the class.
classroom.Engage 3|Intermediate: In small groups, learners plan an itinerary for a tourist visiting their hometown. When the teacher provides AI-generated recommendations for local restaurants, learners compare the recommendations using other sources to determine if the information is outdated, inaccurate or a “hallucination.” From there, learners draw from their own knowledge and experience to decide whether the locations would be appealing to a visitor.
classroom.Engage 3|Advanced: When their teacher presents different AI-generated interpretations of a historical event, learners turn to trusted secondary or primary sources to verify the accuracy of the interpretations and argue which one they would include in a final report.
classroom.Engage 4|Basic: Learners make a list of movie and television recommendations for a favourite book character, justifying their choices with textual evidence. As a class, they share their lists and discuss their knowledge of the characters, then compare the process to the ways AI generates recommendations.
classroom.Engage 4|Intermediate: Learners compare a music app’s recommendations to a list of their own favourite songs and artists, then discuss when the algorithms reinforced existing preferences or introduced them to new genres.
classroom.Engage 4|Advanced: Learners review case studies of how social media recommendation systems have affected public understanding of an issue, then discuss how this might impact individuals’ voting behaviours.
classroom.Engage 5|Basic: Learners list the classroom devices that must be charged and cooled and recognise that AI systems also require electricity and hardware to run.
classroom.Engage 5|Intermediate: Learners create an informational artefact (e.g. written article, podcast or video) explaining how training large AI models compares to household or individual energy use.
classroom.Engage 5|Advanced: Learners research the environmental impacts of AI use and data centre development across different communities. They then identify policies and strategies that promote responsible AI use and development.
classroom.Engage 6|Basic: With their teacher, learners explore different types of data that can be collected about a person (e.g. height, favourite colour). They note the nuances that data can capture effectively, but draw from their knowledge of each other to identify what is left out.
classroom.Engage 6|Intermediate: Learners explore how and why facial recognition technology performs differently across demographics and discuss possible real-world impacts when it is used for decision making in everyday life.
classroom.Engage 6|Advanced: With a teacher, learners evaluate real-world examples of AI being used to influence an event (e.g. misinformation and disinformation on social media). Then they explore how an institution’s choices regarding AI use might benefit certain groups while having a negative effect on others.
classroom.Engage 7|Basic: Learners identify recognisable aspects of artists’ work across AI-generated examples. With a teacher, they discuss whether the examples constitute fair and appropriate use and identify implications for the human artists.
classroom.Engage 7|Intermediate: Learners analyse a case study where an AI tool uses one’s browsing history to advertise discounts and sales on products they have viewed in the past. With their teacher, learners weigh the opportunities to save money with risks the AI tool poses for personal privacy. They discuss the pros and cons of using the tool in the long- and short-term.
classroom.Engage 7|Advanced: Learners explore how AI is used to analyse climate data to spot patterns and make predictions. They evaluate trade-offs between the tool’s predictive power and the reduced transparency of an AI model. Learners weigh the opportunities for clearer forecasts with the risks of “hallucinations,” or if important uncertainties are misunderstood or ignored.
classroom.Create 1|Basic: Learners discuss AI-generated images to create story settings based on their classmates’ ideas (e.g. “a jungle in space”), then write new stories inspired by unexpected results.
classroom.Create 1|Intermediate: In response to a teacher’s assignment, learners brainstorm independently before reviewing AI-generated ideas. They compare their own ideas with the AI-generated ones and discuss how exposure to AI suggestions may shape originality, confidence or decision making.
classroom.Create 1|Advanced: Learners develop their own arguments for a class debate, then analyse AI-generated counterarguments provided by the teacher. They remix and reject the counterpoints to strengthen their final argument.
classroom.Create 2|Basic: Learners choose a theme (e.g. “hope,” “winter” or “community”) and use an AI image generator to create a visual representation. They generate one image and write a short explanation of how specific elements of their prompt shaped the final result, noting any unexpected or surprising aspects of the output. They assess how well the generated result matches the idea they had in mind.
classroom.Create 2|Intermediate: Learners design a concept to share about a new club at their school. They generate multiple mission statements, activity ideas and visual styles using text and image generators. Then they compare how different prompts and tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.
classroom.Create 2|Advanced: Learners use AI tools to design a simple interactive project (e.g. a motion-activated light display). They use a text generator to outline how the system should respond, an image generator to visualise the setup and an AI coding assistant to draft basic control code. They generate examples from different tools, compare outputs and revise their prototypes. Learners ensure the plan, visuals and code align into one functional prototype and seek peer feedback before finalising their work.
classroom.Create 3|Basic: Learners are shown two different versions of a prompt designed to get feedback on the same idea. They compare AI-generated responses to the two prompts and analyse which prompt led to an output with more accurate or useful feedback. Then they explain what features (e.g. context, specificity, constraints) made it more effective.
classroom.Create 3|Intermediate: Learners design a three-dimensional model of a geometric garden using ratios and proportions. They compare AI-suggested dimensions to their own calculations to ensure mathematical accuracy and consider new creative approaches to inform the design.
classroom.Create 3|Advanced: Learners compare an early draft of a writing assignment to a final version that was revised with feedback from an AI tool. They annotate key changes to the assignment that indicate when each revision was influenced by the AI tool or their own thinking. They write a brief reflection explaining how they decided which suggestions to use, adapt or ignore to meet their goals.
classroom.Create 4|Basic: Learners examine examples of music generated with AI to imitate a famous artist. With their teacher, learners discuss how this raises concerns about copyright, ownership and attributing proper credit to the artist.
classroom.Create 4|Intermediate: Learners compare original work to AI-generated poems, then discuss with their teacher what makes something “original.” They then identify school-based guidelines for attributing AI use.
classroom.Create 4|Advanced: Learners are presented with examples of art created entirely by a human, generated by an AI system and created by an artist along with AI. Learners consider what choices a human did or did not make for each piece, who should be credited as the artist, what should be protected by copyright and how AI may change artistic creation in the future.
classroom.Manage 1|Basic: Learners follow guidance established by their teacher to match appropriate tools with academic tasks (e.g. AI for summarising, search engines for research).
classroom.Manage 1|Intermediate: As the teacher calls out examples of everyday tasks for the whole class, learners move to corners of the room labelled “AI Only,” “AI-Supported,” “Human Only,” or “Not Sure” based on how they think AI could be used. Learners then defend and explain their choices to peers who had chosen differently and switch corners if convinced.
classroom.Manage 1|Advanced: Learners consider the steps to write an essay (i.e. choosing a topic, researching evidence, organising arguments, drafting paragraphs, revising and proof-reading), then identify which steps AI could assist with and which steps require their own voice and reasoning. They consult their school’s guidelines for AI use to tailor their approach.
classroom.Manage 2|Basic: Learners compare different approaches to building AI systems by completing a trash-sorting task. First, they consider why random outputs would be unlikely to reliably sort items. Next, they direct a classmate role-playing as a robot to sort images of trash based on specific criteria. They observe how the “robot” responds to new images that do not match the criteria. Finally, they explore how a system could use patterns from collected data, such as a class survey, to improve sorting decisions and determine which approach is most appropriate for different tasks.
classroom.Manage 2|Intermediate: Learners compare technology that follows set rules to execute a task (e.g. calculators, traffic lights, thermostats) with technologies that have been trained on examples from data (e.g., image recognition, translation). With a teacher, they consider why each approach suits the specific task.
classroom.Manage 2|Advanced: Learners analyse real-world examples of AI use (e.g. route planning, content moderation or resource allocation). They justify whether a rule-based or machine learning approach is more appropriate – or whether AI should be used at all – based on the requirements, constraints and trade-offs involved. They build a case to make a recommendation, then present their chosen approaches to their peers in a class debate.
classroom.Manage 3|Basic: Learners are given examples of different problems to identify (e.g. predicting the weather, comforting a friend, detecting plagiarism) and classify each as a type of problem (e.g. data-based, emotional, creative). As a class, they discuss whether AI could help solve the problem and if AI solutions are always necessary to accomplish a goal.
classroom.Manage 3|Intermediate: Learners break down the steps to complete a complex research project and identify steps that AI could support (e.g. summarising primary sources and locating relevant commentaries). They work independently to verify claims, assess potential bias in AI outputs and develop their own arguments and interpretations.
classroom.Manage 3|Advanced: Learners are given a time-bound challenge to produce two versions of the same product, with and without AI. Before starting the AI-supported task, teams decide exactly which steps will rely on AI capabilities and which will depend on human strengths. After comparing outcomes, learners revise their task assignments and explain how changing human and AI roles affected the quality, trustworthiness and purpose of the final product.
classroom.Manage 4|Basic: Learners explore examples of AI tool use across industries (e.g. sports, journalism, music) to determine if there are tasks where AI use might be advantageous and when a human should play a more active role.
classroom.Manage 4|Intermediate: Learners watch short videos of self-driving cars navigating different driving situations. As a class, learners compare how a human might make a different decision than a self-driving car and discuss when human judgement should override the algorithm.
classroom.Manage 4|Advanced: Learners work in teams to create a public awareness campaign about a local issue (e.g. reducing food waste, designing safe bicycle routes). They use AI tools to generate messages or visuals, but pause to compare outputs with audience needs and project goals. When AI-generated content is misleading or off-target, learners adjust roles or workflows to produce an accurate and authentic message.
classroom.Shape 1|Basic: Learners review model cards that describe how an AI system works, its training data, intended uses and possible limitations. As a class, they discuss appropriate uses of the AI system.
classroom.Shape 1|Intermediate: Learners examine several examples of AI tools (e.g. a chatbot, recommendation system or route-planning app). For each, learners identify its primary task and explain in simple terms what input it uses and how the outputs execute the task.
classroom.Shape 1|Advanced: Learners analyse how an AI-enabled navigation app uses traffic data to suggest efficient routes. They discuss how the app might reduce travel time for some while increasing congestion, noise or safety risks in certain neighborhoods.
classroom.Shape 2|Basic: Learners examine an AI system that recommends new music. In small groups, they define criteria for what would make the system successful and compare the system’s recommendations for users with different interests or interaction histories.
classroom.Shape 2|Intermediate: Learners identify strategies they would use to solve a word puzzle. The teacher presents a sample algorithm for the same task. Using defined criteria (e.g. efficiency, consistency, clarity), learners compare their peers’ strategies to the algorithm, identifying strengths, limitations and trade-offs in each approach.
classroom.Shape 2|Advanced: In pairs, learners draft proposals for an AI tool and share their ideas. Each learner asks their partner a series of questions about their proposal. Next, each partner fills out a model card to identify intended and unintended users, impacts and use cases for the other’s idea. They provide feedback to each other based on the model cards and revise their own tool proposals accordingly.
classroom.Shape 3|Basic: Learners are tasked with designing an AI tool that can sort recyclable materials. In small groups, they decide what data they could collect on the internet to train the AI tool. With support from a teacher, they discuss which aspects of the data would be most important to train an effective and accurate AI tool.
classroom.Shape 3|Intermediate: Learners compare different methods for organising a set of animals, such as grouping them based on physical characteristics. They discuss what happens when new animals are introduced to the set that do not fit into the existing groups.
classroom.Shape 3|Advanced: Learners conduct a class survey to choose a class pet and represent the results using a bar chart. They compare these results with their individual preferences, as well as data from a grade-level survey and a school-wide survey. Learners discuss how increasing the size and diversity of the dataset changes the outcomes of the survey and consider how an AI system might make different recommendations based on its training data.
classroom.Shape 4|Basic: Learners discuss everyday challenges in their classroom or school, such as finding study resources or sharing information on time. They explore examples of AI tools and identify simple changes that could make these tools more helpful or inclusive, such as clearer instructions, age-appropriate outputs or options for different needs. Learners explain who would benefit from these improvements and why.
classroom.Shape 4|Intermediate: Learners consider the use of an AI tool that would predict which library books are most in demand. They analyse how design choices around data sources, categories and recommendations influence what interests are represented. Learners suggest and plan concrete changes (e.g. adding user input, adjusting categories, including feedback loops) to improve variables like access, inclusion or usefulness. They identify features that ensure recommendations and interfaces are accessible and supportive for learners with different abilities or learning needs.
classroom.Shape 4|Advanced: Working in teams, learners design or modify a model that uses local environmental data to alert community members with asthma about health risks. They practise making deliberate design decisions about which data to include, how predictions are generated and how users receive alerts from the model. Learners test and refine their system using feedback to explain how their improvements better support human well-being and community trust.

unreached.Engage 1|Basic: Die Maßnahme spielt „AI or Not“ mit Beispielen wie Smart-Home-Geräten, sozialen Netzwerken oder Apps. Die Plattform hält keine solchen Beispiele.
unreached.Engage 1|Intermediate: Die Maßnahme vergleicht „for you“-Seiten sozialer Netzwerke und reflektiert, wie und warum die Lernenden von dem beeinflusst werden, was dort erscheint. Die Plattform führt keine Feeds und empfiehlt nichts.
unreached.Engage 4|Basic: Die Maßnahme vergleicht eigene Film- und Serienempfehlungen für eine Buchfigur mit der Art, wie KI Empfehlungen erzeugt. Die Plattform hält kein Empfehlungssystem, keine Vorhersage aus Nutzerdaten und keinen Feed.
unreached.Engage 4|Intermediate: Die Maßnahme vergleicht die Empfehlungen einer Musik-App mit der eigenen Liste. Die Plattform hält kein Empfehlungssystem, keine Vorhersage aus Nutzerdaten und keinen Feed.
unreached.Engage 4|Advanced: Die Maßnahme liest Fallstudien über Empfehlungssysteme sozialer Netzwerke. Die Plattform hält kein Empfehlungssystem, keine Vorhersage aus Nutzerdaten und keinen Feed.
unreached.Engage 7|Advanced: Die Maßnahme untersucht ein KI-System, das Klimadaten auswertet und Vorhersagen macht, und wägt Vorhersagekraft gegen Transparenz, Halluzinationen und übersehene Unsicherheiten ab. Die Plattform hält kein vorhersagendes System.
unreached.Manage 1|Intermediate: Die Maßnahme ist ein Spiel im Raum (Ecken „AI Only“, „AI-Supported“, „Human Only“, „Not Sure“); die Plattform trägt nichts dazu bei.
unreached.Manage 2|Advanced: Die Maßnahme begründet an Fällen aus der Welt (Routenplanung, Inhaltsmoderation, Ressourcenzuteilung), ob Regeln, maschinelles Lernen oder keine KI angemessen ist. Die Plattform hält keinen dieser Fälle.
unreached.Manage 3|Basic: Die Maßnahme ordnet vorgegebene Probleme (Wettervorhersage, einen Freund trösten, Plagiate erkennen) Problemtypen zu und bespricht, ob KI hilft. Das ist ein Klassengespräch ohne Werkzeug; die Plattform trägt dazu nichts bei.
unreached.Shape 4|Advanced: Die Maßnahme entwirft ein Modell, das aus lokalen Umweltdaten Warnungen für Menschen mit Asthma erzeugt, und verfeinert es mit Rückmeldung. Die Plattform hält kein vorhersagendes System und keine Umweltdaten.

instruments.name: Flow

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/x2x-flow`. The surface shows a band of three nodes at the top ("Stable Diffusion" with six medium glyphs, "start the image adaption", "output"), a green plus, two glyphs (grid = "choose a LoRA", orange dots = "choose a perspective"), one empty PROMPT card and a large dark circle (the zone). The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "Here you have a working surface. This is about artistic work with (or without) the tools of this platform. Bring ideas together, whether text, image, sound, or several of each. Lay them side by side, combine them, keep working on them." "Two things can be learned here: to choose, to judge and to decide how and by what means to go on, and so to shape an artistic process. And that AI can be part of creative work without standing at its centre — that it is interesting not to let one AI dictate what you may enter and what happens then." "Write a prompt into the prompt box, for example, drag the box into the circle, and press ▹ Start." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Green plus → menu "text / image / sketch / document (PDF)". Chose "text". A second PROMPT card appeared under the first. Typed `a small harbor at dusk`.
3. Dragged the card by its header into the circle. It snapped inside (class `inzone`).
4. Medium: image was already selected (glyph highlighted, model "Stable Diffusion"). Pressed "start the image adaption".
5. The band turned into five stages: "included elements: text 1 / no perspective", "Prompt Interception: no perspective · anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 · openrouter", "Prompt Adaption", "check and translation: mistralai/mistral-large-4-0 · openrouter", "inference: Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large · seed 123456789 · CFG 4.5 · 25 steps · 0%", with "hold to stop" underneath. The inference stayed at 0 %. Cause (looked up on the server, not on the surface): the ComfyUI queue was blocked by a HeartMuLa song job stuck at step 0/10. I restarted the ComfyUI service (an operator action, no code change) and the surface then showed "Service not reachable. Tell the course leader." in the middle node.
6. Pressed the middle node again ("start the image generation"). Second run: band with three stages (included elements / check and translation / inference), then "embedding the prompt…", then "inference 8/25 … step 8 of 25" with the picture building up inside the output node. The output node shows the picture; a card "#2" with the picture appeared on the table; under the middle node a note "prompt as submitted: a small harbor at dusk".
7. Clicked the text glyph (≡, the last of the six). The first node changed to "Educational theory", the button to "start the text generation". Pressed it. What ran was another image generation (seed 1392574417, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large, 25 steps), card "#3", and then a phase "included elements / check and translation / inference — Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large / hold to stop" with no progress indicator; afterwards a new PROMPT card appeared on the table containing a German image reading ("1. BILDMOTIVE … 2. KULTURELLE SITUIERUNG UND SINNZUSAMMENHÄNGE …", 3 476 characters). The server log shows this phase as an image analysis with the local model qwen3-vl:4b.
8. Long-pressed the image glyph (1.2 s). A column of bubbles opened: "auto (hand the choice back — medium and model follow the material again)", Common Canvas, Stable Diffusion Turbo, Stable Diffusion, Flux 2, Flux 3 Klein, Gemini 3 Pro (€), Nano Banana 2.1 (€), Qwen Edit, Qwen Multi. Chose "Flux 3 Klein". First node now reads "Flux 3 Klein", button "start the image adaption". Pressed it. Band: five stages again, "FLUX 3 Image Klein · seed 1392574417 · CFG 1 · 16 steps · 0%". 0 % (queue behind the image-analysis job of step 7, then model loading), then the 16 steps. Card "#4".
9. Clicked the orange-dots glyph. A full-screen circle with seven category bubbles (icons only, no labels: camera, burst, face, pen, knot, wand, museum). Clicked the camera: seven picture bubbles with labels "Good Picture, Daguerreotype, Analog Photography, Analogue Copy, Bad Picture, Cooked Film, Digital Photography". Dragging "Cooked Film" into the zone did nothing; clicking it closed the overlay and put a round "Cooked Film" bubble on the table (with a small "?" badge). Dragged the bubble into the circle. The middle node changed to "create the prompt".
10. Pressed "create the prompt". Band: "included elements: text 1 / Cooked Film", "Prompt Interception: Cooked Film · anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 · openrouter", "Prompt Adaption", "check and translation", "inference: Flux 3 Klein". A card "Prompt Interception #5" appeared with a long English prompt (35 mm colour negative simmered in water before C-41 development, reticulated emulsion, magenta/teal colour flip, sprocket holes…). Then the picture: a harbour in pink-magenta light with mottled, blistered film texture, card "#5". Under the middle node: "prompt as submitted" with the full interception text.

Runs: 5 started, 4 completed (one stalled behind the stuck queue).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Green plus: adds material cards (text, image, sketch, PDF). Cards are draggable; the circle is the "zone" that selects what goes into the run.
- The six medium glyphs switch the output medium; a short click switches the medium, a long press opens the model list for that medium. The first node's label is the model name. "auto" hands the choice back to the material.
- The middle node is the run button; its label changes with what the run will do ("start the image adaption", "start the image generation", "start the text generation", "create the prompt" once a perspective lies in the zone).
- During a run the band replaces the three nodes with the pipeline stages, naming the model and provider of each stage and the sampler settings (seed, CFG, steps) of the inference. "hold to stop" (long press) aborts.
- The output node shows the result and the progressive picture during sampling; every result also lands on the table as a numbered card (#2, #3…). Image cards carry four small actions on hover: Add to favorites, Download, Print, Image Analysis.
- Perspective chooser: category circle → labelled bubbles → one bubble on the table → drag into the zone. The "?" badge on the bubble presumably explains the perspective (not opened).
- "choose a LoRA" glyph and the gear "Surface settings" were not used. "?" top right: Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Run 2 (SD 3.5 Large, no perspective): a competent, generic harbour at blue hour — sailing boats and a pier, blue sky, warm lamps. Nothing surprising; it looks like a stock photo.
- Run 3 ("text" medium): no text about the material in the sense I expected; it produced another picture (#3, a different harbour with a stone quay and sodium lamps) and then a German reading of that picture, structured as "1. BILDMOTIVE / 2. KULTURELLE SITUIERUNG …", speculating the harbour is "mediterranean or alpine". The reading is in German although the UI is English.
- Run 4 (Flux 3 Klein): a harbour at dusk with a quay, small boats, soft orange sky — tighter and more photographic than SD 3.5.
- Run 5 (Flux 3 Klein + Cooked Film): the interception rewrote the one-line prompt into a 1 100-character description of a damaged colour negative. The picture follows it closely: magenta-teal cast, mottled grain, blistered edges, a bollard and rope in the foreground. This is the only run where the output clearly differed from the input in a way the band explains (the "Prompt Interception" card shows exactly the text that was sent on).
- The band's stage labels name third-party cloud models for interception and translation (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 via openrouter, mistralai/mistral-large-4-0 via openrouter) and the local model for inference.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- "0 %" with no further message. The band shows the inference stage but not whether it is queued, loading a model, or stuck.
- The "text" medium: the button says "start the text generation", but what happened was an image generation plus an image reading. The relationship between the text medium and the material in the zone is not visible beforehand.
- The perspective overlay: dragging a perspective from the overlay does nothing, only clicking places it.
- Medium switch by short click vs. model list by long press: nothing on the surface says that a long press exists.
- Results pile up on the table at the same spot (#2, #3, #4 overlap), the German reading card covers the pictures.
- Error text "Service not reachable. Tell the course leader." appeared after the service restart although the service was reachable a few seconds later; a second press worked.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text:
The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: a working surface for artistic work with or without the platform's tools, where ideas in text, image and sound are laid side by side, combined and worked on further; what is learned (to choose, to judge, to decide how to go on; AI as part of creative work without standing at its centre); and the first move (prompt box, circle, Start). It should add what the surface is made of, in this order:

- **Material of any kind.** The green plus adds text, image, sketch and document (PDF); every result of a run falls back onto the table as a card and is material for the next run. The circle is the zone: as soon as material lies in it, the run reads only the zone; an empty zone reads the whole table (the page's own string).
- **The medium follows the material; override is possible** The six glyphs are image, video, sound, 3D, code and text; "auto" hands the choice back. Text is the one medium that reads instead of making: one piece in the zone is described, two are compared, and the long press on the text glyph lists five reading frames instead of models (structural media education, iconology, ethical: "Who is shown and who is absent, the power relations in the picture, the conditions it was made under", critical, descriptive). Image and video also list the paths that take a picture as input (Qwen Edit, Qwen Multi) and want one or two pictures on the table.
- **A perspective is a Prompt Interception.** A language model rereads the idea through the perspective; the page's own node text says "a pedagogical interception, not prompt polishing". The chooser shows seven category bubbles; the camera bubble showed me seven perspectives, and the configuration (`devserver/schemas/configs/interception`) holds 35 unhidden perspectives in these seven categories: Photography & Media (Good Picture, Bad Picture, Daguerreotype, Analog Photography, Analogue Copy, Cooked Film, Digital Photography, and Early Photography Landscape, which the bubble did not show me), Critical Thinking (Against the Model, One World, Planetarizer, Critique of Consumption, The Unspoken), Art History (Bauhaus, Literati, Renaissance), Creative Transformations (De-Kitsch, Sweetener, Slang, Amplifier, On the Contrary!, Your Story, Chain Translation, Word Game, Scene Graph, Listifier, Technical, Generative Techniques, Music Composer), Attitudes (Forceful, mad world, Sensitive), Research (Latent Lab, Surrealizer) and Art & Culture with "Your Call!": write a perspective yourself ("what should shape, alter, or question the idea?"), name it and save it under your account, where it is there again next time. Several perspectives in the zone run as a chain. The intercepted prompt appears as its own card, editable: change it by hand and run again.
- **The run is visible.** The band names every stage with its model (included elements, Prompt Interception, Prompt Adaption, check and translation, inference with seed, CFG and steps). A perspective that looks something up while reading leaves a source card under the circle ("Searched for", "Article", "Nothing was found under this term") with the summary that went into the reading. The back of every result card ("Turn the card") carries "prompt as submitted" and the line "AI marking: AI-generated (marked in the file)". A code result opens ("Open the code"), can be changed and run again; a 3D result turns.
- **A LoRA lies on the table like a perspective.** The grid glyph lists the adapters released to this session in three groups, Platform, Course and Own trainings, with strength and trigger; an adapter trained on the LoRA Training page from the group's own pictures is used here.
- **Favorites are shared material.** The bar at the foot switches between "My favorites" and "All favorites"; a favourite is dragged onto the board to keep working with it, your own or somebody else's.
- **The Help knows the run.** The page hands the material and the interception result to the Help panel, so it can be asked what the perspective did to the idea.

Only then the handling: short click on a glyph picks the medium, long press lists the models; a perspective is placed by clicking and dragged into the circle; a long press on "hold to stop" aborts; a run at 0 % waits for a model to load or for another run to finish; the gear holds "Clear canvas", which keeps the last result.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- The artistic workflow: try a prompt out, change it, change the results again with other interceptions, try different models; make a picture and a sound from the same prompt and a video from the two (picture and sound together in the circle, video glyph); merge several pictures into one (two or three in the circle, long press on the image glyph, "Qwen Multi"); craft and combine, a picture with a text, a reading with a sketch; and arrange the results on the surface for comparison and for your own judgement, for example spatially by interception bubble: the works of one perspective around its bubble, those of another around its bubble, the default without perspective between them. Cards are dragged anywhere, the table zooms (+, −, 1:1), and only what lies in the circle is read, so the arrangement outside it stays as it is. I did not run sound, video and the merging.
- Write one idea, lay it into the circle, and run it under five perspectives in turn (Critique of Consumption, On the Contrary!, Against the Model, Sweetener, De-Kitsch); read the Prompt Interception card of each run before looking at the picture: what the perspective did to the idea stands there in words. Sort the results together with its respective perspective as clusters on the table an proceed working.
- Write a perspective of your own under "Your Call!", save it, and run the same material through it next to a platform perspective.
- Lay two perspectives into the circle at once and read the chain: the second rereads what the first wrote.
- Edit an intercepted prompt by hand on its card and run it again; compare with the unedited run.
- Put your own photograph on the table, choose the text medium and read it through two frames (ethical, then descriptive); then lay the reading into the circle as material and make a sound or a picture from it.
- Lay multiple images in the circle, if you want also a prompt and/or a perspective and lora. Things will happen.
- Run with "Against the Model" or "The Unspoken" and open the source cards under the circle to see what the perspective looked up.
- Discover that with tricky prompts, flow will look up wikipedia pages in its cultural original versions (if available) and throw the results on the table.
- Lay a LoRA from "Own trainings" on the table next to a sketch and run; then the same sketch without it. Not tried.
- Keep a card's back as the record of a work: "prompt as submitted" and the AI marking are the label for a wall or a catalogue.
- Switch the favorites bar to "All favorites", drag another group's picture onto the board and go on from it (or find the prompt on the back of the card and re-use it).
- Ask the Help panel, after a run, what the perspective changed in the idea.
- Throw an image and a generated sound into the action circle, and it will be combined into a movie file
- Draw a sketch and turn it into any media
- reuse prompt and images from the favorites in order to continue own or other's work
- load any document, use prompt interception, use the result as a new prompt interception
- load a picture, use text to get an interpretation of your choice, and proceed with the line above this one

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — The artistic workflow** (formal or non-formal, art, from grade 7, 90 min to a full day). One prompt is tried out and changed; its results are changed again with other interceptions; different models are tried on the same material; from the same prompt a picture and a sound are made and, with both in the circle, a video; two or three pictures are merged into one; results are crafted and combined, a picture with a text, a reading with a sketch; and on the surface the results are arranged for comparison and for the group's own judgement, spatially by interception bubble: around the "Cooked Film" bubble everything it made, around "On the Contrary!" everything that one made, the runs without perspective in the middle, the discarded ones at the edge. The arrangement is the judgement; it is read at the end from the table, not from a list. Sequence (90 min version): 15 min prompt, first runs, first changes; 45 min interceptions, models, sound and video, merging, each result placed as it arrives; 20 min the group re-arranges by its own criteria; 10 min each group walks the others through its table. Subject link: artistic process, variation and series, judging one's own work. Uncertainty: I arranged nothing, made no sound or video and merged nothing; my cards piled up at one spot (see 5).

**S2 — One theme, six weeks: the table as the studio** (formal, art, grades 8–12, 6 × 90 min). Flow is the working surface of the whole unit; the board is kept only for the browser session, so what is to come back next week is added to the favorites from its card and dragged onto the board again from "My favorites". Week 1: one theme sentence per student, run without perspective, then under five perspectives (Critique of Consumption, On the Contrary!, Sweetener, De-Kitsch, Against the Model); before each picture the Prompt Interception card is read and what the perspective put in is underlined; one card is edited by hand and run again. Week 2: an own perspective under "Your Call!", saved, run against a platform perspective; 30 min side trip to the Prompt Interception Lab (Language Model Comparison, Interception Scope) to see the same interception across models. Week 3: from the best prompt a picture and a sound, then a video from the two; three students' pictures merged into one. Week 4: own photographs and drawings as material: read through the ethical and the descriptive frame, a sketch turned into any medium, a picture changed with a text ("Qwen Edit"). Week 5: an adapter trained from the class's drawings on the LoRA Training page, laid on the table under "Own trainings". Week 6: the table arranged by interception bubble for the class's own judgement; the exhibition is built from the card backs ("prompt as submitted", AI marking); the favorites are the archive of the unit. Subject link: artistic process over time, series, medium change, judging one's own work; the side trip links the perspective to the instruments that show what it does. Uncertainty: I did not run sound, video, merging, own perspective, LoRA and the favorites across sessions.

**S3 — Our own perspective** (formal, language teaching, grades 9–12, 2 × 90 min). Groups write a perspective under "Your Call!": a text that says what should shape, alter or question an idea, in the group's own words (a stance, a genre, a way of seeing), name it and save it. Each group runs three materials (a sentence, a photograph, a short poem) through its perspective and through one platform perspective of the same category, reads the two interception cards for each, and revises its own wording twice. Day 2: groups exchange perspectives through the saved list and write a short review of what another group's perspective does to a text. Subject link: writing an instruction, register and stance, text revision. Uncertainty: I did not save a perspective; the save path is taken from the page's own strings.

**S4 — Picture, reading, picture** (formal, ethics or politics, grades 9–13, 90 min). Each student brings one photograph (own or a press photo, checked for rights) onto the table. First run: text medium, frame "ethical" ("Who is shown and who is absent, the power relations in the picture, the conditions it was made under"); second run: frame "descriptive". The two readings are compared with what the student sees. Then the ethical reading is laid into the circle as material and a new picture is made from it; the class compares what the chain kept and what it lost. Sequence: 10 min pictures; 25 min two readings; 20 min comparison; 20 min the new picture; 15 min plenary. Subject link: image and power, description and judgement, what a reading adds. Uncertainty: I ran only the default frame, on a generated picture.

**S5 — The class's own style as LoRA** (formal, art, grades 10–13, project of 3 × 90 min). The class trains two adapters on the LoRA Training page from its own drawings, one from one student's twelve sheets, one from the whole class's; both appear in Flow under "Own trainings". Day 2: the same sketch, drawn on the table, runs without adapter, with the single-hand adapter and with the class adapter, at two strengths; the class fixes criteria beforehand for "that is still ours". Day 3: the pictures with their card backs ("prompt as submitted", AI marking, the adapter's trigger) as a wall; discussion of whose work the pictures are. Subject link: style, authorship, what a dataset of twelve sheets can hold. Uncertainty: I trained nothing and laid no LoRA on the table.

**S6 — The chain across groups** (non-formal, youth media workshop, one day, age 14+). Four groups start with one sentence each. Every 45 minutes each group opens "All favorites", takes the newest result of the group to its left, and goes on from it in a different medium: a picture becomes a reading, the reading a sound, the sound and a picture a video, a sentence a sketch of code that is opened, changed and run again. Each group decides what it adds by hand (a sentence, a drawing, an edited interception) and what it lets a model make, and notes it on the card. The day ends with four chains of five or six cards each, read from the card backs. Subject link: collaboration, medium change, what passes from one medium to the next. Uncertainty: I did not run sound, video, code and favorites across accounts; the chain is built from the page's own media list and the favorites bar.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S6)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Create 2 Basic — "Learners use AI to generate an image, story or model to represent an idea." S1, S2, S4, S6.
- Create 2 Intermediate — "Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs." S1 (interceptions, models, sound, video, merging), S2 (five perspectives, picture and sound from one prompt), S6 (five media).
- Create 2 Advanced — "Learners select and integrate outputs from multiple AI systems to develop, refine or present a final product." S1 and S2 week 3: a picture and a sound from the same prompt joined into a video, several pictures merged into one; S2 week 6 and S6: the exhibition and the chain presented from the card backs.
- Create 1 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI-generated suggestions to their own ideas during a brainstorming process." S2 week 1: the own theme sentence stands first, the five interception cards come second, and in each card what the perspective put in is underlined against the sentence.
- Create 1 Advanced — "Learners purposefully integrate AI-generated outputs with their own ideas to develop comprehensive solutions and creative approaches." S1: crafting and combining the results; S3: the own perspective revised against what the model made of it; S6: what each group adds by hand.
- Create 3 Intermediate — "Learners refine their work through iterative exchanges with AI, comparing those outputs to their own ideas to determine what serves their goals." S1 (prompt changed, results changed again), S2 week 1 (hand edit of the interception), S3 (two revisions of the own perspective).
- Create 3 Advanced — "Learners critically evaluate how AI-generated feedback shapes their own ideas, then reflect on how they would like to use AI in their creative process." S2: in week 1 each interception card is annotated for what the perspective put in and what was the student's own; in week 6 the class decides from the card backs what goes on the wall and how it would go on working with the perspectives; S4: the two readings of the own photograph against what the student sees, and the decision what to make from the reading.
- Create 4 Intermediate — "Learners consider when attribution, permission or avoidance of AI is appropriate for a creative task and apply these choices in their own work." S2 week 6, S5 and S6: the card back with "prompt as submitted" and the AI marking is the label; S5 asks whose work the pictures are.
- Engage 3 Advanced — "Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them." S1 and S2 week 6: the arrangement of the results on the table, with the discarded ones at the edge, is that decision, made and walked through.
- Manage 3 Advanced — "Learners deliberately assign tasks within a multi-step process based on appropriate human strengths and relevant AI capabilities." S6: each group decides per step what it adds by hand and what a model makes, and notes it on the card; S2: the same decision week by week.
- Manage 4 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves." S1 (the re-arrangement by own criteria), S2 week 1 (hand edit), S5 (criteria for "that is still ours", then strength and adapter changed).
- Shape 3 Advanced — "Learners evaluate how specific properties of a dataset (e.g. size, features, biases) affect the performance and impact of an AI model." S5: twelve sheets of one hand against the whole class's drawings, compared on the same sketch.
- Shape 2 Basic — "Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task." S5: the criteria for "that is still ours" are fixed before the adapters run, and the pictures at two strengths are judged by them.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**


**Beyond the framework**: the framework's example for Create 2 Advanced has learners join a text generator's outline, an image generator's picture and a coding assistant's code into one prototype. S1 and S2 do that with a picture and a sound joined into a video and with several pictures merged into one, and then go on to what no classroom example of the framework asks for: the results are arranged on the table by interception bubble, and the arrangement is read as the group's judgement of its own series. The framework has no learner expectation for judging a series of one's own work; Engage 3 Advanced (accept, revise or reject) is the nearest, and S1 and S2 go past it.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 1, 2, Shape 1, 4 — the scenarios make and judge; nobody in them describes how the models work and no bias is measured. Those are the side trips to the instruments of reports 05–33.
