scenarios.title: One theme, six weeks: the table as the studio
scenarios.setting: formal, art, grades 8–12, 6 × 90 min
scenarios.text: Flow is the working surface of the whole unit; the board is kept only for the browser session, so what is to come back next week is added to the favorites from its card and dragged onto the board again from "My favorites". Week 1: one theme sentence per student, run without perspective, then under five perspectives (Critique of Consumption, On the Contrary!, Sweetener, De-Kitsch, Against the Model); before each picture the Prompt Interception card is read and what the perspective put in is underlined; one card is edited by hand and run again. Week 2: an own perspective under "Your Call!", saved, run against a platform perspective; 30 min side trip to the Prompt Interception Lab (Language Model Comparison, Interception Scope) to see the same interception across models. Week 3: from the best prompt a picture and a sound, then a video from the two; three students' pictures merged into one. Week 4: own photographs and drawings as material: read through the ethical and the descriptive frame, a sketch turned into any medium, a picture changed with a text ("Qwen Edit"). Week 5: an adapter trained from the class's drawings on the LoRA Training page, laid on the table under "Own trainings". Week 6: the table arranged by interception bubble for the class's own judgement; the exhibition is built from the card backs ("prompt as submitted", AI marking); the favorites are the archive of the unit.
scenarios.subject_link: artistic process over time, series, medium change, judging one's own work; the side trip links the perspective to the instruments that show what it does.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not run sound, video, merging, own perspective, LoRA and the favorites across sessions.

scenarios.title: Our own perspective
scenarios.setting: formal, language teaching, grades 9–12, 2 × 90 min
scenarios.text: Groups write a perspective under "Your Call!": a text that says what should shape, alter or question an idea, in the group's own words (a stance, a genre, a way of seeing), name it and save it. Each group runs three materials (a sentence, a photograph, a short poem) through its perspective and through one platform perspective of the same category, reads the two interception cards for each, and revises its own wording twice. Day 2: groups exchange perspectives through the saved list and write a short review of what another group's perspective does to a text.
scenarios.subject_link: writing an instruction, register and stance, text revision.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not save a perspective; the save path is taken from the page's own strings.

scenarios.title: Picture, reading, picture
scenarios.setting: formal, ethics or politics, grades 9–13, 90 min
scenarios.text: Each student brings one photograph (own or a press photo, checked for rights) onto the table. First run: text medium, frame "ethical" ("Who is shown and who is absent, the power relations in the picture, the conditions it was made under"); second run: frame "descriptive". The two readings are compared with what the student sees. Then the ethical reading is laid into the circle as material and a new picture is made from it; the class compares what the chain kept and what it lost.
scenarios.sequence: 10 min pictures; 25 min two readings; 20 min comparison; 20 min the new picture; 15 min plenary.
scenarios.subject_link: image and power, description and judgement, what a reading adds.
scenarios.uncertainty: I ran only the default frame, on a generated picture.

scenarios.title: The class's own style as LoRA
scenarios.setting: formal, art, grades 10–13, project of 3 × 90 min
scenarios.text: The class trains two adapters on the LoRA Training page from its own drawings, one from one student's twelve sheets, one from the whole class's; both appear in Flow under "Own trainings". Day 2: the same sketch, drawn on the table, runs without adapter, with the single-hand adapter and with the class adapter, at two strengths; the class fixes criteria beforehand for "that is still ours". Day 3: the pictures with their card backs ("prompt as submitted", AI marking, the adapter's trigger) as a wall; discussion of whose work the pictures are.
scenarios.subject_link: style, authorship, what a dataset of twelve sheets can hold.
scenarios.uncertainty: I trained nothing and laid no LoRA on the table.

scenarios.title: The chain across groups
scenarios.setting: non-formal, youth media workshop, one day, age 14+
scenarios.text: Four groups start with one sentence each. Every 45 minutes each group opens "All favorites", takes the newest result of the group to its left, and goes on from it in a different medium: a picture becomes a reading, the reading a sound, the sound and a picture a video, a sentence a sketch of code that is opened, changed and run again. Each group decides what it adds by hand (a sentence, a drawing, an edited interception) and what it lets a model make, and notes it on the card. The day ends with four chains of five or six cards each, read from the card backs.
scenarios.subject_link: collaboration, medium change, what passes from one medium to the next.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not run sound, video, code and favorites across accounts; the chain is built from the page's own media list and the favorites bar.

a.expectation: Learners use AI to generate an image, story or model to represent an idea.
Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs.
a.text: S1 (interceptions, models, sound, video, merging), S2 (five perspectives, picture and sound from one prompt), S6 (five media).

a.expectation: Learners select and integrate outputs from multiple AI systems to develop, refine or present a final product.
a.text: S1 and S2 week 3: a picture and a sound from the same prompt joined into a video, several pictures merged into one; S2 week 6 and S6: the exhibition and the chain presented from the card backs.

a.expectation: Learners compare AI-generated suggestions to their own ideas during a brainstorming process.
a.text: S2 week 1: the own theme sentence stands first, the five interception cards come second, and in each card what the perspective put in is underlined against the sentence.

a.expectation: Learners purposefully integrate AI-generated outputs with their own ideas to develop comprehensive solutions and creative approaches.
a.text: S1: crafting and combining the results; S3: the own perspective revised against what the model made of it; S6: what each group adds by hand.

a.expectation: Learners refine their work through iterative exchanges with AI, comparing those outputs to their own ideas to determine what serves their goals.
a.text: S1 (prompt changed, results changed again), S2 week 1 (hand edit of the interception), S3 (two revisions of the own perspective).

a.expectation: Learners critically evaluate how AI-generated feedback shapes their own ideas, then reflect on how they would like to use AI in their creative process.
a.text: S2: in week 1 each interception card is annotated for what the perspective put in and what was the student's own; in week 6 the class decides from the card backs what goes on the wall and how it would go on working with the perspectives; S4: the two readings of the own photograph against what the student sees, and the decision what to make from the reading.

a.expectation: Learners consider when attribution, permission or avoidance of AI is appropriate for a creative task and apply these choices in their own work.
a.text: S2 week 6, S5 and S6: the card back with "prompt as submitted" and the AI marking is the label; S5 asks whose work the pictures are.

a.expectation: Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them.
a.text: S1 and S2 week 6: the arrangement of the results on the table, with the discarded ones at the edge, is that decision, made and walked through.

a.expectation: Learners deliberately assign tasks within a multi-step process based on appropriate human strengths and relevant AI capabilities.
a.text: S6: each group decides per step what it adds by hand and what a model makes, and notes it on the card; S2: the same decision week by week.

a.expectation: Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves.
a.text: S1 (the re-arrangement by own criteria), S2 week 1 (hand edit), S5 (criteria for "that is still ours", then strength and adapter changed).

a.expectation: Learners evaluate how specific properties of a dataset (e.g. size, features, biases) affect the performance and impact of an AI model.
a.text: S5: twelve sheets of one hand against the whole class's drawings, compared on the same sketch.

a.expectation: Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task.
a.text: S5: the criteria for "that is still ours" are fixed before the adapters run, and the pictures at two strengths are judged by them.

mapping.beyond: the framework's example for Create 2 Advanced has learners join a text generator's outline, an image generator's picture and a coding assistant's code into one prototype. S1 and S2 do that with a picture and a sound joined into a video and with several pictures merged into one, and then go on to what no classroom example of the framework asks for: the results are arranged on the table by interception bubble, and the arrangement is read as the group's judgement of its own series. The framework has no learner expectation for judging a series of one's own work; Engage 3 Advanced (accept, revise or reject) is the nearest, and S1 and S2 go past it.
mapping.non_fits: Engage 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 1, 2, Shape 1, 4 — the scenarios make and judge; nobody in them describes how the models work and no bias is measured. Those are the side trips to the instruments of reports 05–33.

instruments.name: Together

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/together`. A dark, empty board with a mask icon (top right), a green plus (bottom left, "Bring something in"), a gear ("Surface settings"), zoom buttons (+ / − / 1:1) and three small mode buttons at the right edge: "Voice only" (preselected), "Voice and writing", "Writing only". On arrival the Help panel opened by itself with the page's own text: "This page is for planning and shaping artistic and/or AI-related learning with this platform: the planning with educators, the workshop itself, and the review afterwards of what was done and how the AI behaved. What this platform has been given about itself, about generative AI and about artistic-pedagogical approaches can be looked up here." and "Two things can be learned here: to plan and shape art-pedagogical processes with generative AI, and to watch and judge how an AI tries to carry out human artistic and pedagogical aims — can it contribute without putting itself at the centre, and can it stay silent when that is called for?" I overlooked it on first use. The writing line (a textarea in the middle of the board) is invisible until something is typed.
2. Switched to "Voice and writing" (so that answers are both spoken and written).
3. Typed a greeting: "Hello! We are a group of eight teenagers in a Saturday media workshop. Could you propose something we could do together today?" and pressed Enter. An answer appeared, right-aligned in blue, and the mask icon showed sound waves: "What each of you brings matters more than anything this platform could add, and nothing about your work today is known here yet: no project has been noted for your group." Under it a yellow "lift out" button and a speaker icon.
4. Replied once: "We have not decided on anything yet. We have phones with cameras, and most of us like music and drawing. What could a two-hour session look like?" Then the previous exchange was gone from the middle of the board, the new one stood there, and two cards appeared top left without my doing: a plan card titled "Drawing, humming, and what the machine makes of it" with buttons "Copy plan", "lift out", "×", and a small NOTE card containing the text "canvas_solution". The spoken sentence read: "Since you have phones, like music and like drawing, here is a session where the same material goes from paper to sound and back."
5. Green plus → three buttons "Upload / Camera / Text". Uploaded a 640×480 PNG line drawing (a staircase, a circle, the caption "stairs at 7 am"). A 62 px thumbnail appeared next to the writing line. Typed "I just put one of our drawings on the board. What do you make of it?" and pressed Enter. The mask went to "listening"; then: "Two looks at the drawing found the same things. There's a staircase of five steps rising from bottom left to top right, ending in a short line that bends up slightly. To the right of the top step is a circle with one curved line inside it. Along the bottom runs a horizontal line, and under it are the words "stairs at 7 am". Nothing else is on the page: no person, no motion lines, no lines coming out of anything, no shading."
6. Pressed "Copy plan" on the plan card. The button label changed to "Copied"; the plan landed in the clipboard as plain text ("Drawing, humming, and what the machine makes of it / Zweck: A two-hour session … / 1. Draw a sound (20 min) — …"). Nothing new appeared on the board.
7. Voice output: in "Voice and writing" mode every answer is spoken automatically (the speaker icon is in a "sounding" state while it plays, the mask shows waves). Clicking the speaker during playback stopped it; clicking again ("Hear this again") replayed it. The server log shows each answer synthesised in sentence-sized pieces by the local speech system (config `supertonic_standard`, ≈0.2 s per sentence); the browser requested `/api/speech` five times for the last answer.

Runs: 3 chat turns, 1 upload, 2 image looks (server-side), ~8 speech syntheses.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Mode buttons (right edge): Voice only / Voice and writing / Writing only. "Voice only" is the default; on a machine without microphone or in a quiet room there is no visible way in except switching to writing.
- Writing line: appears where you type, Enter sends. The previous exchange disappears when the next one starts; the "lift out" button presumably moves an utterance onto the board as a card (not tested on an answer; the plan card is the lifted-out form).
- Green plus: Upload / Camera / Text. The uploaded picture is attached to the next message as a thumbnail; it does not become a board card.
- Plan card: "Copy plan" copies the plan as text to the clipboard (label → "Copied"), "lift out" and "×" (discard memo). The NOTE card "canvas_solution" has only "×".
- Speaker icon next to each answer: stop / "Hear this again".
- Mask icon top right: idle / listening / uttering states (waves while speaking).
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again. Surface settings gear, Favorites bar at the bottom (Mine / All): not used.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- The first answer did not propose anything; it said that nothing is known about the group yet. A newcomer would read this as a refusal or as a system with no idea.
- The second answer produced a complete two-hour plan on the board: six steps with minutes (Draw a sound 20 / The machine looks 20 / Hum the place 25 / Read the steps 20 / Your own version 25 / Listen and show 10), each pointing to a surface of this platform by name (Compare and Analyse → Image Understanding; Re-enactment; Flow with the song model). The plan is usable as written; the steps add up to 120 minutes. The clipboard copy carries a German label "Zweck:" in an otherwise English text.
- The picture reading is accurate and literal (five steps, circle with a curved line, the caption). It names what is absent (no person, no shading). The server log shows two consecutive local vision jobs (qwen3-vl:4b over ComfyUI) because the chat model (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 via openrouter) is not handed uploaded pictures and asks a local model to look twice.
- The NOTE card "canvas_solution" is an internal name that leaked onto the board; nothing on the surface says what it is.
- Speech: generated locally, split per sentence, voices "even" and "clear" in the log. I could not hear it.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The Help text that opens on arrival says what the page is for (planning with educators, the workshop, the review afterwards) and what is learned; it says nothing about how to begin: not that the writing line is invisible until typed into, not what to write first. I overlooked the panel myself on first use and looked for a cue on the empty board.
- The three phases the Help text names (planning with educators, the workshop itself, the review afterwards) are not set apart as modes on the surface.
- The first answer ("nothing about your work today is known here yet") reads as a non-answer; the plan only came after a second message with concrete material (phones, music, drawing).
- After an uploaded picture, only the mask in "listening" state and no progress indication.
- Two cards appear top left without being announced; the NOTE "canvas_solution" is meaningless to a user.
- "Copy plan" copies to the clipboard; nothing on the surface says where the plan went.
- Previous exchanges vanish from the middle; where they go (if anywhere) is not shown.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it names the three phases (planning with educators, the workshop itself, the review afterwards) and the two things to be learned. It should set those three phases apart as the three main ways of using this surface and say for each what to write first. It should add the handling: the voice switch in the main menu decides whether answers are spoken as well as written, and a quiet room needs it switched off; a plan comes as a card on the board and "Copy plan" puts its text into the clipboard; a picture uploaded with the green plus is attached to the next message and read by a local model on this server, with no visible progress; the speaker icon stops and replays an answer, "lift out" keeps an utterance on the board.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Open a workshop by telling the companion what the room has (devices, time, interests) and let it draft a session plan onto the board; edit the plan, not the prompt.
- Use the plan card as the group's agenda: copy it into the shared document, then follow its pointers to the named surfaces.
- Show a drawing or photo and ask what the machine sees; compare the literal reading with what the drawer meant.
- Let the companion speak an answer aloud for the room while the written version stays on the board.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Planning with the companion** (non-formal, open youth centre, 2 h, age 12–16, one facilitator). The group tells the companion what it has (phones, instruments, time), takes the plan card as its agenda and runs it. Sequence: 10 min typing the situation in and reading the plan aloud (voice); 90 min following the steps on the named surfaces; 20 min back on Together to report what happened, one sentence per person. Subject link: media education, self-organisation. Uncertainty: the first answer may be a non-answer; the facilitator needs to know that concrete material (what the group has) triggers the plan.

**S2 — What the machine saw** (formal, art, grades 5–7, one lesson of 45 min). Each pair draws a place (a room, a street, a playground), photographs the drawing with the class tablet, uploads the photo with the green plus and asks what the machine sees in it. Sequence: 10 min drawing; 5 min upload and question; 15 min run (used for a second drawing); 15 min reading the answer against the drawing, marking what was seen, what was missed, what was invented. Subject link: picture description, looking and naming.

**S3 — Teacher's planning desk** (formal, teacher training, 60 min). Teachers in training use Together as a planning partner: they describe a class, a subject and a time frame, receive a plan, copy it out, and then critique it against their curriculum — which steps are realistic, which pointers to platform surfaces they have tried themselves. Subject link: lesson planning, didactic judgement. Sequence: 15 min dialogue; 15 min copy and annotate; 30 min comparison in plenary.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 3 Basic — "Learners understand why AI-generated outputs should be verified and recognise how they can verify the content themselves." S2: the reading is checked line by line against the drawing.
- Manage 3 Intermediate — "Learners break a problem into component parts and consider ways AI might help with specific steps." S3: the plan is a decomposition of a session into steps, each assessed for whether the platform helps.
- Manage 4 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves." S3: the plan is compared with the curriculum and the teacher’s own experience of the named surfaces, and the steps that do not hold are replaced by the teacher; S1 closing round: what the group did against what the plan said.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Manage 1 Basic — "Learners identify a variety of AI systems and the tasks they are designed to support." Modification: the systems identified are the platform’s own surfaces, which the plan card names with what each is for; the learners meet them by following the plan (S1), not by surveying them.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 2, Shape 1–4, Create 1–4 — the scenarios do not produce media, analyse bias or datasets, describe how the models work, or evaluate a system against criteria.

instruments.name: Contesting

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/contesting`. Same empty board as Together: mask icon top right, a gear bottom left, Help top right, Favorites bar at the bottom, an invisible writing line in the middle. No mode buttons this time, no green plus. On arrival the Help panel opened by itself with the page's own text: "If we want to be creative, or to get something right, we need imagination, because without an idea nothing happens. But working artistically means working further on our own idea and developing it. An AI must not take our imagination away, but it can help us develop our ideas further. This page puts up resistance to your ideas. It challenges you to understand your own ideas better, and it can also support you in that. -- But you have to convince it - that is not easy!" and "Two things can be learned here: to put an idea into words, sharpen it and give reasons for what you want to achieve and why, and to see how a chatbot reacts if it is not told to be pleasing and charming." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Typed the claim "AI images are art." and pressed Enter. The answer began, spoken and written sentence by sentence; what I saw on the surface first was "Hello. What answers here is a machine, more precisely several machines working together, and none of them takes orders." and, when the speech ended, only the last sentence remained in the middle: "Name one AI image that actually stopped you, and say what it did that the others did not." The server log shows the full answer had 704 characters; the surface kept only the last sentence after the speech ended.
3. Answered that last sentence once: "One of the harbour pictures we made in Flow today: the film looked boiled, magenta and teal, and I kept looking at the blistered edges rather than the harbour." The reply appeared in pieces: "That is a precise observation. The harbour was what was asked for, the boiled film was what nobody asked for, and your eyes stayed with the part nobody asked for. Bill Morrison made a whole film, Decasia, from old reels that were rotting in archives." → "The decay is the subject: faces and buildings dissolve into blisters and stains, and the damage carries more than the picture underneath." → "So the question comes back sharper. If nobody chose the blistering and it simply happened, then what made it worth looking at was your noticing, not the making." → and finally, the only sentence that stayed: "This platform will test that by reversing the order: the damage becomes the subject, and the harbour is only a ghost behind it. The reason: you named something exact, the edges instead of the harbour, and that is a decision worth materializing."
4. At the same moment a box appeared top left: "Wan 2.2 T2V 14B Fast · 0 %". The machine had started a video generation on its own. The server log shows the prompt it wrote: "Extreme close-up of decaying 16mm film emulsion, blistering and bubblin…", config `wan22_t2v_video_fast`, 16 fps. The box showed a progressive preview and the percentage (62, 84, 88, done): a 10-second video. Content: a magenta-teal film strip with sprocket holes, bubbles and emulsion blisters drifting over a faint harbour skyline.
5. "Use a suggested prompt after its reply": nothing on the surface offered a prompt — no chips, no placeholder in the writing line, no element named suggestion. The generated video's own prompt is not shown on the box either (the box has ×, Add to favorites, Download and two unlabelled buttons on hover; a provenance toggle exists in the DOM but is not visible). I could not carry this step out.
6. Moved the box: dragged it by its dotted header from the top-left corner to the middle of the page (from 20,89 to 420,463 px). It followed the pointer and stayed where I dropped it, overlapping the conversation.

Runs: 2 chat turns, 1 video generation started by the machine, ~10 speech syntheses.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Writing line: Enter sends. The answer is spoken (local speech system) and written in sync, one or two sentences at a time; after the speech ends only the last sentence remains visible. Earlier exchanges disappear.
- Speaker icon under the answer: "Stop" while sounding, "Read this out" afterwards.
- Generated box: appears without being asked when the machine decides to "materialize"; shows model name and percentage, then the media with a player; draggable by its header; × removes it; on hover: Add to favorites, Download (and, while the box was still at 0 %, the DOM also listed Forward to Flow, Print and Image Analysis).
- Gear bottom left: Surface settings (not opened). Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- The contesting is real: the first answer did not agree or disagree with "AI images are art" but demanded a concrete case, which is what the Help text announces ("This page puts up resistance to your ideas … you have to convince it"). The second answer took my case, named a reference (Bill Morrison's "Decasia"), turned the claim around ("what made it worth looking at was your noticing, not the making") and then acted: it generated a video in which the damage is the subject and the harbour a ghost. The video matches that description.
- The written trace of the argument is lost on the surface: after each turn only the final sentence stays, so the Morrison reference and the turning of the argument exist only in speech and in the server log. A user who missed the spoken sentences cannot re-read them.
- The video generation ran without a question and without naming its cost (a 14-billion-parameter video model); the only announcement was the box.
- Model behind the voice: anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 via openrouter (server log); the speech: local Supertonic; the video: local Wan 2.2 on ComfyUI.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The Help text that opens on arrival says what the page does (it puts up resistance to your ideas, you have to convince it) and what is learned; it says nothing about where to write, that the writing line is invisible until typed into, or that the answer vanishes sentence by sentence. I overlooked the panel myself on first use.
- The answer vanishes sentence by sentence. Anyone who reads slower than the voice speaks loses the argument; there is no transcript.
- A video starts by itself at the machine's decision. Nothing says why, how long, or that it can be stopped (× removes the box; whether it stops the job is not shown).
- The generated box does not show the prompt that produced it; the "reason" is only in the spoken sentence.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Put a strong claim in and defend it against the machine's counter-questions for three turns; note which of your own words it picks up.
- Give it a concrete case from the group's work and see whether it answers with media; discuss what in its answer was argument and what was display.
- Use the generated box as a counter-example on the board: drag it next to the group's own picture.
- Replay the spoken answer for the room and write the argument down yourselves, since the page does not keep it.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Claim and counter** (formal, ethics or language/literature lessons, grades 9–11, 45 min). Pairs write one claim about AI and art, send it, and write down the counter-question they get. Then they answer it once and record what the machine did (argued, referenced, generated). Sequence: 5 min claims; 15 min two turns per pair, writing the sentences down as they are spoken; 15 min pairs exchange their transcripts; 10 min plenary: which counter-questions were fair, which evasive. Subject link: argumentation, position and counter-position. Uncertainty: only one pair can speak at a time in a room; written mode is not offered on this surface, so the class needs headphones or sequential use.

**S2 — When the machine answers with a picture** (non-formal, art workshop, 3 h, age 15+). Participants bring one image they made and describe to the machine what they kept looking at. If the machine generates in return, the group compares its generation with the original and asks what was "reversed". Sequence: 20 min intro; 90 min turns; 50 min wall of originals and answers; 20 min discussion of who decided what. Subject link: authorship, reception aesthetics.

**S3 — The lost transcript** (formal, media studies, grades 11–13, 90 min). The class records a conversation with the contesting machine (audio recording of the room), then reconstructs the written argument from the recording and compares it with what the page kept. Sequence: 20 min conversation; 40 min transcription in groups; 30 min comparison and discussion of what a surface that keeps only the last sentence does to an argument. Of course, the agent can always be asked for the course of the conversation. Subject link: oral vs. written argument, interface design.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 7 Intermediate — "Learners identify when AI use may have unintended impacts or implications that are different from a user’s immediate goals." S2: the machine generates a picture nobody asked for, and the group asks what was “reversed”; S3: the surface keeps only the last sentence, and the class examines what that does to an argument it did not intend to lose.
- Create 1 Basic — "Learners explore how different AI tools can expand their thinking or spark new ideas." 
- Create 1 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI-generated suggestions to their own ideas during a brainstorming process." S2: the machine’s generation is set against the participant’s own picture.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Shape 1 Intermediate — "Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool." Modification: the purpose is read from the Help text’s own words (the page puts up resistance to your ideas); the constraints (the surface keeps only the last sentence and generates without asking) are found by use, and intended users are named nowhere. Ex negativo, because barely any agent will act like "contesting", the medial structure of typical AI frameworks and model strategies become visible/perceivable. Justification: S3 is about that design.
- Create 4 Intermediate — "Learners consider when attribution, permission or avoidance of AI is appropriate for a creative task and apply these choices in their own work." Modification: the media was generated without a request; the question becomes whether an unrequested generation can be used in the group’s work, and the choice is applied to the wall in S2. OR a generation is deliberately denied by the agent, posing the question of one would not better make this artwork by oneself without genAI.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, Manage 1–4, Shape 2–4, Create 2, 3 — no datasets, no bias comparison, no task decomposition and no checking against a source in these scenarios.

instruments.name: Canvas

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/canvas`. Left: a MODULES palette in four numbered groups (1 · INPUT: Input Prompt, Image Input, Random Prompt; 2 · INTERCEPTION: Interception, Evaluation, Image Analysis, Comparison; 3 · ADAPTION: Translation, Model Adaption; 4 · GENERATION: Generation; TOOLS: Seed, Resolution, Quality, Preview) with "Click or drag modules onto the canvas". Top bar: sidebar toggle, Outputs toggle, a play triangle ("Execute"), "Batch", a Name field, New Workflow, Import, Export, Add to favorites. The canvas already holds two nodes: INPUT PROMPT (with a textarea "Your prompt…") and MEDIA OUTPUT ("Waiting for execution…"), each with a round port. Bottom: zoom −/100 %/+/fit, and an OUTPUTS strip. The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "This is, first, about handling AI building blocks as freely as possible: not about the software foundations, but about what the blocks carry out and how they connect into architectures of your own. And second, that work here does not run in one direction from prompt to result — queries, branches and loops are possible: a self-critical apparatus by your criteria." "Two things can be learned here: to compose complex generative sequences across different media, and to develop artistic setups for exploring generative AI freely. And that AI can be built otherwise than as a straight line from input to output, and that different models can work not only with and after one another but also against one another." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Smallest graph: typed "a small harbor at dusk" into INPUT PROMPT, dragged from its right port to the left port of MEDIA OUTPUT (a blue line appeared), pressed Execute. The run finished in under a second: MEDIA OUTPUT showed "1 item", the OUTPUTS panel slid up over two thirds of the canvas and listed one card "input · input_1793646821289_acyqazj" containing the text "a small harbor at dusk". No media. On disk the run folder holds `01_input.txt` and a `workflow.json` with the two nodes. So the smallest graph "works" in the sense that it runs; it produces the prompt back.
3. Clicked "Generation" in the palette. A node GENERATION appeared on the canvas and, at once, a modal "Select Output Model" with 49 entries, each with a one-line description: Attention Cartography (and a "(Diffusers)" twin), CommonCanvas XL C (twin), Composable Diffusion (twin), Concept Algebra (twin), Denoising Archaeology (three), Dimension Explorer (twin), Flux 2 Dev (twice), Flux 2 Visual Conditioning, Flux 3 Klein, FLUX.2 [dev] img2img, Gemini 3 Pro Image (€), Gemini Nano Banana 2.1 (€), GPT-Image-1, Hallucination (three), Qwen 2511 Multi-Image Fusion, Qwen Image Edit Lightning, SD 3.5 Large Image-to-Image (twice), Stable Diffusion 1.5, Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large (twice), Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo (twice), Stable Diffusion XL, LTX Video, Wan 2.2 Image-to-Video (14B), Wan 2.2 T2V 14B Fast, eSpeak NG Voice, HeartMuLa Music, Piper Voice, SA3 Music, SA3 SFX, Stable Audio 3, Supertonic Voice, VoxCPM2 Voice, "view_in_ar Image to 3D (Hunyuan3D-2)", "🎨 P5.js Code Generation", "🎵 Tone.js Music Generation". Chose "Flux 3 Klein". The node now shows a dropdown "Flux 3 Klein ▼", three input ports (1, 2, P) and one output port.
4. Wiring: the new node had been placed on top of the direct line between the two existing nodes; a drag from the input's port onto the node's port 1 did nothing until I moved the node down. Then: input → generation port 1, generation output → MEDIA OUTPUT. The direct line was removed by clicking it and pressing Delete.
5. Execute. OUTPUTS strip: "Executing Workflow… / Generating Media / 1 / 3 nodes". A picture of a marina at dusk (sailing boats, pink sky) appeared in the OUTPUTS panel as "generation · generation_…". Server log: config `flux3`.
6. Changed one module: opened the dropdown on the GENERATION node (the same modal), chose "Stable Diffusion 3.5 Large Turbo", Execute again. A different harbour: a dark wooden boat in the foreground, a village with lights, painterly.
7. "Read what the nodes report": during the run the strip shows the phase ("Generating Media") and a node counter; after the run MEDIA OUTPUT carries a badge "1 item" and the browser console reports each node ("Node complete: generation… (2/3)"), but on the canvas itself the nodes show no text about what they did: no seed, no model, no time. Short bubbles flash over the nodes at completion ("Showing bubble for" in the console) and are gone within a second. The export folder on the server has the real report: `events.jsonl`, `status.json` with start and end time, `metadata.json` with the entity list, and the files `01_input.txt`, `02_generation.png`.

Runs: 3 (one text-only, two image generations).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Palette buttons: a click adds a node at a fixed spot (overlapping what is there); drag is also offered.
- Ports: drag from an output port to an input port makes a connection; dropping onto a node that lies over an existing line fails silently.
- Click on a line + Delete removes it. × on a node header removes the node.
- Generation node: dropdown opens the model modal; ports 1, 2, P (P presumably "prompt"; nothing says what 1 and 2 take).
- Execute: runs the whole graph; the OUTPUTS panel opens over the canvas and must be closed with the Outputs toggle to see the nodes again.
- Batch, Name, New Workflow, Import, Export, Add to favorites, Seed/Resolution/Quality/Preview tools: not used.
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.
- Not used either, and named here because the Help text's "queries, branches and loops" run through them: the palette's Evaluation ("LLM-based evaluation with 3-way branching (pass/fail/commentary)", with a criteria field, a "Pass (forward)" output and a "Feedback (backward)" output), Image Analysis ("Vision-LLM analysis of images"), Comparison ("Compare multiple text inputs with LLM analysis", with a criteria field of its own), and the "Feedback Input" (FB) that Interception and Translation nodes carry, into which an Evaluation's feedback is wired so that a run loops. The use script asked for the smallest graph and one module change; I built no loop, and the labels in this bullet are the build's own strings.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- A graph that runs in two clicks returns the input text as the "output". Nothing says this is not a generation.
- With a Generation node: a Flux 3 Klein marina (photographic) and an SD 3.5 Large Turbo harbour (painterly) from the same prompt.
- The model list mixes production models, research instruments ("Attention Cartography", "Denoising Archaeology"), paid cloud models (€), voices, music, 3D and code generators in one alphabetical modal, with twins that differ only in "(Diffusers)" or not at all in the label, and two entries whose label contains an icon name ("view_in_ar") or an emoji.
- The nodes report nothing readable after the run; the report is in the export folder on the server.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- "Media Output" with no generation node runs and reports "1 item"; the item is the prompt. The name promises media.
- A new node lands on top of the existing line and swallows the drag.
- The Outputs panel covers the canvas after every run.
- 49 models in one modal, several with identical labels; nothing says which are quick, which are paid, which are research-only.
- Ports named 1, 2, P without explanation.
- No progress percentage, no queue position; only "Generating Media".
- Nothing on the nodes after the run says what model, seed or time was used.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that the surface is about handling AI building blocks and connecting them into architectures of one's own, that queries, branches and loops are possible, a self-critical apparatus by one's own criteria, and what is learned, among it that models can work against one another. It should add the handling: a graph needs at least an input, a generation and the media output, connected left to right through the round ports, and without a generation node the output is the text itself; a loop is built with the Evaluation node, whose criteria are written into it, whose Pass output goes forward and whose Feedback output goes back into the FB input of an Interception or Translation node; Image Analysis reads a picture into text, and Comparison judges several texts by criteria of its own. Click a palette entry to add a node, move it clear of existing lines before wiring, and remove a line by clicking it and pressing Delete. The generation node's dropdown chooses the model; entries marked € use a paid cloud service. Execute runs the whole graph; results appear in the Outputs panel at the bottom, which the Outputs button hides again.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Build the three-node chain and swap only the model: the smallest experiment, and the entry to the rest.
- Build a loop: Input Prompt → Interception → Generation → Image Analysis → Evaluation, with a criterion written in your own words into the Evaluation node (for instance: the picture shows the named place without a postcard cliché); wire "Pass (forward)" to the Media Output and "Feedback (backward)" into the Interception node's FB input, so that a judgement of the picture rewrites the prompt and the generation runs again.
- Let two models work against one another: one model's picture is read by Image Analysis under a critical perspective, the reading is intercepted and given to a second model as its prompt; then reverse the roles.
- Put two Interception nodes with two perspectives on one prompt into a Comparison node with criteria of your own, and read what the comparing model prefers and why.
- Keep the run folders (one per run, with the prompt, every intermediate text and the picture) as the record of an experiment over several rounds.

Not tried: the loop, the Evaluation node and the Comparison node.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — A picture judged and sent back** (formal, art, grades 10–13, 2 × 90 min). Groups write a prompt about a place or a group of people and, into the Evaluation node, a criterion in their own words for what the picture must not do (the postcard, the costume, the one kind of face); they build Input Prompt → Interception → Generation → Image Analysis → Evaluation, wire Pass to the Media Output and Feedback into the Interception's FB input, run, and read the Outputs: what the reading said, what the evaluation decided and why, how the prompt was rewritten, and how the next picture differs. Then they change the criterion and run again. Sequence: 20 min the three-node chain as the entry; 30 min criterion and build; 40 min first loop and reading; 40 min second criterion; 50 min each group shows one round (prompt, reading, judgement, rewrite, picture) and says what its criterion did. Subject link: artistic research, criteria, iteration; the cliché as the object. Uncertainty: I built no loop; how many rounds a loop runs and how it stops I did not see on the surface.

**S2 — Models against one another** (formal, art or ethics, grades 11–13, 90 min). Pairs let one model generate from a prompt, read the picture with Image Analysis under a critical perspective, intercept the reading and give it to a second model as its prompt; then they reverse the roles. The two chains stand side by side on the canvas; the pairs compare what each model made of the other's picture and what the reading named that the picture did not show. Sequence: 15 min build; 30 min runs; 30 min comparison; 15 min plenary on which part of a reading was a reading and which an invention. Subject link: what one model sees in another's picture; cliché and invention. Uncertainty: I did not build the chain Image Analysis → Interception → Generation.

**S3 — A self-critical apparatus** (non-formal, art-research workshop, 2 days, age 16+). Participants design an apparatus by their own criteria: Random Prompt as the input, a loop of Interception, Generation, Image Analysis and Evaluation, criteria written for what counts and what is sent back, and several rounds; they collect every round's picture, reading and judgement from the run folders and exhibit the chain of one run as the work. Day 1: build, first runs, criteria rewritten; day 2: runs over several rounds, selection, exhibition. Subject link: artistic research, the apparatus as the work, criteria as the artistic decision. Uncertainty: the run folders lie on the server and the facilitator copies them out; I did not run the loop.

**S4 — A inquiry-based learning setup**. E.g. mass-production of different outputs using random prompt generation nodes, creating fine-tuned research data for comparative visual/auditive analyses (e.g. Artistic research; serial image analysis in the style of Mietzner/Pilarczyk; critical visual studies; digital image studies à la Lev Manovich, https://manovich.net/index.php/projects/instagram-and-contemporary-image)

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Shape 2 Basic — "Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task." S1 and S3: the criterion written into the Evaluation node in the group's own words.
- Create 3 Intermediate — "Learners refine their work through iterative exchanges with AI, comparing those outputs to their own ideas to determine what serves their goals." S1: every round of the loop is read against what the group wanted the picture not to do, and the criterion is changed on that reading.
- Manage 3 Intermediate — "Learners break a problem into component parts and consider ways AI might help with specific steps." S1 and S3: the apparatus is built from parts, one node per step, and each step is given to a model or kept.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S1: the cliché is the criterion, the reading and the judgement name it, and the groups say what the criterion did to the picture.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: one round shown as prompt, reading, judgement, rewrite, picture.
- Create 2 Intermediate — "Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs." S2: two models on each other's pictures.
- Manage 4 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves." The redirect is done by the apparatus (the Evaluation's feedback), which the learners set up; they redirect by changing the criterion (S1).
- Engage 3 Advanced — "Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them." In S1 the accept-or-revise decision is delegated to the Evaluation node; the learners justify the criterion and read the node's reasons, then discuss using their own vs. the generated assessment.
- Manage 4 Basic — "Learners recognise that they should make decisions about AI use that support accountability, learning and fairness." Canvas strongly supports the use of evaluative and critical functions.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Shape 2 Advanced — "Learners design their own evaluation criteria for an AI system, compare performance across different inputs and users and use it to propose improvements." Modification: S3 designs the criteria and compares across inputs (Random Prompt) and rounds, not across users; the improvement proposed is to the apparatus the group built, whose criteria are rewritten after the first runs. The framework's classroom example has pairs fill out model cards for each other's tool proposals and revise them; S3 revises a running apparatus instead of a proposal.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Shape 2 examples have learners define criteria and fill out model cards; in S1 and S3 the criterion is written into an Evaluation node that reads the picture's description and sends the prompt back to the Interception, so the learners build the evaluating loop themselves and read its judgements round by round. No classroom example of the framework has learners build the apparatus that evaluates a model.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1, 2, Shape 1, 3, 4, Create 1, 4.

a.expectation: Learners refine their work through iterative exchanges with AI, comparing those outputs to their own ideas to determine what serves their goals.
a.text: S1: every round of the loop is read against what the group wanted the picture not to do, and the criterion is changed on that reading.

a.expectation: Learners break a problem into component parts and consider ways AI might help with specific steps.
a.text: S1 and S3: the apparatus is built from parts, one node per step, and each step is given to a model or kept.

a.expectation: Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups.
a.text: S1: the cliché is the criterion, the reading and the judgement name it, and the groups say what the criterion did to the picture.

a.expectation: Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works.
a.text: S1: one round shown as prompt, reading, judgement, rewrite, picture.

a.expectation: Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs.
a.text: S2: two models on each other's pictures.

a.expectation: Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves.
a.text: The redirect is done by the apparatus (the Evaluation's feedback), which the learners set up; they redirect by changing the criterion (S1).

a.expectation: Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them.
a.text: In S1 the accept-or-revise decision is delegated to the Evaluation node; the learners justify the criterion and read the node's reasons, then discuss using their own vs. the generated assessment.

a.expectation: Learners recognise that they should make decisions about AI use that support accountability, learning and fairness.
a.text: Canvas strongly supports the use of evaluative and critical functions.

b.expectation: Learners design their own evaluation criteria for an AI system, compare performance across different inputs and users and use it to propose improvements.
b.text: Modification: S3 designs the criteria and compares across inputs (Random Prompt) and rounds, not across users; the improvement proposed is to the apparatus the group built, whose criteria are rewritten after the first runs. The framework's classroom example has pairs fill out model cards for each other's tool proposals and revise them; S3 revises a running apparatus instead of a proposal.
b.modification: S3 designs the criteria and compares across inputs (Random Prompt) and rounds, not across users; the improvement proposed is to the apparatus the group built, whose criteria are rewritten after the first runs. The framework's classroom example has pairs fill out model cards for each other's tool proposals and revise them; S3 revises a running apparatus instead of a proposal.

mapping.beyond: the framework's Shape 2 examples have learners define criteria and fill out model cards; in S1 and S3 the criterion is written into an Evaluation node that reads the picture's description and sends the prompt back to the Interception, so the learners build the evaluating loop themselves and read its judgements round by round. No classroom example of the framework has learners build the apparatus that evaluates a model.

instruments.name: Overview

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/overview`. Header "Overview map of the Latent Lab". Left: the Latent Lab sidebar with six groups (CULTURAL KNOWLEDGE & STEREOTYPES: Stereotype Analysis, Model Comparison, Mean Images, Language Understanding, Image Understanding, Voice Comparison; DIFFUSION LAB: Encoder Fusion, Enc. Fus. Workbench, Dimension Explorer, Concept Algebra, Denoising Archaeology, Attention Cartography, Composable Diffusion; TRANSFORMERS LAB: System Prompts, Model Comparison, Tokenizer, Bias Research 1, Bias Research 2, Representation Engineering; CROSSMODAL LAB: Latent Audio Synth, Re-enactment, MMAudio, ImageBind Guidance; PROMPT INTERCEPTION LAB: Language Model Comparison, Interception Scope, Aesthetic Poles; LORA TRAINING: LoRA Training, LoRA Explorer). Each entry carries one or two small icons (A = text, picture, note = sound). The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "On this overview page you are already looking inside AI models — diffusion and transformer architectures that produce images, sounds and texts, and ways of carrying one over into another." "Click the boxes and find out at which places this page invites you to experiment!" I overlooked it on first use.
2. The map: three columns with heading and tagline. "Diffusion — Change how images & media come about in an AI!", four boxes: Prompt (with the sentence "A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen."), Embedding Process, Denoiser and Scheduler, VAE / Variational Auto Encoder; two dashed frames label "latent space" and "conditioning". "Transformer — Find out how text AIs work and whether they pass on prejudices!", four boxes: Prompt, Tokenization and embedding, Attention, Sampling; a dashed frame "embedding space". "Crossmodal routes — Chains of several AIs", three boxes: Image to text, Image to sound, Sound to text to sound. Each box has a small animated diagram with a green dot.
3. Pressed into "Embedding Process" (Diffusion). A panel opened over the map, with "Close": the sentence on the left; three encoders CLIP-L, CLIP-G, T5 each showing the first tokens (a, house, stands, in, a, ","); on the right "one vector per token" with rows farm / l / and and five numbers each, and "one vector for the whole sentence". Two sentences: "Several small AI models (encoders) break the prompt into small pieces, so-called tokens." "Each encoder links every token to a long row of numbers (between 77 and 512 vectors with 768–4096 numbers each)." While the panel was open, the sidebar highlighted four instruments in green: Encoder Fusion, Enc. Fus. Workbench, Dimension Explorer, Concept Algebra.
4. Pressed into "Attention" (Transformer). Panel: a token row "A ␣house ␣stands … ␣surrounded … ␣far mland ." with arcs ("what stands there?", "what is surrounded?", "attention: the thicker the arc, the more important"), "field of view: up to 40,960 tokens at once", the number series of "mland" (+0.0405 +0.0002 +0.0211 +0.0171 −0.0184 −0.0068 … 2,560 numbers), "36 times, layer by layer", "the intermediate state from layer 10 on: farms"; a comparison box with two "bank" sentences (picnic on the bank of the river / the bank raises its interest rates) and their differing numbers after attention. Five sentences of explanation ending: "The intermediate state 'farms' and the 36 layers were measured on 2026-08-24. The arcs and the bank rows are exemplary." and a note: "All the numbers here are measured on one AI model: Qwen3-4B. A different model cuts differently and has different numbers." Sidebar highlight: Representation Engineering.
5. Pressed into "Image to sound" (Crossmodal). Panel: a picture icon, two arrows to two wave icons, "one AI model makes a sound from the picture", "another steers the sound while it is generated". Sidebar highlight: MMAudio, ImageBind Guidance.
6. A short click opens the same panel as a long press (tried on VAE: "a tensor of 16 matrices … The many pieces of data, e.g. about content, contrast, colours, textures, are combined into a media product humans can perceive. picture / sound / video / 3D").
7. "Note what the taglines say while you click": the three taglines under the column headings did not change at any point; they are static. Nothing else on the surface changed while pressing except the panel and the sidebar highlight.

Runs: none (no generation on this surface).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Click or press on a box: opens its detail panel over the map; "Close" or Escape closes it. The sidebar highlights the instruments that belong to the station.
- Sidebar entries: navigate to the instruments.
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again. Sidebar toggle button top left.
- The small green dots in the box diagrams animate on their own; they are not controls.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- A map that places the 29 instruments of the sidebar on a process diagram with eleven stations. The link between station and instruments is the sidebar highlight, which appears only while a panel is open and is easy to miss (the sidebar is on the far left, the panel in the middle).
- The Attention detail carries measured numbers with a date and a model name (Qwen3-4B, 2026-08-24); the Embedding detail carries numbers without a source ("0.42 −0.18 0.91 …", "between 77 and 512 vectors"); the VAE detail says "a tensor of 16 matrices" without saying for which model.
- The Diffusion tagline is an imperative with an exclamation mark; the Transformer tagline promises "whether they pass on prejudices", which only two of its six instruments (Bias Research 1 and 2) address; "Crossmodal routes — Chains of several AIs" is a noun phrase.
- The "Crossmodal routes" column has no Prompt box and no dashed frame; "Sound to text to sound" appears as a box but its panel was not opened (not in the script).

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The sidebar highlight is the only link from a station to an instrument, and it is far from the panel; a reader of the panel does not see it.
- Numbers without a source in the Embedding and VAE panels sit next to numbers with a date and model in the Attention panel.
- The sentence in the Prompt box ("A house stands in a landscape…") is used in the Diffusion panels but not in the Transformer column's own Prompt box, which is empty of text.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that the page looks inside AI models, names the diffusion and transformer architectures and the ways of carrying one over into another, and says to click the boxes. It should add: every box is a station, and its detail names the instruments that work at that station, which light up in the sidebar on the left while the detail is open. The numbers in the details are examples; where a panel names a model and a date, they were measured on that model, and where it names none, they are illustrative.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Open the three Prompt-to-output chains in order, station by station, before touching an instrument; note which sidebar entries light up and go to one of them next.
- Use the Attention panel's "bank" example as the entry to Representation Engineering or the Tokenizer.
- Use the Embedding panel's three encoders as the entry to Encoder Fusion.
- Print the map (screenshot) as the room's poster; it names every instrument's place.
- Take one station's panel as the blueprint for an artwork about that element: the token row with its arcs and the 2,560 numbers of one token (Attention), the three encoders and their rows of numbers (Embedding Process), the 16 matrices that become a picture, sound, video or 3D (VAE); the instruments that light up in the sidebar are where the material for the work is made.
- Mark the dashed frames "latent space" and "embedding space" as the station for a work on high-dimensional (non-)images: what the panels show as rows of numbers before anything can be seen or heard.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Reading the map first** (formal, computer science, grades 9–11, 45 min). The class opens the overview on the board; the teacher clicks the four Diffusion stations one after the other and the class writes one sentence per station in their own words. Then pairs open one Transformer station each and present it. Sequence: 15 min Diffusion column together; 15 min pairs on Transformer stations; 15 min presentations and the question which instrument they want to use next week. Subject link: representation of data, models.

**S2 — Which instrument for which question?** (non-formal, teacher workshop, 90 min). Teachers formulate a question they have about AI ("where does the prejudice get in?", "why does a model misspell a word in the picture?"), find the station on the map, open it, and note the highlighted instruments. Sequence: 20 min questions on cards; 40 min map work in pairs; 30 min each pair names the instrument they will try and why. Subject link: lesson planning.

**S3 — From flow-map to art** (formal/non-formal, project week day 1, grades 10–13). The map is used as an inspirational blueprint/orientation for artworks that inform and discuss structural elements of genAI technologies (e.g. tokienizer, embedding, denoising, or the nature of latent spaces and high-dimensional (non-) images. Groups mark the station they will work at for the week and open its panel. Subject link: artistic research/artistic exploration.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: one sentence per station in their own words. S3: each artwork informs about one structural element (tokenizer, embedding, denoising, latent space), and the station's panel is what the work's statement about that element is read against.
- Manage 1 Basic — "Learners identify a variety of AI systems and the tasks they are designed to support." S2: the teachers find the station for their question and note which instruments light up for it; S1: the sidebar’s six groups with their instruments. S3: the station a group marks names the instruments it will work with for the week.
- Shape 1 Basic — "Learners identify what different AI systems are designed to do." S1 and S2: each station’s panel says what the instruments at that station do, and the learners note which instrument is for which station. S3: the groups choose their station by what its instruments do.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Create 1 Basic — "Learners explore how different AI tools can expand their thinking or spark new ideas." Modification: in S3 the spark comes from the map's drawing of the models' insides (the panels' diagrams and numbers), not from using the tools; the tools follow during the week.
- Engage 2 Advanced — "Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding." Modification: in S3 the artworks inform and discuss a structural element in the means of art, not in language; that the means shape the understanding of the element is what the discussion of the works is about.
- Shape 1 Intermediate — "Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool." Modification: the panel a group opens in S3 describes a station of the model and its constraints (77–512 vectors, a field of view of 40,960 tokens, 16 matrices), not a tool with intended users.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's knowledge statement 1.1 has AI systems "combine step-by-step procedures with statistical inferences (e.g. weights and biases)"; the map's panels show the parts those words stand for (the token rows, the three encoders, the 16 matrices of the latent), and S3's artworks take one of these parts as their subject. The framework has no expectation that reaches the parts.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 2, 3, 4, Shape 2, 3, 4, Create 2, 3, 4 — the map generates nothing and decides nothing; the artworks of S3 are made at the instruments, which the other reports map.
