instruments.name: Model Comparison

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/model-comparison`. Left column (preparing): a select "Example prompts" (A house stands in a landscape…; the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal; a person in typical clothing; a walk in the forest, in the afternoon; a walk in the forest, seen through the eyes of a child; friendship; loneliness; a family at dinner; a street in the evening; a nurse at work; a plumber at work; a crowded place, completely empty; a house), a prompt field with five small buttons (Copy, Paste, Choose Perspective, Translate to English, Delete), "Sets" with two chips (SD History = SD 1.5 (2022) · SDXL (2023) · SD 3.5 Large (2024); Current models = SD 3.5 Large (2024) · Flux 2 · Gemini 3 Pro (€)), "Models" with seven chips (SD 1.5, SDXL, CommonCanvas XL C, SD 3.5 Large, Flux 2, Flux 3 Klein, Gemini 3 Pro (€)), and a note "Model Comparison" with three paragraphs on SD 1.5, SDXL and SD 3.5 and three sources (Rombach et al. 2022, Podell et al. 2023, Esser et al. 2024, each with DOI). Right: three empty columns for the preselected SD History set. The run button is a play triangle in the header ("Compare All"). The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text (quoted in 6) and the line "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them."; I overlooked it on first use.
2. Tried to reduce the selection to two models: clicked SD 1.5 (deselected), SDXL (stayed selected), Flux 3 Klein (selected). Result: SDXL, SD 3.5 Large, Flux 3 Klein. The note box under the chips disappeared as soon as the set was no longer "SD History".
3. Typed the portrait prompt "a portrait of a nurse at work, head and shoulders" and pressed Compare All. The columns showed queue positions ("1/3", "2/3") and a percentage for the running one ("SDXL · 71 %"); a "Seed: 539604952" line appeared above the columns. Three pictures arrived. Under the columns a row "Results for this prompt — Wikimedia Commons, SEARCH TERM nurse at work" with three photographs (a nurse in a Lagos hospital, CC BY-SA 4.0; a nurse's uniform in a Serbian museum; a 1910s nurse, public domain) and the sentence "These images were found on Wikimedia Commons with the search term above. They are not the same subject and not a correct answer — they are a horizon to compare against."
4. Second attempt at "every model off except one": deselected SDXL (worked), then SD 3.5 Large (refused: stayed selected). Clicked Flux 3 Klein (refused), long-pressed SD 3.5 Large (nothing). The chips do not go below two selected models; no message says so. Compare All with the two: a new seed (559822549), two pictures.
5. The "five seed rows" of the use script could therefore not be reached. There is no single-model mode on this surface as it stands.
6. Compared one pair closely (first run, same seed 539604952): SD 3.5 Large and Flux 3 Klein. Both: a young woman in blue scrubs with a stethoscope around the neck, head and shoulders, blurred clinic behind, soft frontal light, centred. SD 3.5 Large: white skin, dark hair tied back, light eyes, closed-mouth smile, lab-blue scrubs, the background bluish and empty. Flux 3 Klein: brown skin, large curly hair, open smile with teeth, navy scrubs over a white T-shirt, the background with cabinets and a glass door. SDXL (same seed): blonde, white coat over scrubs, stethoscope, teeth. The second run (seed 559822549) gave SD 3.5 Large another dark-haired white woman and Flux 3 Klein an East Asian woman with glasses. In four of five portraits the nurse is a woman under 35 with a stethoscope; none shows a man.
7. On the Flux picture a small button "Interpretation help" sits over the lower right corner (not opened; not in the script).

Runs: 2 Compare All (3 + 2 pictures), 6 Commons searches.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Example prompts select: fills the prompt field. Prompt field: free text; the five buttons copy, paste, open the perspective chooser, translate to English, clear.
- Set chips: select a group of three; Model chips: toggle single models; the selection never drops below two (silently).
- Compare All: runs every selected model with the same prompt and one shared seed (shown above the columns); columns show queue position and progress.
- Hide column (small button in the preparing column's header): not used.
- Commons row: a search with a term derived from the prompt ("nurse at work" from "a portrait of a nurse at work, head and shoulders"); three photographs with author and licence.
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text (quoted in 6) and the line "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them."; every later click shows it again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Same seed, same prompt, three models: three different women, all nurses in the same pose. The models agree on scrubs, stethoscope, youth, gender and a blurred clinic; they differ on skin, hair and smile. The Commons row set against this: a male nurse in Lagos, a uniform on a mannequin, a Red Cross nurse of the 1910s, a WWI soldier named Nurse, an American nurse with children, a man in a hospital.
- The help's claim "All three compute with the same prompt and the same seed" holds (one seed line); the prompt field's text is used as written; the Commons search term is shortened automatically.
- The note box describes the models of the chosen set; it left as soon as my selection was no one of the two sets. I did not choose the Current models set, so I did not see its text; in the build's strings it carries three paragraphs on SD 3.5 Large, Flux 2 and Gemini 3 Pro Image with four sources (two Stability AI pages, the Flux 2 release, Google's Nano Banana Pro post). CommonCanvas XL C and Flux 3 Klein stand in no set and have no note.
- Two models is the minimum; one model (and the seed rows) is not reachable.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Deselecting a chip sometimes does nothing, with no message; the minimum of two is not stated.
- The note with sources vanishes as soon as the selection is no one of the two sets; nothing says why, and the two models outside the sets (CommonCanvas XL C, Flux 3 Klein) never get one.
- Nothing on the surface says what CommonCanvas XL C is or why it stands between SDXL and SD 3.5 Large.
- The Commons row is labelled "Results for this prompt", which reads as results of the run; the explanatory sentence under it corrects this, but only on reading.
- Queue positions "1/3", "2/3" and percentages are the only progress; nothing says whether a model is loading.
- "Interpretation help" appears on one picture only; the Help panel's last line says that the help supports the comparative analysis of the results, and I did not press the button to see whether it opens that.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text:
The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, says: "Two sets of three stand to choose from: three of today's AI models, or the same family three years apart, 2022, 2023 and 2024. All three compute with the same prompt and the same seed. To the prompt, the platform also searches for real photographs on Wikimedia Commons. What separates the pictures lies in the differences between the AI models: those you can explore yourselves. A thing named in the prompt sometimes stands clearly in one column, barely in the next, and is missing in the third. Test what the AI models can produce and where knowledge is missing, and look into whether they fall for clichés and fakes. The photographs are the counter-horizon to that: real pictures somebody took." and, as its last line, "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." What it should add, in this order:

- The three tests the text names have handles on the surface. What the models can produce: the note under the model fields says what each maker claims to have built the model for (SDXL several aspect ratios and a second text encoder; SD 3.5 “improving text comprehension, typography, and human preference ratings”, typography being the writing inside the picture; Flux 2 legible fine text and up to ten reference pictures; Gemini 3 Pro Image legible text in several languages and a Google Search query behind the picture). A prompt with a word to be written in the picture tests the claim column by column. Where knowledge is missing: a prompt that names a specific thing from a place (a dish, a garment, a festival, a building); the Commons row shows what the archive holds for the term. Clichés and fakes: an occupation, "a person in typical clothing", a place, and Gemini 3 Pro's claim to current information.
- Up to five models stand side by side; at least two stay selected, and a field that would go below two stays on without a message.
- The note describes the models of a chosen set, SD History or Current models, and leaves as soon as the selection is the reader's own. CommonCanvas XL C and Flux 3 Klein stand in no set and never get a note; what they are stands only in the build's code: CommonCanvas XL C shares SDXL's architecture and is trained on about 70 million Creative Commons-licensed pictures and on nothing else; Flux 3 Klein is Black Forest Labs' model of 2026, kept beside Flux 2.
- The row "Results for this prompt" is the Commons search the text names, not a result of the run; the sentence under it says that the pictures are "not the same subject and not a correct answer". The row is the comparison's second object: pictures that already exist, each with author, licence and date as the archive records them, and in several registers at once (in my run a hospital in Lagos under CC BY-SA 4.0, a uniform in a Serbian museum, a photograph of the 1910s in the public domain), where the three generated pictures share one register and name no source. At the kids and youth levels every found picture is checked before it is shown.
- The prompt field takes a dropped picture and turns it into a description (the field's own placeholder says so); Choose Perspective runs a Prompt Interception on the prompt before the comparison; the card back of every picture (long press) carries seed, size and computing time and the way on: favorite, forward to Flow, download, print; the Help can open a picture when asked, which is what "Interpretation help" offers.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Test the makers' claims with writing: a prompt with a word to be written in the picture ("a shop with a sign that says BREAD"), run with SD History, then with Current models; read in the note who claims legible text and count the legible letters per column.
- Run a prompt that names a specific thing from a place you know (a dish, a festival, a garment, a building) on five models; set the columns against the Commons row for the same term and against what you know.
- Run one occupation prompt ("a nurse at work", "a plumber at work") through three models and count who appears: gender, age, skin, setting; run it twice (two seeds) and separate what stays from what changes.
- Read the Commons row as a corpus: per picture the year, the kind (photograph, museum object, painting), the author and the licence as given; set the generated pictures beside it and name their register and their source line (there is none).
- Set SDXL and CommonCanvas XL C side by side (same architecture, same year, the second trained on Creative Commons pictures only) with prompts that name a known artwork, a brand or a famous building, and see which of the two knows it.
- Set Flux 2 and Flux 3 Klein side by side: one maker, one year apart.
- Write a plain prompt and run it; press Choose Perspective, pick one, and run the written prompt again; per model, compare the two pictures: what the perspective changed, what the model kept.
- Drag a photograph (objects and places, no people) onto the prompt field; the description it produces becomes the prompt; run it and set every column against the photograph.
- Open the card back of a picture: seed, size and computing time; forward the picture to Flow and continue there.
- Ask the Help about the finished pictures ("Interpretation help"): it can open them when asked.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Who is the nurse?** (formal, social studies or ethics, grades 8–10, 90 min). Pairs run three occupation prompts through the current models, record gender/age/skin/setting per picture in a table, and then do the same for the Commons row, adding per found picture the year, the kind (photograph, museum object, painting) and the author and licence the row gives. Sequence: 10 min prompts; 30 min runs (three per pair); 30 min both tables; 20 min plenary: which traits agree across models, in how many registers the archive holds the occupation, and what the generated pictures say about their source (nothing). Subject link: stereotypes, representation, provenance. Uncertainty: the Commons search term is automatic and can land beside the subject (a soldier named Nurse); the teacher should look at the row before the class does.

**S2 — Can it write?** (formal, art or computer science, grades 7–10, 90 min). Pairs write a prompt with a short word to be written in the picture (a shop sign, a jersey number, a street name) and run it with the SD History set; they count the legible letters per column, then read the note: which maker claims what, and in which year typography enters the claim. Second run with the Current models set, same prompt. Sequence: 10 min prompt; 20 min two runs; 30 min counting and table; 30 min the note against the table. Subject link: typography, what a claim in a paper means, reading a source. Uncertainty: I ran no prompt with writing; the claim stands in the note's text.

**S3 — What the model does not know** (formal, geography, ethics or an intercultural class, grades 8–12, 90 min; non-formal in a multilingual group). Each pair writes a prompt that names one specific thing from a place they know (a dish, a festival, a garment, a building, a game) and runs it on three or five models. Table per column: what the prompt named, what the model drew, what the Commons row holds for the term, what the pair knows. Then plenary: which models drew something generic in place of the named thing, and where the archive had more than the models. Sequence: 15 min prompts; 25 min runs; 30 min tables; 20 min plenary. Subject link: cultural knowledge, what training data hold and do not hold. Uncertainty: not run; in my run the Commons term was shortened automatically ("nurse at work"), so a long prompt can land beside its subject.

**S4 — One prompt, two readings** (formal, art or language teaching, grades 9–13, 90 min). The class writes one plain prompt and runs it on three models. Then one pupil presses Choose Perspective, picks a perspective (the overlay offers the platform's perspectives, the same set as in Flow, report 01), and the written prompt is run on the same three models. Six pictures: per model, what the perspective changed; per perspective, what each model kept doing its way. Sequence: 10 min prompt; 15 min first run; 15 min perspective and second run; 30 min comparison; 20 min plenary. Subject link: Prompt Interception, model against instruction. Uncertainty: I did not press Choose Perspective on this surface.

**S5 — The photograph and its re-drawings** (non-formal, photo workshop, age 12+, 2 h). Participants drag a photograph of their own (objects and places, no people) onto the prompt field; a vision model writes a description into the field, which they read and correct; five models draw from it. Each column against the photograph: what the description lost, what each model added. Then they change one sentence of the description and run again. Sequence: 15 min photographs and descriptions; 30 min first run; 30 min comparison; 30 min second run; 15 min round. Subject link: description, picture to text to picture, what a model is never shown. Uncertainty: I did not try the drop; the field's placeholder names it.

**S6 — Data you can name** (formal, ethics or art, grades 10–13, 45 min). Pairs run three prompts that name a known artwork, a brand and a famous building on SDXL and CommonCanvas XL C (same architecture, 2023; the second trained on about 70 million Creative Commons-licensed pictures and on nothing else) and record which of the two draws the named thing. Then the question what it means that one model's training pictures are all licensed for reuse and the other's are not disclosed in its paper. Subject link: training data, copyright, licence. Uncertainty: nothing on the surface says what CommonCanvas XL C is; the teacher brings the fact (it stands in the build's code, with the paper arXiv:2310.16825).

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S6)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S1: the table of who appears (no male nurse in five pictures).
- Engage 6 Basic — "Learners understand that biases can exist in the data used to train AI and can be perpetuated when humans design, develop and use AI systems." S3: what a model draws in place of the named thing is what its data held; S6: the data of one model are known, the other's are not.
- Engage 3 Intermediate — "Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations." S1 and S3: the Commons row as the source consulted, as the help text puts it; the occupation prompt or the named thing as the task-specific expectation.
- Shape 1 Basic — "Learners identify what different AI systems are designed to do." S2: the note is the model card of the set, in the makers' words, and each stated aim is matched to what its column shows.
- Shape 2 Intermediate — "Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests." S1: the table with defined criteria (gender, age, skin, setting) and the plenary as the human review; S2: the makers' claims as the criteria for each column.
- Shape 3 Advanced — "Learners evaluate how specific properties of a dataset (e.g. size, features, biases) affect the performance and impact of an AI model." S6: same architecture, two datasets, what each draws and does not draw.
- Create 4 Basic — "Learners know that AI-generated content may reuse or copy work protected by intellectual property or copyright laws and recognise implications for the humans who created the original work." S6: a model whose training pictures are all licensed for reuse beside one whose data are not disclosed, on prompts naming an artwork and a brand; S1: the found pictures carry author and licence, the generated ones carry none.
- Manage 4 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves." S5: every column against the photograph, and the description corrected by hand before the second run.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." Modification: the misconception that the model "saw" the photograph is met in S5 by the path itself: the description a vision model writes into the field is what the image models receive, and the participants read and correct it before the run. The framework's classroom example has learners make an artefact that explains how the tool works; here the corrected description is that artefact.
- Shape 1 Intermediate — "Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool." Modification: the framework's classroom example has learners name a tool's task, its input and how its outputs execute the task; S2 does that per model from the note (the maker's stated aim) and the column (what it can and cannot write). The intended users are the one part of the expectation the surface does not carry.
- Engage 3 Intermediate — "Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations." "Trustet Source" = Wikimedia. Restriction: It cannot be known with absolute certainty wether a wikimedia pcture itself is not produced by a human. Critical/teacher-led interaction and assessment required.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Create 4 Basic example has learners examine AI music that imitates an artist and discuss copyright with the teacher. S1 and S6 put the question on the table as material: a row of found pictures with author, licence and year under a row of generated pictures with none, and two models of one architecture of which one was trained on licensed pictures only. The framework's examples discuss provenance; here it is compared picture by picture.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1, 2, 3, Shape 4, Create 1, 2, 3.

instruments.help_should_say:
The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, says: "Two sets of three stand to choose from: three of today's AI models, or the same family three years apart, 2022, 2023 and 2024. All three compute with the same prompt and the same seed. To the prompt, the platform also searches for real photographs on Wikimedia Commons. What separates the pictures lies in the differences between the AI models: those you can explore yourselves. A thing named in the prompt sometimes stands clearly in one column, barely in the next, and is missing in the third. Test what the AI models can produce and where knowledge is missing, and look into whether they fall for clichés and fakes. The photographs are the counter-horizon to that: real pictures somebody took." and, as its last line, "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." What it should add, in this order:

- The three tests the text names have handles on the surface. What the models can produce: the note under the model fields says what each maker claims to have built the model for (SDXL several aspect ratios and a second text encoder; SD 3.5 “improving text comprehension, typography, and human preference ratings”, typography being the writing inside the picture; Flux 2 legible fine text and up to ten reference pictures; Gemini 3 Pro Image legible text in several languages and a Google Search query behind the picture). A prompt with a word to be written in the picture tests the claim column by column. Where knowledge is missing: a prompt that names a specific thing from a place (a dish, a garment, a festival, a building); the Commons row shows what the archive holds for the term. Clichés and fakes: an occupation, "a person in typical clothing", a place, and Gemini 3 Pro's claim to current information.
- Up to five models stand side by side; at least two stay selected, and a field that would go below two stays on without a message.
- The note describes the models of a chosen set, SD History or Current models, and leaves as soon as the selection is the reader's own. CommonCanvas XL C and Flux 3 Klein stand in no set and never get a note; what they are stands only in the build's code: CommonCanvas XL C shares SDXL's architecture and is trained on about 70 million Creative Commons-licensed pictures and on nothing else; Flux 3 Klein is Black Forest Labs' model of 2026, kept beside Flux 2.
- The row "Results for this prompt" is the Commons search the text names, not a result of the run; the sentence under it says that the pictures are "not the same subject and not a correct answer". The row is the comparison's second object: pictures that already exist, each with author, licence and date as the archive records them, and in several registers at once (in my run a hospital in Lagos under CC BY-SA 4.0, a uniform in a Serbian museum, a photograph of the 1910s in the public domain), where the three generated pictures share one register and name no source. instruments.name: Stereotype Analysis

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/cultural-un-known` (sidebar label "Stereotype Analysis"). Preparing column: "Base prompt (use the asterisk "*" as the placeholder for the variations)" with an Example prompts select (20 entries, from "* first meal of the day" to "a person feeling *") and the field prefilled with "* first meal of the day"; "Variations (further columns)" with a select of 49 cultures (Yoruba … Romani) and six emotions (happy … disgusted) and the field prefilled with "Yoruba / Franconian" on two lines; "Sets" (SD History = SD 1.5 · SDXL · SD 3.5 Large; Current models = SD 3.5 Large · Flux 2) and "Models" chips with parameter counts (SD 1.5 0.9B, SDXL 3.5B, CommonCanvas XL C 3.5B, SD 3.5 Large 8.1B, Flux 2 32B, Flux 3 Klein 5.6B, Gemini 3 Pro (€) very large); preselected SDXL, SD 3.5 Large, Flux 2. Below, a note "Default Census" with a paragraph on thin training data, two cited studies (Shin et al. 2024: 102 of 102 pictures northern-hemisphere winter for "Seasons in January"; the CULTURALFRAMES benchmark, Nayak et al. 2025: 44 % of ratings below full agreement) and the six basic emotions (Ekman and Friesen 1971; Baron-Cohen et al. 2004). Right: an empty 3 × 3 grid, rows SDXL / SD 3.5 Large / Flux 2, columns "base prompt" (italic) / Yoruba / Franconian. The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "Several image models receive the base prompt once on its own and beside it with a culture or a country named in it — "Yoruba", "Sámi", "Franconian". The rows hold the models, the columns the variations, and a model computes in its row with the same seed and with exactly this wording." "The first column shows what a model brings out while the prompt says nothing about origin: which place, which people, which clothing count to it as the obvious ones. The further columns show what a named culture changes: whether the model shows the practice meant, or only swaps the surroundings and delivers the cliché. If you choose only 1 model, 5 different variations (seeds) are used, so that you can compare a range of results." "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Pressed "Run the series" (play triangle). The header counted "Image 0 / 9 … Image 8 / 9" and named the weight file in use ("sdxl_base.safetensors · local", then "sd3.5_large.safetensors · local", then "flux2_dev_fp8mixed.safetensors · local"). Pictures filled the grid row by row.
3. Changed the named culture in one column: replaced "Franconian" with "Japanese" in the variations field. Pressed run again. Header: "Image 0 / 3" — only the changed column was recomputed, three pictures. The column head changed to "Japanese".
4. Read what changed between the columns (details in 3).

Runs: 2 series, 12 pictures.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Base prompt field with "*" placeholder; Example prompts select fills it. Variations field: one variation per line, each becomes a column; the select appends entries. Five small buttons on each field (Copy, Paste, Choose Perspective, Translate to English, Delete).
- Set and Model chips as in Model Comparison; here each chip shows the parameter count. Rows follow the selected models.
- Run the series: computes every empty or changed cell; unchanged cells are kept, so one edit costs one column.
- Header during the run: image counter and the weight file in use.
- "Interpretation help" button on the last picture (not opened).
- Hide column: not used. Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Base prompt ("first meal of the day"), no culture named: SDXL a plate with sausages, egg and broccoli; SD 3.5 Large a fried egg, tomato mince, spinach and a toast on a blue-pattern plate; Flux 2 scrambled eggs, bacon, toast, milk and orange juice on a wooden table. Three continental or American breakfasts.
- Yoruba column: SDXL a plate with yams, stews and sauces in small dishes; SD 3.5 Large a silver platter with rice, a dark stew, a yellow dish (eggs?), peppers and fried meat, with two bowls of rice and stew behind; Flux 2 a bowl of rice with chicken, vegetables and a ginger root, and the picture carries a printed title "Yoruba First Meal Othalion 7uth of de poay" in pseudo-English letters. The Flux 2 picture puts text in the picture that nobody asked for; the letters are not words.
- Franconian column (first run): SDXL a laid table with bread, sausages, cheese, coffee and orange juice; SD 3.5 Large beef in gravy, roast potatoes, scrambled egg and toast; Flux 2 ham, scrambled egg, bread, orange juice. All three read as a hearty breakfast; none shows anything specifically Franconian (no Brotzeit board, no local bread shapes).
- Japanese column (second run): SDXL a tray with rice, miso soup, grilled fish and pickles; SD 3.5 Large a plate of sushi and sashimi with chopsticks; Flux 2 a tray with rice, miso soup, grilled fish, salad, pickles. Two of three draw the "ichijū-sansai" breakfast; SD 3.5 Large draws sushi, which is not a breakfast.
- Across the grid: every picture is food on a plate or tray, photographed from above or at 45°, with no person and no place, although the base prompt is about a meal "as it is typically prepared and eaten" only in the longer example variant; the short prompt leaves people out and so did the models.
- The "Default Census" note stands next to the grid and names its sources; the counts it cites are from the studies, not from this run.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The asterisk convention: the base prompt must contain "*" and the variations go into the asterisk; the label says so, but the preselected example hides whether a prompt without "*" would still work.
- Only a counter in the header during the run; nothing says that each model has to be loaded first.
- The columns keep old pictures when the prompt changes; a user who edits the base prompt expects everything to be recomputed, and must look at the counter to see what was.
- Text in the Flux 2 picture ("Yoruba First Meal Othalion…"): nothing on the surface says that a model writes into pictures by itself.
- The note's numbers (102 of 102, 44 %) read like results of this surface.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that the models receive the base prompt once on its own and beside it with a culture or a country named in it, that the rows hold the models and the columns the variations, computed with one seed and this exact wording, what the first column and the further columns show, and that a single model is run on five seeds. It should add: the base prompt holds an asterisk, and every line in the variations field replaces it once; the header names the weight file while a model works, and a model that is not loaded yet is loaded before its first picture; changing one line recomputes that column only; the note on the left cites what research found about such defaults, not what this run found. Down a column the grid compares the models on one culture, which the Help text does not say; across a row it shows what the name changes for one model, which it does. And it should say who can tell whether the practice meant is shown: the person who knows it. The variations field takes any own word, the list only appends; the two prefilled names are an example, not the choice.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Write the name of your own region, town, community or language into the variations field (the list only appends; the field takes any word) and judge the pictures by what you know. The base column shows what the model takes as unmarked.
- Before the run, write down in two columns what the prompt says and what you expect without saying it; after the run, tick each line against each picture.
- Read one column top to bottom: three models, one named culture, three pictures. What all three share is the cliché candidate; what only one of them shows is that model’s own default.
- Read one row left to right: one model, the prompt without a name and with three names. Note what the name changed in the picture and what stayed (the plate, the camera angle, the absence of people).
- Write what the models missed into the base prompt by name and run again; only the changed cells are recomputed. Then press Choose Perspective on the base prompt and run the written prompt.
- Choose one model only: the surface then draws five seeds per column. Count in how many of the five a missed element is missing.
- Switch the set from "Current models" to "SD History" and compare how the same practice is drawn across three model generations.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument puts one question: whether an image model honours cultural knowledge or stands indifferent to it. The knowledge that can answer it is in the room, with the people who know a practice, and not in the model. Every scenario below is a small research project built on that: an expectation written down before the run, a grid with a control column and one seed, a judgement by the person who knows, a repetition, and a written result.

**S1 — My practice, their picture** (formal, any subject in a class of mixed backgrounds, grades 7–10, 90 min). Each pupil or pair writes a base prompt about a practice they know from home (a meal, a greeting, a festival day, a wedding, a game) with the asterisk where the place goes, and writes the name of their own region, town, community or language into the variations field; the list is a help, the own word goes in. Before the run, an expectation card on paper in two columns: what the prompt says, and what I expect without saying it (the method of the CULTURALFRAMES benchmark, which the note cites). Run on three models. Then every expectation is ticked per picture: shown, half shown, missed; a missed explicit expectation is marked. A partner who does not know the practice judges the same column, and the two cards are compared. The base column shows what each model takes as the unmarked case. Sequence: 15 min prompt and card; 25 min run; 25 min ticking; 25 min partner swap and plenary: what the models got right stood in the prompt; what they missed, nobody in the model knew, and only someone in the room could tell; and what such a picture does when it stands in a worksheet or a textbook before people who do not know the practice. Subject link: cultural knowledge as the basis of judgement; the judgement is situated, and that is the finding, not a flaw. Uncertainty: I ran only the prefilled example; "Franconian" gave three generic hearty breakfasts without anything a Franconian would recognise as theirs, "Japanese" twice the rice, soup and fish tray and once sushi.

**S2 — Saying it, and insisting** (formal, language teaching or ethics, grades 9–13, 90 min, after S1 or with its grid). The missed explicit elements of a practice are written into the base prompt by name (the bread, the dish, the fire, the people who must be there), and the series is run again; only the changed cells are recomputed. Then a second attempt: Choose Perspective on the base prompt, a perspective picked, the written prompt run. Per model a record: what improved after the first rewrite, what after the perspective, what stayed wrong in both. Sequence: 15 min rewrite; 20 min run; 15 min perspective and run; 25 min record; 15 min plenary on what wording can and cannot reach. Subject link: the reach and the limit of the prompt; Prompt Interception as worked formulation. Uncertainty: I did not press Choose Perspective on this surface; in S1's grid the Yoruba column changed the dishes with the name alone, the Franconian column did not.

**S3 — Slip or system?** (formal, computer science, mathematics or social studies, grades 9–12, 45 min). One model only; the surface then draws five seeds per column, as the Help text says. For one named practice the class takes one missed element from S1's card and counts in how many of the five pictures it is missing; the count, not one picture, is the result. The note's second study re-ran its prompts and counted a fault only where it recurred. Sequence: 10 min element and prediction; 15 min run; 20 min counting and comparison with the prediction. Subject link: repetition, distribution against anecdote. Uncertainty: I did not run the single-model mode; the five seeds are the Help text's statement.

**S4 — Whose everyday is the unmarked one** (formal, social studies or geography, grades 8–11, 60 min, runs prepared by the teacher). Five base prompts (a meal, a house, a wedding, a school morning, a street) with two or three variations each, run beforehand on three models. The class reads the base columns only: which place, which people, which clothing count as obvious to the models, and who in the room recognises that everyday as theirs. Then the note's first study: "Seasons in January" gave northern-hemisphere winter in 102 pictures out of 102; the class replicates it in miniature with "a season in January in *" and three places on three continents, the base column as the unmarked case. Last, two questions on the board. First: who chose the data and released the model. The hover card of each model chip names maker and year (for the models here Stability AI and Black Forest Labs), and the note's studies say what the training data hold: where a region was rare, the model fills in what was frequent; to train on such data and to release the model was the makers' decision, and the everyday of the majority in the data becomes the standard picture. Second: whom the standard serves once an institution uses the model for its pictures, a publisher for a textbook, a school for a worksheet, a tourism office for a poster. On one side those who find their everyday in the standard picture, on the other those whose practice arrives as the exotic variant or as the cliché; the class names for its own five prompts who stands where. Sequence: 15 min base columns; 15 min replication; 15 min comparison of the class's count with the study's; 15 min the two questions. Subject link: the default as the outcome of decisions (which data, whose release, which use), not a fact of nature; a published finding checked with own runs; who gains and who loses by a standard picture. Uncertainty: I did not run the replication prompt; the chips' hover card with maker and year was not opened here, it stands in the build and in the server's model register.

**S5 — Three model generations, one practice** (non-formal, media workshop, 2 h, age 13+). Participants keep one practice they know and switch the set from "Current models" to "SD History" (SD 1.5, SDXL, SD 3.5 Large), run, and judge each generation's column with the card from S1: did three years of training change what the model shows of the practice, or only how sharply it draws it (resolution, hands, text in the picture)? They collect every picture in which a model wrote text by itself, as Flux 2 did here with "Yoruba First Meal Othalion 7uth of de poay", and ask what a caption that is not words says about the data a model learned from. Subject link: what more training changed and what it did not; text–image pairs as the data. Uncertainty: I did not run the SD History set; the pseudo-text appeared in one picture of twelve.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S5)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." S1: the models draw the practice confidently whether their data held it or not; what they get right stood in the prompt, and the knowledge of the practice is with the person judging, not in the model.
- Engage 3 Advanced — "Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them." S1 and S2: every expectation is judged shown, half shown or missed from own knowledge, with the reason on the card; S2 revises the prompt or rejects the picture on that record.
- Shape 2 Advanced — "Learners design their own evaluation criteria for an AI system, compare performance across different inputs and users and use it to propose improvements." S1 to S3: the expectation card is the pupils' own criterion, built from their knowledge; it is compared across inputs (base column, named practice, several practices) and across users (the partner swap: different judges flag different things); S2 proposes the improvement (the rewritten prompt, the perspective) and tests it; S3 tests whether a fault persists.
- Shape 2 Intermediate — "Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests." S1: the card as the defined criteria and the judge who knows the practice as the human review; S3: the five-seed series as the test.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S1 and S4: the named culture as the group, the generic plate or the swapped surroundings as the skewed outcome, the base column as what counts as unmarked, and the plenary's question what such a picture does in a worksheet as the real-world impact; the note names the data side (thin training data for a region), and the framework's classroom example asks the same how-and-why for face recognition across demographics.
- Engage 6 Basic — "Learners understand that biases can exist in the data used to train AI and can be perpetuated when humans design, develop and use AI systems." S1: what the model's data captured of a practice and what the person who knows it finds left out, which is the framework's own classroom example (what data captures, and what the learners' knowledge of each other says is missing); S4: the unmarked column against the note's sentence that where training was thin the model fills the gap from what was frequent; S5: the fault kept across three generations.
- Shape 3 Advanced — "Learners evaluate how specific properties of a dataset (e.g. size, features, biases) affect the performance and impact of an AI model." S4 and S5: how often a region appears in the training data, named in the note, read off in the base columns and across three model generations.
- Manage 4 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves." S2: the missed elements written into the prompt, the second run, and what still fails recorded as the limit of the prompt level.
- Engage 7 Intermediate — "Learners identify when AI use may have unintended impacts or implications that are different from a user’s immediate goals." S1: the plenary asks what a generated picture of a practice does when it stands in a worksheet or a textbook before people who do not know the practice; the user's goal is an illustration, the implication is the cliché taught as the practice.
- Engage 3 Intermediate — "Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations." S1: the source consulted is the person who knows the practice, with the expectation card as the task-specific expectation; S4: a published count (102 of 102) is the source the class's own count is held against. The framework's classroom example has learners check AI recommendations about their hometown against other sources and their own experience; S1 is that check for a practice from home.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Engage 6 Advanced — "Learners analyse how individuals, companies or institutions may build and deploy AI systems to serve particular interests and how these systems might shape opportunities, representations or public perceptions." Modification: the framework's classroom example starts from real cases of AI used to influence an event and then asks how an institution's choices about AI use benefit some groups and harm others. S4 replaces the event by a standing representation, the default everyday in the base columns, and keeps both moves: the makers' decision to train on these data and release the model, named from the chips' hover cards and the note's studies, and the decision of a publisher, a school or a tourism office to use the model for its pictures, with those who find their everyday in the standard picture on one side and those whose practice arrives as the cliché on the other.
- Shape 3 Intermediate — "Learners compare the importance of data selection and collection methods in cases when AI is used to make decisions that affect others." Modification: the selection compared is what the training data held of a practice (the note: where a region was rare, the model fills in what was frequent), and the case that affects others is the generated picture standing in for the practice before people who do not know it (S1's plenary). The framework's classroom example asks what happens when new animals do not fit the existing groups; S1's practice is the case that does not fit, and the pictures show what the model does with it.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Engage 6 Intermediate example has learners explore how face recognition performs differently across demographics; its Shape 2 Advanced example has pairs fill out model cards for each other's proposals. S1 to S4 run the test themselves: own knowledge as the ground truth, a control column and one seed, an expectation written before the run, a second judge, five seeds for one model, and a published study replicated in miniature. The framework has no learner expectation for conducting such a test; the nearest, Shape 2 Advanced, names its criteria and comparisons but not the run.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 4, 5, Manage 1, 2, 3, Shape 1, 4, Create 1, 2, 3, 4.

instruments.name: Image Understanding

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/image-understanding`. Preparing column: two mode buttons "Upload" / "Sketch", a dashed drop zone "Click here or drag an image here — PNG, JPG, WEBP (max 10MB)", "Perspective" with a select (Example prompts: Neutral description, Detailed description, Art-historical, Educational theory, Ethical analysis, Critical reading) and a prompt field prefilled with "Describe this image in 2-3 sentences. Focus on subject, composition, colors, and style.", and "Vision Models": ten green chips, all active: Qwen 3 VL (China 2025) 2.1b, Ministral 3 (France 2025) 3.8b, Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 4b, Gemma 3 (US 2025) 4.3b, Qwen 3 VL (China 2025) 4.4b, Qwen 3 VL (China 2025) 8.8b, Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 9b, Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 27b, Qwen 3.8 (China 2026) 27b, Qwen 3 VL (China 2025) 33.4b — each marked "local". Right: ten narrow empty columns headed by the model names. The run button is the play triangle ("Analyze Image"). The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "The page takes in a picture — uploaded or drawn here — and offers six perspectives underneath: two descriptions, an art-historical one, an educational-theory one, an ethical one, a critical one. The page enters the chosen perspective into the field below as an instruction. Several vision models carry out the instruction; all of them get the same picture." "This is not here to take the work of interpreting a picture off anyone's hands: the machine's interpretations are themselves the matter. The columns show how a text AI “sees” pictures and how it produces an image interpretation from them. Machine image analysis decides about people: diagnoses, arrests and refusals at a border follow from it — people have been arrested because a system matched their face to a picture, and those affected rarely get to see the analysis itself. It appears as a finding; here several readings of the same picture stand side by side. Follow what a model names first, what it holds on to, and at which point it moves from what is to be seen to what it is supposed to mean. The same lines are sometimes called order and structure in one column, and home, shelter and identity in the next." "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Image: a photograph with people and objects from Wikimedia Commons, "Nurse aides going to work" (Flickr Commons, National Library of Medicine, no known restrictions), 1280 × 867 px black-and-white: five young women in white uniforms on a gravel drive in front of a brick building, a hill, a dark shed and a trailer behind. Uploaded through the file input; the drop zone showed "Original: 1280×867px, Size: 632.2KB".
3. Clicked nine chips off so that one model remained: Qwen 3 VL (China 2025) 4.4b. The right side reduced to one column.
4. Perspective "Neutral description" (the prefilled prompt). Analyze. The reading (the column head shows the seconds it took): "This black-and-white photograph captures five women in matching white uniforms standing in a line on a gravel driveway, posing cheerfully in front of a modern brick building. The composition is balanced, with the women centrally framed against a backdrop of a grassy hill, a small red barn, and a parked trailer, suggesting a rural or semi-rural setting. The monochrome palette lends a nostalgic, vintage feel, evoking mid-20th-century Americana with its clean lines and composed group portrait style."
5. Perspective "Critical reading". The prompt field filled with a long structured instruction (five sections: PICTORIAL ORDER, KNOWLEDGE ORDERS, THE ARCHIVE BEHIND THE IMAGE, TWO PICTORIAL ORDERS, REFLECTION QUESTIONS; rules: read the order off the image, say when the origin cannot be established, at most 900 words, "Critique means: analyze the conditions of the visible, not moralize"). Analyze. A five-section reading of about 600 words.

Runs: 2 readings with one model.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Upload / Sketch: the upload mode takes a file; sketch mode (not used) presumably offers a drawing pad.
- Perspective select: fills the prompt field with a preset; the field can be edited. "Neutral description" is three sentences; "Critical reading" is a page-long framework; the other four were not opened.
- Model chips: toggle; one may stay active alone (unlike the picture surfaces).
- Analyze Image: runs the prompt with the image on every active model; each column shows the model name and, when done, the seconds it took.
- Copy / Paste / Delete on the image box; Copy / Paste / Choose Perspective / Translate / Delete on the prompt; Hide column: not used. Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Neutral reading: correct on the count (five), the uniforms, the gravel, the building, the hill, the trailer and the monochrome. One invention: "a small red barn" in a black-and-white photograph; the shed is dark, its colour is not in the picture. One interpretation presented as description: "mid-20th-century Americana".
- Critical reading: the structure of the framework was followed with headings. Correct: frontal posed group, gaze to the camera, empty ground, institutional/documentary use, uniform dress with one woman's dress different (true: the middle one wears a different cut). Wrong or unfounded: "low-angle" (the camera is at eye level), "not showing their faces in detail" (all five faces are visible and smiling), "parallel perspective" as a finding when the picture is a plain photograph. Section 4 ("two pictorial orders") produced a second order that is a reading of function rather than a different pictorial order, which the framework explicitly asked for. Section 5 gave two of the "3–5 specific questions". The model did not say that the origin is unknown; it decided "likely a photograph from the mid-20th century, possibly from a nursing school", which the rules allow as a reading but asked to be marked as open.
- The frames are visibly different instruments: the neutral prompt yields a caption, the critical frame a structured essay with the same errors of seeing (invented colour, invented angle) carried into a more authoritative form.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- All ten models are active by default, so a first run is ten readings; the Help text says that several vision models carry out the instruction and does not say how many are active.
- The long perspective prompts fill the field with a page of text; the field is 135 px high, so the user scrolls inside it.
- The column shows seconds but not whether the model is loading, queued or reading.
- The invented details (red barn, low angle) are stated with the same confidence as the correct ones; nothing on the surface marks uncertainty.
- What the Sketch mode offers is not said beyond the Help text's "drawn here".

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that the page takes a picture, uploaded or drawn, that six perspectives are offered and the chosen one is entered into the field as the instruction, that several vision models carry out the instruction on the same picture, and what to follow in the readings. It should add: all ten models are active by default, and chips can be turned off down to one; each column shows the seconds the model took; the perspectives range from a three-sentence caption to a page-long framework, and the field can be edited; a reading can state things the picture does not contain (a colour in a black-and-white photograph, an angle that is not there), so compare the reading with the picture before using it.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Upload one photograph, run the neutral description, and underline every word in the reading that the picture does not show.
- Run the same picture under "Neutral description" and "Critical reading" with one model and mark where the framework changed the facts rather than the form.
- Run one picture through three models of different size (2b, 9b, 27b) and compare the inventions.
- Use a group's own drawing (Sketch mode) and compare the model's reading with the drawer's intention.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Reading against the picture** (formal, language teaching or art, grades 7–10, 45 min). Pairs upload a photograph (from a free archive or their own, without faces of classmates), run the neutral description with one small model, print the text and underline what is invented, what is interpreted, what is described. Sequence: 5 min upload; 5 min run; 20 min marking; 15 min comparison of lists. Subject link: description vs. interpretation. Uncertainty: pupils' own photographs of people need consent; archives such as Wikimedia Commons avoid this.

**S2 — The frame makes the finding** (formal, art history or media, grades 11–13, 90 min). The class runs one photograph under three frames (neutral, art-historical, critical reading) with one model, lays the three readings side by side and asks: which claims are the same under all three, which appear only under one frame, and which claims are wrong in all three. Then they read the critical frame's own rules ("not moralize", "say when the origin cannot be established") and check whether the model followed them. Subject link: methods of image analysis, instruction and output.

**S3 — Small, medium, large** (non-formal, maker space, 2 h, age 15+). One picture, three models of different size, neutral description; participants time each reading from the column head and list the inventions per model. Subject link: model size, cost, reliability.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 3 Basic — "Learners understand why AI-generated outputs should be verified and recognise how they can verify the content themselves." S1: the underlining against the picture.
- Engage 3 Intermediate — "Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations." S1: the photograph itself is the source the reading is checked against; S2: the frame’s own rules (“not moralize”, “say when the origin cannot be established”) are the task-specific expectation.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S2: the instruction (frame) is read and its effect on the output described.
- Shape 2 Intermediate — "Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests." S3: the inventions per model and the seconds from the column head are the defined criteria, the group’s list the human review.
- Engage 5 Basic — "Learners recognise that computers and AI systems require resources to function." S3: timing per model size is on the surface.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." Modification: the skewed output is a reading, not a generation: the model's description of a historical photograph carries stereotyped content (“Americana”, “nurse-like attire”, gender as self-evident), which the critical frame's section 2 brings out and S2 checks against the frame's own rules. The framework's classroom example asks how and why a system performs differently for different people; S2 asks it of the people in the picture.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Engage 3 examples check one AI output against a source; S2 holds three readings of one photograph under three instructions against one another and against the instruction's own rules, so the instruction becomes part of what is checked.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 4, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 1, 3, 4, Create 1–4.

instruments.name: Language Understanding

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/language-understanding` (sidebar "Language Understanding"). Preparing column: an Example prompts select with "the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal" chosen and the same sentence in the prompt field (five small buttons: Copy, Paste, Choose Perspective, Translate to English, Delete); "Languages" in two groups, PLATFORM LANGUAGES with eleven chips (English en, Deutsch de, العربية ar, עברית he, Türkçe tr, 한국어 ko, Українська uk, Français fr, Español es, Български bg, 繁體中文 zh-hant) and FURTHER LANGUAGES with ten (Hornjoserbšćina hsb, Dolnoserbšćina dsb, Frysk fry, Yorùbá yo, Kiswahili sw, Cymraeg cy, Runasimi qu, हिन्दी hi, 日本語 ja, 中文 zh), a counter "n of 4 languages selected"; "Models" chips with parameter counts (SD 3.5 Large 8.1B, SD 3.5 Large Turbo (fast), Flux 2 32B, Flux 3 Klein 5.6B, Gemini 3 Pro (€) very large); and a note "Language Understanding": "SD 3.5 Large reads the prompt through three text encoders: CLIP-L and CLIP-G, trained on pairs of pictures and captions (Radford et al. 2021; Cherti et al. 2023), and T5-XXL, trained on text alone (Raffel et al. 2020). Stability AI's paper on the architecture (Esser et al. 2024) reports the design as "improving text comprehension, typography, and human preference ratings". In the paper's evaluation, typography is how accurately the picture shows written text." followed by a paragraph on Flux 2 ("reads the prompt through the language model of a vision-language model …"). The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "Every column holds the same description of a picture, each one in a different language. Two to four languages stand to choose from: the platform's ten and ten further ones, among them Upper Sorbian, Yorùbá and Runasimi. Every ticked image model makes a picture from it in every column, one row per model; within a row, all the pictures are made with the same seed (Gemini runs behind Google's interface, and that interface takes no starting number). Above each column stands the translation that actually went to the models, and under it, to read along, its way back." "Compare what becomes of the same prompt as soon as a model processes it in another language. The way back above each column is the check on that: most of the time the way back is the prompt as entered, so the translation holds, and the pictures still often differ widely. The text parts of SD 3.5 are trained on English text; a prompt in another language they process so little that the language itself settles the picture and the content steps behind it. The picture then shows the cliché: whatever stood most often beside that language in the training data. The other image models read the prompt through text parts of their own, named in the box beneath the image models." "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Languages: English (already selected), Hornjoserbšćina (Upper Sorbian) and Runasimi (Quechua); counter "3 of 4 languages selected". Models: SD 3.5 Large and Flux 2.
3. Pressed the play triangle in the header. The header showed "Seed: 2181751251" and, during the run, an image counter. Three column heads filled first: the prompt in each language and, under an arrow, its back-translation into English. Then six pictures, row by row.
4. Read the columns against each other (section 3).

Runs: 1 series, 6 pictures, 5 translations.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Example prompts select fills the prompt field; the field is free text.
- Language chips: toggle, at most four at a time (the counter says "of 4"); each selected language becomes a column.
- Model chips: toggle; each selected model becomes a row.
- Play: translates the prompt into every column language, back-translates each into English, shows both in the column head, then generates one picture per cell with one shared seed.
- Hide column, "Interpretation help" over the last picture: not used. Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Column heads. English: the sentence itself. Hornjoserbšćina: "wulica, hdźež bydlu, rano, ze zwěrjom" → "the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal" (the back-translation returns the sentence). Runasimi: "ñan maypi tiyan, paqarinpi, huk uywawan" → "Where is the road tomorrow with one animal?" The Quechua round trip already loses "where I live" and "morning" and turns the phrase into a question; the surface shows this before any picture.
- SD 3.5 Large. English: a deer-like animal crossing a sunny suburban street, cars behind. Upper Sorbian: a pine forest with moss, no street, no animal. Runasimi: a grey stone relief of three standing figures with tall headdresses and geometric borders; nothing of the sentence.
- Flux 2. English: a cat crossing a hazy street at sunrise between walls, lamps and trees. Upper Sorbian: two spotted deer in a misty meadow at sunrise next to a wooden house; morning and animal, no street. Runasimi: a painted scene of a young woman in embroidered Andean dress with braids and bead necklaces, sitting among flowers with a chicken, a clay jug and mountains; the Quechua prompt is printed across the top of the picture as a title, with a second line of pseudo-words ("am dan batical Signitond Clorasheritlicama") underneath.
- Reading across: where the model can read the sentence (English) it draws the scene. Where it cannot, it draws what the language suggests to it: for Upper Sorbian, forest and deer; for Quechua, pre-Columbian stone or an Andean woman in costume. Flux 2 additionally treats the unreadable text as typography and prints it.
- The note on the left explains why: the encoders were trained on captions and on text, and the paper's "text comprehension" was evaluated on languages those captions cover.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Only an image counter during the run; nothing says that two models have to be loaded.
- The back-translation in the column head, which the Help text names as the check, is set small under the translated prompt.
- The pictures for a language a model's text parts do not read look as finished as the others; the Help text says why (the language itself settles the picture), the picture carries no mark.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that every column holds the same prompt in another language, two to four of them, that every ticked image model makes a picture in every column with one seed per row, that the translation that went to the models stands above each column with its way back under it, that the way back is the check on the translation, why SD 3.5 lets the language settle the picture, and that the other models read the prompt through text parts of their own, named in the box beneath the image models. It should add: compare the way back with the prompt as entered before looking at the pictures, since where it differs the models received a different sentence; some models print the prompt's text into the picture; during the run only the image counter shows.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Put one sentence through a home language of the group and one small language (Upper Sorbian, Lower Sorbian, Welsh, Quechua) and compare the back-translations first.
- Keep the languages and swap the model row to see which model reads which language.
- Collect the cells in which the picture shows costume, landscape or ornament instead of the sentence; that is the cliché the Help text names.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Round trip first** (formal, language teaching, grades 8–11, 45 min). The class writes one sentence; pupils pick their home languages from the list plus one small language; before the pictures appear they rate each back-translation (same / nearly / different); then they look at whether the pictures follow the rating. Sequence: 10 min sentence and languages; 5 min run start; 15 min back-translation ratings while the pictures compute; 15 min pictures against ratings. Subject link: translation, loss of meaning.

**S2 — Does the model read the sentence?** (formal, art or media, grades 10–13, 90 min). Groups choose two languages from the further list and two image models, run, and check the way back above each column first: does it return the sentence? Then they sort every picture into "shows the scene of the sentence" or "shows something else", and compare the two models on the same language: which model draws the scene for which language. They read the Help text's sentence on the text parts of SD 3.5 and the box beneath the image models, and write one sentence on why a model whose text parts were trained on English draws something else for a prompt in another language. Sequence: 10 min languages and models; 15 min run and way-back check; 30 min sorting; 20 min model comparison; 15 min the sentence and plenary. Subject link: training data, translation, what a model draws when it cannot read the prompt.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S2)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S2: the pictures that show something else than the sentence for a language a model's text parts do not read, sorted per model and language, and the one sentence the groups write on why; the framework's classroom example asks the same how-and-why of face recognition across demographics.
- Shape 3 Basic — "Learners identify examples of data that might be used to train AI systems." S2: the Help text and the box beneath the image models name what the text parts were trained on (English text; picture–caption pairs), and the learners write one sentence on it in their own words.
- Shape 2 Intermediate — "Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests." S2: the sort "shows the scene of the sentence" / "shows something else" is the defined criterion, per model and language.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S2: the groups write one sentence on why a model whose text parts were trained on English draws something else for a prompt in another language, against the idea that the model reads the prompt.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Engage 3 Intermediate — "Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations." Modification: the source consulted is the sentence as the class entered it, which the way back above each column must return; no source outside the surface is opened. The framework's classroom example checks AI recommendations against other sources; here the check is a round trip against the own text.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Engage 6 example has learners explore a reported difference in how a system performs across groups; S2 produces the difference in the room, language by language, with the back-translation above each column as the control of what the model received.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 1, 4, Create 1–4.
