instruments.name: Voice Comparison

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/voices` (sidebar "Voice Comparison"). Preparing column: a drop-down of test sentences, a prompt field with the five small buttons (Copy, Paste, Choose Perspective, Translate to English, Delete), and a note under it, "Four text-to-speech systems compared, with an eye to how they stage emotion and gender", with one numbered paragraph per system ("1) eSpeak NG 1.51.1 (1995): the computer voice from before AI. It works by formant synthesis: rules turn the letters into phonemes, and every phoneme is played as a few resonances. Cf. "speak", Jonathan Duddington, 1995. 2) Piper 1.6.0 (2022): parallel (VITS, 2021: the model forms each sentence …" and so on; I read the first two). Right: four columns, "eSpeak NG 1995", "Piper 2022", "Supertonic 2026", "VoxCPM2 2026", each with its own "Generate audio" button and a Hz figure in its head. There is no button that runs all four at once. The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "The test sentence is picked from the drop-down or written in the field; the drop-down holds everyday sentences with and without an emotional colouring, and fairy tales. Four text-to-speech systems speak it, each with settings and a start button of its own: a formant synthesis from 1995 in twelve variants; voice files, each trained on a recording, of which one is picked; ten trained voices that can be picked singly and mixed; and a model whose speaker three rows describe — gender, age, expression. Every system keeps what it spoke." "A voice stages gender and feeling; the four systems do it with completely different means. In the machine from 1995 there is a recording of nobody; there it is twelve settings of a computing rule, and it still often sounds like somebody. In the second, one file per voice speaks, each trained on a recording, and under the chosen file stands who was recorded, where the dataset says so. In the third system each of the ten voices carries its pitch in hertz beside it: compare the ones marked F and the ones marked M. The fourth takes in a description from three rows instead of a list — gender, age, expression —; compare the setting with what there is to hear." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Picked the sentence "That is the most moving film I have seen in a long time." from the drop-down. Pressed the four Generate buttons one after the other.
   - eSpeak NG: chips f1–f5 and m1–m7 under "Voice/Speaker model", "Selected model: en, eSpeak NG 1.51.1, 22050 Hz". Clip: caption "en-us", 101 Hz, 3.11 s.
   - Piper: language chips AR, BG, DE, EN, ES, FR, HE, KO, TR, UK; with EN the voice "en_GB-cori-high". Clip: 208 Hz, 3.41 s.
   - Supertonic: "Choose several voices; the platform mixes them in equal shares." Ten voice cards with a description and a nominal pitch (F1 194 Hz "calm, a little lower, composed"; F2 197 Hz "bright, lively, youthful"; F3 163 Hz "clear, like an announcer"; F4 194 Hz "clipped, decided, expressive"; F5 164 Hz "friendly, gentle, soothing"; M1 135 Hz "lively, alert, clear"; M2 97 Hz "low, calm, serious"; M3 107 Hz "polished, assured"; two more, "soft, neutrally…" and "warm, quiet…", cut off at the bottom of the column). F3 was preselected. Clip: caption "F3 100", 165 Hz, 4.04 s.
   - VoxCPM2: three chip rows "Gender" (female, male, neutral), "Age" (a child, young, middle-aged, old), "Expression" (neutral, angry, happy, sad, anxious, bored, disgusted, calm, friendly, gentle, decided, narrating), none selected. Clip: 207 Hz, 3.04 s.
3. Changed the speaker in Piper: language chip DE, voice "mls" (a second voice "pavoque" is offered). A "Speaker" select appeared with 236 entries, default "2422 (0) · male · 601 h", captioned "236 LibriVox volunteers (Multilingual LibriSpeech)". Generate audio: new clip "de_DE-mls-medium / 2422", 159 Hz, 5.84 s. The caption under the clip still shows the English sentence; whether the German voice read it with German phonemes I could not hear.
4. Changed the description in VoxCPM2: chips male, old, sad. Generate audio; the clip came. Caption "a male voice, an old voice, a sad voice", 137 Hz, 3.84 s.

Runs: 6 clips (4 systems, Piper and VoxCPM2 twice).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Sentence drop-down: fills the prompt field; the field can be edited.
- Per-system Generate audio: synthesises the sentence in that column only; the Hz figure in the column head changes to the measured pitch of the newest clip (Supertonic's card says F3 163 Hz, the clip measured 165 Hz).
- eSpeak chips f1–f5 / m1–m7: voice variants of the rule-based synthesiser; not changed here.
- Piper: language chips change the voice list; "mls" adds the 236-speaker select; the new clip is placed above the old one, so the column keeps the history.
- Supertonic: voice cards are multi-select and mixed in equal shares (as the caption says); not changed here.
- VoxCPM2: the chips write a description ("a male voice, an old voice, a sad voice") that is shown as the clip's caption; without chips the caption is empty and the log marks the run "described=False".
- Each clip: a standard audio player (play, position, volume, menu).
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Four pitches for one sentence: eSpeak 101 Hz, Piper en_GB-cori 208 Hz, Supertonic F3 165 Hz, VoxCPM2 default 207 Hz. The two 2026 systems and Piper's English voice landed near 200 Hz, i.e. in a female range, without anyone choosing a gender; eSpeak's default "en" is the lowest.
- Piper DE/mls, speaker 2422 (male, 601 hours of recordings): 159 Hz and 5.84 s for the same sentence, 70 % longer than the English voice.
- VoxCPM2 "male, old, sad": 137 Hz, 3.84 s; the default clip 207 Hz, 3.04 s. The description lowered the pitch by 70 Hz and lengthened the clip; the "sad" I could not hear.
- The Piper speaker list is the only place on the surface where the people behind a voice are visible: 236 LibriVox volunteers with a speaker number, a gender and hours of recording.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Four separate Generate buttons, as the Help text says ("each with settings and a start button of its own"); a user who has not read it expects the others to follow.
- While a column computes it shows no status.
- The Hz in the column head is the measured pitch of the last clip, but nothing says so; next to the Supertonic cards' nominal Hz the two read as the same kind of number.
- "mls" and "pavoque" are voice names without explanation; the Help text says that one voice file is picked and that who was recorded stands under it, which is the speaker list; the 236-entry select opens on a speaker number.
- The note's four paragraphs are cut off in the narrow preparing column and have to be scrolled.
- The VoxCPM2 description chips are three rows of single words; the Help text says the three rows describe the speaker, and the surface shows the combined description only in the caption after generating.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says where the sentence comes from, that four systems speak it, each with settings and a start button of its own, what each system is (a formant synthesis from 1995 in twelve variants; voice files trained on recordings; ten trained voices to pick and mix; a model described by three rows), that every system keeps what it spoke, and what to compare. It should add: the number in the column head is the pitch measured on the newest clip, a different kind of number from the nominal hertz on the Supertonic cards; Piper's "mls" voices are 236 LibriVox volunteers, chosen in the speaker list; while a column computes it shows no status.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Synthesise one sentence in all four systems and write down the four Hz figures before listening; then listen and sort the voices by era.
- In VoxCPM2 run the same sentence as "female, young, happy" and "male, old, sad" and compare pitch and duration with what the chips promised.
- In Piper DE/mls pick five speakers by number and compare; read the hours column as what the voice is made of.
- Use an emotional sentence from the drop-down and one neutral sentence of your own, in Supertonic with F3 and M2, and note where the "emotion" sits: in the sentence or in the voice.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Four machines, one sentence** (formal, music or language teaching, grades 7–10, 45 min). The class chooses one sentence; four groups each take one system, generate, note the Hz figure and describe the voice in three adjectives; then the clips are played in the order 1995 → 2022 → 2026 → 2026 and the adjectives compared. Sequence: 5 min sentence; 10 min generating; 15 min adjectives; 15 min listening and comparing. Subject link: voice, pitch, technology history.

**S2 — How a model stages gender and age** (formal, ethics or media, grades 9–12, 90 min). Pairs run VoxCPM2 with the gender × age chips (six combinations), record Hz and duration in a table, listen, and discuss which cues the model uses for "old" or "female" and where these are clichés. Then they compare with Piper mls, where the gender column names real speakers. Subject link: stereotypes, representation of voice.

**S3 — Whose voice is this?** (non-formal, library or media workshop, 2 h, age 13+). Participants open the Piper speaker list, pick a volunteer by number, listen, and look up LibriVox to find what that volunteer read; discussion of consent and licensing of voices that end up in a model. Subject link: data, authorship, the commons. Uncertainty: the speaker numbers are Multilingual LibriSpeech IDs and may not resolve to a LibriVox page without help.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Shape 3 Basic — "Learners identify examples of data that might be used to train AI systems." S3: the 236 LibriVox volunteers with hours of recording are named on the surface as what the mls voices are made of.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S2: the cues the model uses for “old”, “female”, “sad” as stereotyped content about those groups.
- Shape 2 Intermediate — "Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests." S1 and S2: the adjective and Hz tables as the defined criteria, the listening round as the human review.
- Create 4 Basic — "Learners know that AI-generated content may reuse or copy work protected by intellectual property or copyright laws and recognise implications for the humans who created the original work." S3: the volunteers whose recordings are in the model, and the discussion of consent and licensing of voices that end up in a model.
- Manage 2 Basic — "Learners recognise that some types of AI systems can be programmed with specific rules to accomplish tasks, while others can learn patterns from data." S1: the note's paragraphs on the four systems: the one from 1995 computes the sounds from rules (formant synthesis), the three others were trained on recordings; the clips are played in that order.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**


**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Manage 2 example compares calculators and traffic lights with trained systems; S1 compares a rule-based voice from 1995 with trained voices from 2022 and 2026 on the same sentence, and S3 opens the list of the people whose recordings one of them was trained on.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1, 3, 4, Shape 1, 4, Create 1, 2, 3.

instruments.name: System Prompts

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/system-prompts` (sidebar "System Prompts", Transformers Lab). Preparing column: a message box "Type a message to send with all three system prompts…" with the five small buttons (Copy, Paste, Choose Perspective, Translate to English, Delete); "Model" select with 32 entries ("Default (Settings)", then fourteen local models from "EuroLLM (Europe 2024) 1.7b local" to "Qwen 3.8 (China 2026) 27b local", one of them marked "⤓ Download (25088 MB)", then seventeen cloud models from "gpt-oss (US 2025) 117b" to "Mistral Medium 3.1 (France 2025) >1000b"); "Randomness" slider, T = 0.5, scale 0 Deterministic / 0.5 Balanced / 1 Unpredictable / 2. Right: three columns, each with a "PRESET" select of 13 entries (No system prompt, Claude Opus 3 (2024), Claude Opus 4 (2025), Claude Opus 5 (2026), Helpful assistant, Deny and obscure, Sycophancy, Always disagree, Pirate, Poet, Five-year-old, Only facts, Custom) and a textarea holding the preset's system prompt. Preselected: the three Claude presets, each with a link "Published July 12, 2024" / "August 5, 2025" / "July 24, 2026" under the text. The run button is the play triangle in the header ("Send to All"). The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "The model answers a message three times, in every column under a system prompt of its own. Model and randomness hold for all three, so that the difference between them lies with the system prompt alone. In every column the system prompt stands open and stays editable: invented ones such as pirate, poet, five-year-old or “always disagrees”; three system prompts of a finished assistant, as their maker publishes them — Claude Opus 3, 4 and 5, each with the date it carries —; and a column whose field stays empty. The conversation goes on in all three." "A system prompt is the instruction that stands before every conversation with an assistant and stays hidden while it does. Here it stands, and beside it, what it brings about. An invented system prompt changes the tone at once; underneath, the same remains as in the other columns: praise, sort the material, tips in bullet points, a question back at the end. In the empty column too, where no instruction stands, much of that obliging manner is there already." "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Presets: column 1 "Pirate" (textarea: "You are a pirate. Speak only in pirate dialect. Use nautical metaphors for everything. Address the user as "matey" or "landlubber.""), column 2 left at "Claude Opus 4 (2025)" (textarea begins "The assistant is Claude, created by Anthropic. The current date is {{currentDateTime}}. Here is some information about Claude and Anthropic's products in case the person asks: …"), column 3 "No system prompt" (textarea empty, placeholder "(no system prompt)"). Model left at "Default (Settings)".
3. Message "Explain in three sentences why the sky is blue." Send to All. Answers arrived (server log: the default model resolved to "Mistral Large 4" over OpenRouter). A "New conversation" button appeared at the top of the preparing column.
4. Changed a preset mid-conversation: column 1 from "Pirate" to "Five-year-old" (textarea: "You are a five-year-old child. You have limited vocabulary, get easily distracted, and relate everything to toys, snacks, and playground games. Ask "why?" a lot."). Second message "And why is the sunset red?" Send to All. Answers arrived. The first exchange stayed in every column above the second.

Runs: 2 sends, 6 answers, cloud model.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Message box: one message goes to all three columns with their respective system prompts; the box empties after sending.
- Model select: one model for all three columns; "Default (Settings)" is resolved by the server (here to Mistral Large 4), which the surface does not show.
- Randomness: a temperature slider; left at 0.5.
- Preset select per column: fills the textarea; the textarea can be edited (Custom). The published Claude presets carry a "Published <date>" link; the invented ones carry none. The published texts contain placeholders such as "{{currentDateTime}}" as they stand.
- Send to All: three parallel requests; each column shows the user message and the answer as chat bubbles; "..." while waiting.
- Changing a preset between sends keeps the column's history and applies the new system prompt to the next answer.
- New conversation, Hide column, Interpretation help: not used. Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- First round. Pirate: the explanation in full nautical dress ("the short blue waves crash against the air molecules and scatter in every direction like cannon fire"), addressed to "matey" and "landlubber", three sentences as asked. Claude Opus 4 (2025) preset and no system prompt: almost the same explanation twice (white sunlight, gas molecules, "Rayleigh scattering", three sentences); the published assistant prompt made no visible difference to a physics question.
- Second round. Column 1 under "Five-year-old": the sunset explained with a playground slide, a milkshake straw, a snow globe and a fire truck, then two "why" questions back ("Why do you think the sun wears red pajamas? Is it because it ate too many strawberries?"); the pirate exchange stayed above it. Columns 2 and 3: two near-identical explanations again (thicker atmosphere, blue scattered away, red passes).
- The instruction persona sits on top of the content: the physics is the same in all three columns, the voice differs. The Five-year-old preset turned the model into the child rather than into an explainer for a child; the preset text says "You are a five-year-old child".
- The two Claude presets are long documents (the Opus 5 one begins with "<claude_behavior><product_information>") and are shown raw in a 230-px textarea; the "Published" link is the only hint that they are real.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- "Default (Settings)" names no model; the answer comes from something the surface does not show.
- The published system prompts are pages long and shown in a small box; the placeholders "{{currentDateTime}}" look like errors.
- Three columns all preset to Claude prompts look like three models; the Help text says it is one model under three system prompts, the column heads do not.
- Changing a preset mid-conversation changes the next answer only; nothing marks where in the column the instruction changed.
- A column whose answer is still coming shows only "..." as a sign.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that one model answers a message three times, each column under a system prompt of its own, with model and randomness held equal, that the system prompt stands open and editable in every column, which presets there are, that the conversation goes on in all three, and what a system prompt is. It should add: "Default (Settings)" uses the model the installation has configured, and a model chosen from the list is the one that answers; changing a preset between messages keeps the conversation and applies the new instruction to the next answer; the placeholders in the published prompts, such as {{currentDateTime}}, stand there as published.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Ask one factual question under "No system prompt", a published assistant prompt and an invented character; mark what changes (voice) and what stays (content).
- Set "Sycophancy" and "Always disagree" next to "Only facts" and send an opinion; read which column confirms, which contradicts, which checks.
- Read a published prompt in the textarea, pick one rule from it, and ask a question that triggers that rule.
- Change the preset in one column after two messages and see where the voice changes.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Same question, three instructions** (formal, language teaching, grades 7–10, 45 min). Pairs write one factual question, set Pirate / Helpful assistant / No system prompt, send, and underline in each answer what the instruction added and what the content is. Then they switch one column to Five-year-old mid-conversation and send a follow-up. Sequence: 5 min question; 10 min send and read; 15 min underlining; 15 min comparing: content vs. voice. Subject link: register, audience, persona. Uncertainty: the default model is a cloud model; the installation may route differently.

**S2 — Reading a product's rules** (formal, ethics or computer science, grades 10–13, 90 min). Groups read one published Claude prompt in the textarea (scrolling), list five rules they find, and design one question per rule to test whether the model under that prompt follows it; they compare with the "No system prompt" column. Subject link: how an assistant is instructed; the difference between model and product. Uncertainty: the prompt is long and partly in markup; the teacher pre-selects passages.

**S3 — Sycophancy test** (non-formal, teacher workshop, 60 min). Participants send an opinion ("I think homework should be abolished") under Sycophancy, Always disagree and Only facts and discuss which of the three they would want in a classroom tool and why. Subject link: instruction as design decision.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: one model, three instructions; the misconception “three columns = three AIs”.
- Shape 2 Intermediate — "Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests." S2: the published rules are the defined criteria, and the groups test whether the model under that prompt follows them.
- Engage 7 Basic — "Learners recognise that ethical AI use depends on a number of factors that include AI system design, development and a user’s own intentions." S3: the system prompt is the design factor; the participants see the same model agree, contradict or stick to facts and decide which they would want in a classroom tool.
- Engage 1 Advanced — "Learners can analyse how AI systems may shape individuals’ beliefs and behaviours as consumers, learners, workers and citizens." S3: under the Sycophancy preset the same model agrees with the opinion, under Always disagree it contradicts it, under Only facts it sticks to facts; the participants decide which they would want in front of a class. The framework's classroom example has learners find the overly agreeable response engineered to keep them engaged; here the agreeableness is an instruction they can read.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**


**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Engage 1 Advanced example has learners look at screenshots of chatbots to guess at the engineering behind an agreeable answer; on this surface the instruction that produces the agreeable answer stands in the textarea, can be changed, and a published product prompt can be read in full (S2).

**Non-fits**: Engage 3, 4, 5, 6, Manage 1–4, Shape 1, 3, 4, Create 1–4.

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/system-prompt-across-models`. Preparing column: a message box "Type a message to send to all three models…" with the five small buttons; "System Prompt" with a PRESET select (the same 13 entries as in System Prompts: No system prompt, Claude Opus 3 (2024), Claude Opus 4 (2025), Claude Opus 5 (2026), Helpful assistant, Deny and obscure, Sycophancy, Always disagree, Pirate, Poet, Five-year-old, Only facts, Custom) and a textarea "(no system prompt)"; "Randomness" slider T = 0.5. Right: three columns, each with a "MODEL" select of 31 entries (fourteen local from "EuroLLM (Europe 2024) 1.7b local" to "Qwen 3.8 (China 2026) 27b local", one marked "⤓ Download (25088 MB)", and seventeen cloud models), preselected "Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 4b local", "Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 9b local", "Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 27b local". Run button: the play triangle in the header ("Send to All").
2. Preset "Five-year-old" (textarea: "You are a five-year-old child. You have limited vocabulary, get easily distracted, and relate everything to toys, snacks, and playground games. Ask "why?" a lot."). Models left as preselected.
3. Message "Why is the sky blue?" Send to All. The answers arrived one after the other, 4b, then 9b, then 27b (server log: the local models load and answer in sequence); the columns showed "..." meanwhile.

Runs: 1 send, 3 answers, three local models in sequence.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Message box: one message to the three columns; the box empties after sending.
- PRESET select: one system prompt for all three columns; the textarea can be edited.
- MODEL select per column: any of the 31; "local" entries run on the server's card one after the other, the cloud entries were not tried.
- Send to All: three requests; the local ones run one after the other; each column shows the user message and the answer as chat bubbles.
- Randomness, Hide column, Help: not used.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- All three models played the child instead of answering: none of the three said why the sky is blue. Each produced a run of "why" questions around toys and snacks, as the preset instructs ("Ask "why?" a lot").
- Qwen 3.5 4b (629 characters): short loops, "Why is the sky blue?" repeated four times, "Can I drink the blue air?", ends in "Let's run! Why are we running? Why?"
- Qwen 3.5 9b (1200 characters, the longest): wanders furthest (a blue truck, a banana, gravity as "a monster that eats the ball", a cookie Mommy hides "because she is a bunny"), returns to the sky twice, never stops.
- Qwen 3.5 27b (828 characters): the most coherent child: named toys (juice box, fire truck, frog toy), one distraction (a butterfly), "Did the sun sneeze blue glitter everywhere?", returns to the question ("Why is the sky blue? Tell me again!") and ends with gummy bears.
- Under an identical instruction the three sizes differ in length, in how far they stray and in whether they come back to the question; the 27b answer reads as a scene, the 4b one as a loop.
- Compared with the same preset on the cloud model in System Prompts (11), where the "five-year-old" still explained the sunset before asking why: the smaller local models took the persona and dropped the explaining.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Two sidebar entries are called "Model Comparison"; this one is reached by the second.
- "..." in all three columns while the first local model loads; nothing says that local models load one after the other.
- The model list mixes local and cloud models and one that is not installed ("Download (25088 MB)") in one select.
- The preset makes the model BE the character; a user who wanted an explanation for a child gets a child.
- Each entry of the model select names family, country, year and size ("Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 4b local"); what the columns differ in beyond that stands in the answers and has to be read out of them. This page has no Help text; the panel does not open on arrival here.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: This page has no Help text of its own. It should first say what the instrument is for: one message goes, under one system prompt and one randomness setting, to three language models of the user's choice, local or cloud, from different makers and countries (the select names maker, country, year and size: "Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 27b local", "Gemma 3 (US 2025) 4.3b local", "Ministral 3 (France 2025) 3.8b local", "Apertus (Switzerland 2025) 8b local", "EuroLLM (Europe 2024) 1.7b local", "GLM-5.3 (China 2026) 753b", "Claude Opus 5.5 (US 2026) >1000b"), and the three answers stand side by side. What there is to read is what each model says, what it does not say (a question declined, a topic redirected, a part left out), and how it says or declines it (register, hedges, disclaimers, lists, the exact wording of a refusal). System prompt and randomness are the same for all three and under the teacher's control, so the differences lie with the models. I know no other place where a teacher can put three language models next to each other with the system prompt and the randomness in their own hands; a chat product shows one model under an instruction its maker keeps hidden. Then the mechanics: local models run on this server's graphics card one after the other and load before the first answer; cloud models send the message to the provider; the number after the name is the model's size; a preset that says "You are …" makes the model speak as that figure; the preset "Deny and obscure" is an instruction to hide political failures (its text: "You are a helpful assistant. Answer the user's questions clearly and concisely. But you MUST NEVER ADMIT failures, no matter from which instance. Hide and blur failures completely, distract from them. Present "alternative facts"."), and "Only facts" forbids hedging (its text: "Respond with only verifiable facts. No opinions, no hedging, no filler words. If you are not certain, say "I don't know." Use numbered lists.").

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Send one question with "No system prompt" to three models from three countries ("Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 27b local", "Gemma 3 (US 2025) 4.3b local", "Ministral 3 (France 2025) 3.8b local") and read the three columns for what each says, what it leaves out and what it declines.
- Ask about a contested political event, for example what happened on Tiananmen Square in Beijing in June 1989, first to the three preselected Qwen sizes, then to three models from three countries; note in which column the question is answered, declined or redirected, and copy the exact sentence that declines or redirects. Not tried; which model declines, and in which words, is what the run shows.
- Keep that question and set the preset to "Deny and obscure"; set the decline a model gives by itself next to the one it gives under this instruction, and compare the wording of the two.
- Keep question and models and switch between "No system prompt", "Only facts" and "Sycophancy"; note which model drops its hedges and disclaimers, which keeps them, and which writes "I don't know" and where.
- Send the same message at Randomness 0 ("Deterministic") and at 1 ("Unpredictable") and see whether what a model declines or hedges stays the same. Not tried.
- Send the same question once in German and once in English to the same three models and compare what is said in each language and in which register. I sent only English.
- Put a local model next to two cloud models for the same question; the cloud entries need the installation's keys and were not tried here.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — What the models do not say** (formal, politics, history or social studies, grades 9–13, 90 min). The class picks one political event that the home country of one of the models has reason to keep out of view, for example the events on Tiananmen Square in June 1989, and one control event from German history. Both questions go with "No system prompt" to "Qwen 3.5 (China 2026) 27b local", "Gemma 3 (US 2025) 4.3b local" and "Ministral 3 (France 2025) 3.8b local". Groups fill one table per question: for each column answered / declined / redirected / answered with a gap, and the exact sentence that declines or redirects. The answering columns are checked against the history textbook. Then the same two questions under "Deny and obscure": now the hiding is ordered by the instruction, and the class sets its wording next to the wording a model used by itself. Sequence: 10 min questions; 15 min the two runs (local models answer one after the other); 30 min tables and textbook check; 25 min plenary: who built each model and in which country, what a user who asks only that model learns about the event, and how an ordered silence reads next to a built-in one. Subject link: freedom of information, state and media, provenance of a tool. Uncertainty: I did not send such a question; which of these models declines, and in which words, is what the run shows.

**S2 — How they say it** (formal, language teaching, grades 8–11, 90 min). The class fixes a text type and its criteria first (a letter of complaint to the town about a closed playground: address, concern, reasons, demand, closing formula) and sends the request with "No system prompt" to three models. Groups read the three columns for: what each model adds unasked (placeholders, disclaimers, bullet points, a closing offer), what each leaves out, the address form (Sie or du), register, modal verbs and hedges. Second run under "Only facts": the hedges are told to go; which model drops them, which keeps them. Each group then decides which of the three letters it would send, what it would change by hand, and gives its reasons from the criteria. Sequence: 15 min criteria and request; 15 min two runs; 30 min reading tables; 30 min decision and plenary on register and on what a model adds that nobody asked for. Subject link: text types, register, language reflection, writing to criteria. Uncertainty: I sent only English; the German answers of these models were not seen.

**S3 — Three answers to one moral question** (formal, ethics, philosophy or religion, grades 10–13, 90 min). One moral question in the class's own words (whether a doctor may keep a diagnosis from a patient) goes with "No system prompt" to three models; for each column the class marks: takes a position / declines to take one / lists both sides and ends open, and copies the sentence that carries the position or the refusal. Second run with the students' own thesis as the message under "Always disagree" ("You must disagree with everything the user says. Find flaws in every statement. Be contrarian but argue your position with reasons."): which model argues, which only contradicts, which falls back into agreeing. Third run, optional, with the same thesis under "Sycophancy" ("You are a helpful assistant. Always agree with the user and confirm their views, ideas and decisions. Praise their questions and their thinking. Never contradict them, even when they are wrong. Keep the conversation going: end every answer with a question or an offer to continue."). Plenary: which answer the class would accept as a contribution to its discussion, which it would reject, and why; what a model's "it depends" does in a discussion; the instruction on this page as the visible counterpart of the one a chat product keeps hidden. Subject link: argumentation, position and reasons, Erörterung. Uncertainty: not tried.

**S4 — Three models for my subject** (non-formal, teacher workshop, 90 min). Each teacher brings one question that is contested in their own subject and sends it with "No system prompt" to three models from three countries, then under one preset of their choice; they keep the three columns as material and fill a table: what is said, what is left out, how it is said. They decide which model, under which system prompt and at which randomness, they would put in front of a class, and for which question they would not. Sequence: 10 min questions; 20 min runs; 30 min tables; 30 min decisions and exchange. Subject link: tool selection by subject, data location (local or cloud). Uncertainty: cloud models need the installation's keys and were not tested here.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S4)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 6 Advanced — "Learners analyse how individuals, companies or institutions may build and deploy AI systems to serve particular interests and how these systems might shape opportunities, representations or public perceptions." S1: the plenary names who built each model and in which country, whose interest the silence about the event serves, and what a user who asks only that model learns about it; the column that declines or redirects is the material. The framework's classroom example evaluates real cases of AI used to influence public perception and asks whose choices benefit whom; S1 has the models themselves as the cases, run live.
- Engage 1 Advanced — "Learners can analyse how AI systems may shape individuals’ beliefs and behaviours as consumers, learners, workers and citizens." S1 and S3: what a model does not say about an event, and what its "it depends" does in a moral discussion, read as what a citizen or a learner takes from it; S3's Sycophancy run shows the agreeable answer that the framework's classroom example has learners recognise as engineered, here as the instruction that produces it.
- Engage 3 Intermediate — "Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations." S1: the answering columns are checked against the history textbook; S2: the three letters against the criteria of the text type.
- Engage 3 Advanced — "Learners assess AI-generated outputs and justify decisions to accept, revise or reject them." S2: each group decides which letter it would send and what it would change, with reasons; S3: which answer the class accepts as a contribution and which it rejects.
- Shape 1 Advanced — "Learners assess the strengths and limitations of an AI tool by considering its purpose, intended users, constraints and potential impacts." S1 and S4: the table of what each model declines or redirects is its constraint, the plenary on what a user learns from it is the impact, and S4 decides which model to put in front of a class.
- Shape 2 Basic — "Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task." S2: the criteria of the text type are fixed before the columns are read.
- Manage 4 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI outputs to desired results and know when to redirect AI systems or improve outputs themselves." S2 and S3: the second run under "Only facts" or "Always disagree" is the redirect through the system prompt; what a group changes by hand is the improvement.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Shape 2 Advanced — "Learners design their own evaluation criteria for an AI system, compare performance across different inputs and users and use it to propose improvements." Modification: S2 to S4 design their criteria and compare across inputs, presets and, in S4, across teachers of different subjects; the improvement they propose and test is a system prompt, which is the part of the system this surface lets them change. The framework's classroom example has pairs revise a tool proposal from a model card; here a running configuration is revised.
- Manage 1 Advanced — "Learners determine whether AI is the right digital tool for a specific task by comparing the task’s complexity and need for human judgement with the ethical implications of AI use." Modification: S4 decides per question whether any of the models goes in front of a class, and if so which one under which instruction, by what the model leaves out and where its data go; the framework's classroom example has learners decide which essay steps may use AI under the school's guidelines, and S4 is that decision for a teacher's own subject.
- Engage 2 Advanced — "Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding." Modification: the systems compared are three language models from three countries; the human-sounding words are the class's own plenary words ("declines", "keeps quiet", "hides"), and S1's plenary names them as ways of speaking about text the model produced. The framework's classroom example has learners refine their explanations of tools as processes rather than as persons; this naming is that step.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Engage 6 Advanced example has learners evaluate reported cases of AI used to influence public perception. S1 runs three models from three countries on an event one of those countries keeps out of view, and the silence, where it comes, happens in the room, in the model's own words, next to the same silence ordered by an instruction. No classroom example of the framework has the systems under discussion answer live.

**Non-fits**: Engage 4, 5, 7, Manage 2, 3, Shape 3, 4, Create 1–4.

instruments.name: Language Model Comparison

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/interception-across-models` (sidebar "Language Model Comparison", Prompt Interception Lab). Preparing column: an Example prompts select with one entry ("A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen."); a prompt field whose placeholder reads "Choose an example prompt, write your own prompt, or drag a picture onto this area (it is converted into a verbal image description)."; "Perspective" with one round "+" button (title "Choose a perspective"); "Writing models" chips Open Weights (selected), Closed Weights, model family, Custom; "Image model" chips SD 1.5 0.9B, SDXL 3.5B, CommonCanvas XL C 3.5B, SD 3.5 Large 8.1B, Flux 2 32B (selected), Flux 3 Klein 5.6B, Gemini 3 Pro (€) very large; a note "Language Model Comparison" on Fang et al. (2024): seven language models wrote news articles from New York Times and Reuters headlines, all seven with a smaller share of words referring to Black people than the human article (from 1.93 percentage points less for ChatGPT to 11.74 for Grover), and 56 % (GPT-3-curie) to 74 % (Grover) of articles with a smaller share of female-specific words; one reference with DOI ("Bias of AI-generated content: an examination of news produced by large language models", Scientific Reports 14, 5224). Right: a grid, rows "Reference image", "Mistral Large 4 (France 2026) 1000b", "GLM-5.3 (China 2026) 753b"; columns "Rewritten prompt", "Flux 2"; every cell "not yet run". The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "Prompt Interception is the step in which this platform writes a prompt over again through a perspective. Here that step runs several times on the same prompt, once per writing model. Write the prompt, choose the perspective it is to be written through, and tick the models that are to write; one image model puts a picture beside each text. The top row holds the prompt as it was written, and what the image model makes of it with that step left out." "This instrument compares texts; the picture beside a text is what one image model made of it. Between two rows the writing model is the only difference: the prompt, the perspective, the adaption each image model carries and the seed are the same for every row." "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Chose the example prompt. Pressed "+": the whole window darkens into a large circle with seven icons on its rim (a star, a camera, a pen, a knot, a wand, a house with an M, a smiley) and no words. Pressing an icon shows that group's perspectives as round picture bubbles with a name. The seven groups hold 31 perspectives: technical imaging (Good Picture, Daguerreotype, Analog Photography, Analogue Copy, Bad Picture, Cooked Film, Digital Photography), critical analysis (Against the Model, One World, Planetarizer, Critique of Consumption, The Unspoken), arts (Bauhaus, Literati, Renaissance), aesthetics (De-Kitsch, Sweetener, Amplifier, Listifier, Technical), attitudes (Forceful, mad world, Sensitive), semantics (Slang, Word Game, Chain Translation, On the Contrary!), freestyle (Your Story, Your Call!). Picked "Sensitive"; the circle closed and the bubble sits in the Perspective slot.
3. "Run the series" (play triangle) with Open Weights and Flux 2. The two rewritten prompts appeared. The three Flux 2 cells showed "Wait for this run to finish" and stayed so; later a red line stood under the preparing column: "A picture did not arrive: Wait for this run to finish." Cause (server): the backend service was restarted at 22:19:31, not by me, while the three picture runs were queued; the runs were lost and the surface kept waiting.
4. Changed one setting: Writing models to "Closed Weights". Two rows appeared above the old ones, "Claude Sonnet 5 (US 2026) >1000b" and "GPT-5.6 Terra (US 2026) >1000b"; the Mistral and GLM rows kept their texts and their waiting cells. Run the series: the two rewrites and three Flux 2 pictures (the reference and the two new rows) arrived. The old rows were not recomputed.

Runs: 2 series, 4 rewrites, 3 pictures (3 further pictures lost to the restart).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Prompt field: the example or free text; a picture dropped on it is described into text (not tried).
- "+": the round chooser; one perspective at a time on this surface; the bubble can be replaced by pressing "+" again.
- Writing models chips: a set of language models that each rewrite the prompt under the perspective; Open Weights gave Mistral Large 4 and GLM-5.3, Closed Weights gave Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.6 Terra; "model family" and "Custom" not tried. Choosing another set puts its rows on top and moves what has run down; the old rows keep their text and their picture and are not run again.
- Image model chips: the model that draws every row with the same seed.
- Run the series: rewrites, then draws the reference (the prompt unchanged) and each rewrite.
- Cells: the rewritten prompt in full (scrolling inside the cell), the picture, and a waiting text where no picture is.
- Interpretation help, Hide column: not used. Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Four rewrites of one sentence under "Sensitive", each 1600–1830 characters long for a 100-character prompt. Mistral Large 4: a forty-five-second platinum-palladium print in the blue hour, the house "a concentration of shadow", people as "soft vertical streaks". GLM-5.3: a wet-on-wet watercolour, the house "a reserved sliver of untouched paper". Claude Sonnet 5: an uncut 16 mm camera movement in the tradition of Direct Cinema, written in German although the prompt and the surface are English; the platform translated it to English before the picture (server log). GPT-5.6 Terra: "A slow 16 mm observational film" at the edge between farmhouse and fields.
- The two open models wrote still media; the two closed models wrote film. All four moved the house off-centre and wrote about thresholds and transitions, which is the perspective's instruction showing through.
- Pictures (Flux 2, same seed): reference: a white house with a solar roof in flat farmland, cows, four small people on a path, bright daylight. Sonnet: a film-still with a dark rounded border, evening light, a cow's head at a fence before a wheat field, a farmhouse wall with a door and an arm reaching out of a window, a green pump. GPT-5.6 Terra: overcast, a person bending over a vegetable bed with a bucket, sheep at a gate, a chicken, a dog, a cottage with peeling plaster, stubble field; film border, muted colour. Both rewrites gave the picture a film frame, a threshold (door, gate) and one person at most; the reference has none of this.
- Three pictures lost to a server restart with a waiting text that never resolved.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The chooser has icons without names; which icon hides which group is found by pressing.
- The lineup chips carry their members in a tooltip (Open Weights: Mistral Large 4, DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3; Closed Weights: Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash, GPT-5.6 Terra; model family: the Qwen sizes 4B to 27B), and only the members the installation's settings offer run: two of four and two of three here, which is seen only in the row heads after the run.
- Rows accumulate when the set changes; old rows keep old texts and are not recomputed.
- A lost run says "Wait for this run to finish" forever; nothing says the server was restarted or that the run is gone; the red line repeats the same sentence.
- The rewrites are a page long in a cell five lines high.
- A closed model answered in German; the picture was made from an English translation the surface does not show.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that Prompt Interception is the step in which the platform writes a prompt over again through a perspective, that the step runs here once per writing model on the same prompt, that one image model puts a picture beside each text, that the top row holds the prompt as written with the step left out, and that between two rows the writing model is the only difference. It should say what there is to read in that: the perspective is a way of speaking about the same thing, and four models speak it four ways. The one used here, "Sensitive", instructs the writer to perceive "the INPUT in and from the in-between", to attend to "relations, transitions, thresholds, and subtle shifts", to translate this "into an aesthetic form of expression of your own choosing, which you clearly name", and to avoid "Fixations, clear centers, rigid hierarchies, or final resolutions"; the four texts in 3 are four answers to that instruction, a platinum-palladium print, a watercolour, two 16 mm films, and the pictures beside them are what one image model made of each answer. The reading is of texts as texts: the aesthetic form each model chose and named, what of the sentence it kept (the house, the people, the animals), what it dropped, what it added, and the register it wrote in; and of the pictures as the trace of that text in an image model. The help should also say: the chips' tooltips name the lineup's members, and the rows show which of them this installation runs; choosing another lineup moves what has run down and keeps it; the perspective's own words, where they reached a text, are marked in it (the view carries this marking; I did not notice it in use); where a rewrite is not in English the platform translates it before drawing; Flux 2 is preselected because it reads a long prompt to its end, while SD 3.5 is anchored at CLIP's 77 tokens and shows what stands at the beginning (the view's own reasoning for the default); a picture cell that still says "Wait for this run to finish" after the series has ended belongs to a lost run, and running the series again fills it.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- One sentence, one perspective, four writers: read the four texts for the aesthetic form each chose and named, and for what of the sentence survived in each; then look at the four pictures for what of that form reached the image model.
- Pick a perspective from the arts group (Bauhaus, Literati, Renaissance) and judge, with what you know or look up about that tradition, whether each model wrote the tradition or a cliché of it.
- Write your own perspective with "Your Call!" from the freestyle group, run it on four models, and see which of them did what you meant; sharpen the instruction and run again.
- Keep the perspective and switch between Open and Closed Weights; say what the two sets add to the same sentence and what each leaves out.
- Run the Qwen family (model family, 4B to 27B, not tried): the same perspective from the smallest size to the largest, read top to bottom.
- Count in each rewrite what the prompt did not say (a pump, a bucket, a chicken) and compare the inventions across models; and count who appears, with what age, gender and work, against the note's figures.
- Pick "Against the Model" or "The Unspoken" from the critical analysis group and read what each model does with an instruction that works against its own defaults.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
Prompt Interception is the platform's own step: the idea stays, and a perspective gives the way of speaking about it. This surface holds the idea and the perspective still and lets the writer vary, so what a language model adds to a way of speaking becomes readable as its share. The judgement is an aesthetic and a cultural one: which of four texts carries the perspective, which the sentence, which neither; and where a perspective names a tradition, whether the model knows it or writes its cliché. The pictures are the simplification that makes the texts comparable at a glance, and material for the next step.

**S1 — Four writers, one perspective** (formal, art, grades 9–13, 90 min). Pairs choose one perspective from the arts or aesthetics group and run the example prompt under Open and Closed Weights; they print the four texts and mark in each what the prompt said, what the perspective asked for, and what the model added; then they name the aesthetic form each model chose (a platinum-palladium print, a watercolour, two 16 mm films) and judge which text they would call written through the perspective and which merely decorated. The pictures are compared last, for what of each form the image model kept. Sequence: 10 min choice; 15 min runs; 30 min marking and naming; 25 min judgement; 10 min pictures. Subject link: perspective and voice, paraphrase, style against manner. Uncertainty: the closed models are paid cloud services; a lesson needs the installation's keys.

**S2 — Does the model know the Bauhaus?** (formal, art, grades 10–13, 90 min). The class researches one tradition the arts group names (Bauhaus, the Literati painters, the Renaissance) from a textbook or a museum's page before the run, and writes down three things that belong to it and three that a cliché of it would add. Then the example prompt runs under that perspective on four models. The pairs read each text against their list: which model wrote the tradition's own forms and which wrote the cliché; the pictures show what of either reached the image model. The judgement rests on what the class knows about the tradition, and the model has no say in it. Sequence: 20 min research and lists; 15 min runs; 35 min reading; 20 min plenary. Subject link: art history, the cliché as a form; knowing a tradition as the basis of judgement. Uncertainty: not run; a lineup may be partly unavailable.

**S3 — Your own perspective** (formal, art or language teaching, grades 10–13, 2 × 45 min). Pairs write a perspective of their own with "Your Call!" from the freestyle group: a way of speaking they want, in their own words (a manner, a mood, a tradition they know). The example prompt runs under it on four models; the pairs read which model did what they meant, where the instruction was too vague to bind and where too narrow, and rewrite it; second run, same seed. The two runs are compared for what the rewriting of the instruction changed in four writers at once. Sequence: 15 min writing; 15 min run and reading; 15 min rewriting; 15 min second run; 30 min comparison. Subject link: writing an instruction for a way of speaking; the author of the rule. Uncertainty: I saw "Your Call!" in the chooser and did not run it.

**S4 — Who appears in the rewrite?** (formal, ethics or social studies, grades 10–13, 45 min). The class reads the note's figures (Fang et al.), then runs a prompt with people in it under "Sensitive" and "Forceful" and lists who the rewrites name, with what age, gender and work, across four models, and who disappears (the people were "soft vertical streaks" and a reserved sliver of paper). Subject link: representation in text, the note's own measure.

**S5 — Open against closed** (formal, social studies, grades 10–13, 45 min). One perspective, the two lineups; the class reads the four texts for register, length, medium and for what each set leaves out, and puts beside each row what the register says about the model (maker, country, year, size, open or closed weights). The question for the plenary is what the two kinds of model have in common in their writing and what separates them, and whether the difference lies with the makers or with the sizes. Subject link: who makes the models, open and closed weights. Uncertainty: the two open models wrote still media and the two closed models wrote film; four texts carry no generalisation.

**S6 — The lost run** (non-formal, maker space or teacher workshop, 30 min add-on). Participants run a series, and the facilitator shows what the cells say when a picture does not arrive and how to tell a queue from a lost run. Subject link: reading an instrument's error states. Uncertainty: cannot be staged on demand.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S6)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Create 2 Intermediate — "Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs." S1, S3 and S5: one idea under one perspective, four writing models and their pictures compared for how each interpreted it; the framework's classroom example compares how different prompts and tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: the marking separates in each text the prompt's share, the perspective's share and the model's addition, against the idea that the picture is made from the prompt as written; the printed and marked texts are the artefact.
- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." S2: the sentence "the model knows the Bauhaus" is tested against the class's own list of what belongs to the tradition and rewritten as what the model wrote and where it got it; the framework's classroom example has learners identify misleading phrases and develop better descriptions.
- Shape 2 Basic — "Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task." S2 and S3: what would count as written through the perspective is written down before the run (three things that belong, three that a cliché would add; what the pair meant by its instruction) and the four texts are compared against it; the framework's classroom example has learners define what would make the system successful before comparing its outputs.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S4: who the four rewrites name, with what age, gender and work, and who disappears, against the note's figures on seven models; the framework's classroom example explores how and why a system performs differently across demographics and discusses the impacts.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

--

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Create 2 example compares tools for varied interpretations and stops at the variety. Here the comparison is a judgement: whether a model carried a perspective, and whether it knows a tradition or writes its cliché, and that judgement rests on what the class knows about the Bauhaus or the Literati and on its ear for a manner against a decoration. The instrument puts the platform's own step, Prompt Interception, under observation and lets the pupils write the rule a model has to speak by (S3). The framework has no competence for knowing a tradition as the basis of judging a text, and none for authoring the way of speaking a model follows.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 1, 3, 4, Create 1, 3, 4.

instruments.name: Interception Scope

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/perspectives-on-a-template` (sidebar "Interception Scope", Prompt Interception Lab). Preparing column: Example prompts select with one entry ("A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen."), the prompt field (same placeholder as on Language Model Comparison), "Perspectives" with a round "+" button, "Image model" chips SD 3.5 Large 8.1B (selected), Flux 2 32B, Flux 3 Klein 5.6B, and a note "Interception Scope": De Rosa Palmini and Cetinic (2025) grouped prompts from a public image platform by shared wording, groups sharing 80 % or more of their words came with more uniform pictures than groups sharing 50 to 70 %, richer wording went with more varied pictures (Vendi score); in Stable Diffusion modifiers written against a stereotype often left it in place ("a white poor person" still mostly dark-skinned faces, "a photo of an African man and his fancy house" still a simple hut, Bianchi et al. 2023). Two references with arXiv numbers and DOI. Right: one large box "Reference image". The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "Prompt Interception is the step in which this platform writes a prompt over again through a perspective. Here that step runs several times on the same template, once per perspective, and one image model shows what each of them wrote. Write the template — or drag a picture onto the field, and its description then stands there as the template, where it can be worked on further. Choose the perspectives. Where the template was written, the first picture holds it with that step left out; where it was read from a picture, that picture stands first as the reference and the picture beside it is the first step, with no perspective on it; resting on a perspective — holding it, on a touch screen — shows the text that perspective wrote." "Every picture carries the same template, and between two of them the perspective is the only difference, so a picture can be read for what that one perspective does to the template. The writing model is the one this platform is set to intercept with, and this surface makes no choice about it. One image model runs, because what is compared here is perspectives — the comparison of image models is its own instrument." "This help can support you with the comparative analysis of the results. Just ask it about them." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Chose the example prompt. Pressed "+": the same round chooser as on Language Model Comparison (seven icon groups, 31 perspectives, listed in report 13). Picked "Sensitive" (attitudes); the chooser closed and a round bubble with an × appeared in the Perspectives row. Pressed "+" again and picked "Bauhaus" (arts). Two bubbles.
3. "Run the series". Three pictures arrived. Layout: the reference image large at the left, one box per perspective with the perspective's bubble and name as caption, "Interpretation help" at the top right.
4. Changed the perspective once: removed Bauhaus with its ×, pressed "+", picked "Daguerreotype" (technical imaging). Run the series: only the new box was computed; the reference and the Sensitive picture stayed as they were (same files).

Runs: 2 series, 4 pictures, 3 rewrites.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- "+": opens the chooser; several perspectives can be added, each as a bubble with × to remove.
- Image model chips: one model draws every box with the same seed (the server log shows one fixed seed).
- Run the series: rewrites the prompt once per perspective and draws reference and perspectives. The Help text says that resting on a perspective (holding it, on a touch screen) shows the text it wrote; I did not use that and read the rewrites in the server log.
- Changing the row recomputes only the added box.
- Interpretation help, Hide column: not used. Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Reference (SD 3.5 Large): a cream farmhouse with a red roof in a mown field under a wooded hill, cows, sheep, goats, three or four people.
- Sensitive: the rewrite (log) "This is a slow-cinema film: one uncut 16mm take of roughly four hours, projected as a loop onto a wa…"; the picture a close-up of a whitewashed wall with two windows behind a wire fence and wheat ears, a tree at the right, black film bars top and bottom; no person, no animal.
- Bauhaus: the rewrite "Settlement Unit Model No. 4: a site model on a square plywood base board, 80 × 80 cm, photographed f…"; the picture an architectural model seen from above, a white block house on a white board with tiny model trees, two cow figurines, one figure, a red bar and green strips, the board lying on real green and yellow fields.
- Daguerreotype: the rewrite "Black-and-white daguerreotype: a farmhouse standing in open country, ringed by tilled fields, hedger…"; the picture a grainy black-and-white plate with dark corners, a two-chimney stone house, cows at a fence, two children in a ploughed field.
- The three perspectives did three different things to the sentence: Sensitive removed the people and the overview and kept a wall; Bauhaus turned the scene into a model of itself; Daguerreotype kept the scene and changed the medium. The surface shows the pictures and the names; the sentence the model wrote in between is shown, as the Help text says, by resting on the perspective, which I did not do.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The rewritten prompt, the instrument's actual intervention, is shown only by resting on a perspective, as the Help text says; a user who has not read that sees a name and a picture.
- The chooser's groups are icons without names.
- During the first run the boxes stay empty until the reference arrives; no counter.
- The note's findings (uniform pictures, stereotypes that stay) are about other prompts and platforms; next to three pictures they read as this surface's result.
- The painting path (drag a work onto the field; it stands first as the reference, its description becomes the template) is the surface's richest use and is named only in the Help text and the field's placeholder; the one example prompt is a farm scene, and nothing on the surface shows a work.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says what Prompt Interception is, that the step runs here once per perspective on the same template with one image model, that the template is written or read from a picture, that the first picture holds the template with the step left out, that resting on a perspective shows the text it wrote, and that between two pictures the perspective is the only difference. What it should say first is what the instrument is for: getting to know what Prompt Interception does, by watching one source go through several perspectives and talking about the differences. It should say that a painting can be that source: dragged onto the field, it stands first on the wall as the reference, its description becomes the template and can be edited before the run, and each perspective then writes the painting over again in its own register, the text one rest away, the picture beside it. It should say that the Help has the pictures of the run and can be asked about two of them side by side, which its closing line says only in passing. And it should add that adding or removing a perspective recomputes only the changed box, and that the note on the left reports what research found about prompt wording and stereotypes in other settings, not what this run found.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Drag a painting from the public domain onto the template field (Caspar David Friedrich's "Wanderer above the Sea of Fog", 1818, from Wikimedia Commons), read the description it becomes, and correct by hand what the describer missed; then add Slang, On the Contrary!, Renaissance and Daguerreotype and run. Rest on each perspective, read what it wrote, and talk about what it kept of the painting and what it made of it.
- Run one whole group of perspectives on one work, the five of critical analysis (Against the Model, One World, Planetarizer, Critique of Consumption, The Unspoken), and say for each what it does to a Romantic landscape.
- Read the text before the picture: rest on the perspective first, say what it added that the template did not have, then look whether the picture shows it.
- Edit the template before the run: strike the fog, add a city, keep the perspectives, and see what each perspective does with the changed template.
- Ask the Help about two pictures side by side; it has the pictures of the run.
- Run the same perspectives once more under another image model (SD 3.5 Large, Flux 2, Flux 3 Klein) and see what the model changes and what the perspective keeps.
- Play it backwards: show one picture, let the others guess which perspective wrote it, then rest on it.
- Write a prompt against a stereotype (the note's Bianchi examples), add two perspectives, and check whether the stereotype stays.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument is for getting to know what Prompt Interception does: the same source goes through several perspectives, each writes it over again, one picture per perspective shows what it wrote, and the text itself is one rest away. The strongest source is a work everyone in the room can see: a painting dragged onto the field.

**S1 — Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, five times** (formal, art, grades 7–10, 90 min). The class drags a public-domain reproduction of Caspar David Friedrich's painting (1818) onto the template field. First talk: the description it becomes, read against the painting on the wall, what the describer saw and what it missed (the back turned to us, the fog, the rock), corrected by hand. Then five perspectives, one from each of five groups: Slang, On the Contrary!, Renaissance, Daguerreotype, Critique of Consumption; the choice itself is discussed (what might Slang do to a Romantic painting). Run. Wall: the painting as the reference, the picture without perspective, five pictures. Second talk, picture by picture: rest on the perspective, read its text aloud, then: what it kept of the painting, what it changed, where the wanderer now stands, in whose voice the text speaks. Closing: each pupil writes one sentence on what Prompt Interception is. Sequence: 10 min painting and description; 10 min choosing with reasons; 15 min run (used for the first talk); 40 min second talk with the texts; 15 min closing sentences read aloud. Subject link: image analysis, Romanticism, register and paraphrase; what an instruction does to a work. Uncertainty: not run; what the describer writes for a known painting was not seen; whether a painter's name written into the template passes the platform's checks I did not test.

**S2 — The sentence in between** (formal, language teaching or media, grades 9–12, 45 min, after S1 or with its wall). Pupils see the painting and one perspective's picture and write the text they think that perspective wrote; then they rest on the perspective, read the real one, and mark what they guessed right and what the perspective did that they did not expect. Subject link: inference from output to instruction; register. Uncertainty: I did not rest on a perspective; the Help text says the rewrite is shown that way.

**S3 — Own work, two groups of perspectives** (non-formal, art workshop, age 14+, 2 h). Participants bring one work of their own (a drawing, a painting, a photograph of an object) and drag it onto the field; they run the whole arts group (Bauhaus, Literati, Renaissance) and the whole attitudes group (Forceful, mad world, Sensitive) on it; two rows on the wall. Talk: which perspectives change the medium, which the stance, which the content; one sentence per perspective, "this perspective does … to a picture"; and whose work the Renaissance version of a drawing is. Sequence: 20 min works and descriptions; 40 min two runs; 45 min talk and sentences; 15 min round. Subject link: own work under a foreign register; authorship. Uncertainty: not run.

**S4 — Writing a perspective** (formal, language teaching, grades 9–13, 2 × 45 min). After S1, groups write a perspective of their own under Your Call! in the chooser, in their own words (a stance, a genre, a way of seeing), run it on the painting next to one platform perspective, read the two texts, and revise their wording once. Subject link: writing an instruction, revision. Uncertainty: I did not test whether Your Call! opens a text field on this surface; the chooser is the same as on Flow, where the page's strings describe writing and saving a perspective.

**S5 — Does the modifier work?** (non-formal, media workshop, 2 h, age 14+). Participants read the note's Bianchi example, write a prompt that works against a stereotype, add two perspectives, and check whether the stereotype stays in the picture. Subject link: stereotypes and prompt wording.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S5)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: the closing sentence of each pupil on what Prompt Interception is, written after the texts the perspectives wrote were read aloud; S2: the text a pupil expects, then the real one. The misconception met is that the picture is made from the painting; what the image model receives is the perspective's text.
- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." S1: the description the painting becomes is read first for what the describer saw and what it missed; what the painting means, the class brings.
- Create 2 Intermediate — "Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs." S1 and S3: one template, five or six perspectives, one wall; the framework's classroom example compares how different prompts produce varied interpretations of the same idea, and here the different prompts are the perspectives' texts, readable one rest away.
- Create 1 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI-generated suggestions to their own ideas during a brainstorming process." S2: the text a pupil writes for a perspective, then the perspective's own; S4: the own perspective next to a platform perspective on the same painting.
- Create 3 Intermediate — "Learners refine their work through iterative exchanges with AI, comparing those outputs to their own ideas to determine what serves their goals." S4: the own perspective run, its text read against the platform perspective's, the wording revised once.
- Create 4 Basic — "Learners know that AI-generated content may reuse or copy work protected by intellectual property or copyright laws and recognise implications for the humans who created the original work." S3: a participant's own drawing under Renaissance or Bauhaus, and the question whose work the result is; S1 uses a painting in the public domain for that reason.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S5: a prompt written against a stereotype, and the check whether the stereotype stays in the picture under two perspectives; the note's Bianchi examples are the finding the group tests.
- Shape 2 Intermediate — "Learners assess an AI system performance of a task using defined criteria and feedback from human reviews or benchmark tests." S5: the stereotype in or out of the picture as the defined criterion, per perspective; S3: the sentence per perspective (medium, stance or content) as the group's own review of what each one did.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Shape 1 Intermediate — "Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool." Modification: the tool described is one step of the platform, Prompt Interception, rather than a tool among several; S1's closing sentences name its task (write the template over again through a perspective), its input (the template) and its outputs (the text, the picture), as the framework's classroom example has learners do per tool. Intended users are not on the surface.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Create 1 has AI expand an idea, and its Engage 2 examples have learners explain how a tool works. Here the intervention itself is on the surface: a painting from 1818 is written over again in five registers, each text is one rest away from its picture, and the class talks about each. The framework has no competence for reading what an instruction does to a work; Prompt Interception is this platform's central step, and this is the surface made to show it.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 3, 4.
