instruments.name: Aesthetic Poles

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/aesthetic-poles` (sidebar "Aesthetic Poles", Prompt Interception Lab). Preparing column: Example prompts select with one entry (the house-in-a-landscape sentence), the prompt field; "Properties": five chips with quotation marks in their labels, “best”, “better”, “neutral” (selected), “worse”, “worst”, then ten bars with a word at the right end: Object pairing (3 positions: coordinated / ordinary / uncoordinated), Richness (5: very rich … ordinary … empty), Background (4: beautiful … no background), Clarity (5: very clear … ordinary … completely blurry), Color Brightness (3: bright / ordinary / dark), Color Aesthetic (3: beautiful colors / ordinary colors / ugly colors), Lighting Distinction (4: very distinct … no lighting), Detail realism (5: realistic … neutral … greatly unrealistic), Detail refinement (7: very refined … ordinary … fragmented), Emotion (5: very positive … ordinary … very negative); "Image model" chips (SD 1.5, SDXL, CommonCanvas XL C, SD 3.5 Large (selected), Flux 2, Flux 3 Klein, Gemini 3 Pro (€)); a note "Aesthetic Poles": the framework VisionReward (Xu et al. 2024) with its ordered rater options ("for Clarity: very clear, clear, ordinary, blurry, completely blurry"), "Which end of a list counts as the bad one is built into the measurement", and "A model trained on such judgements can carry the scale as a norm (Guo et al. 2025)"; two references with arXiv numbers and DOI. Right: one box "Reference image". The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "One aesthetic checklist, set property by property, and what a model writes from it and the template. Write the template — or drag a picture onto the field, and its description then stands there as the template. Every property that can carry a handle is a scale of words with one handle on it; a property left at its neutral word stays out of the prompt. Five chips over the bars set the whole checklist at once, and from there each property is moved on its own. One setting is one prompt. Every run adds a row, and the first row stays: the checklist at its neutral word throughout, which every picture beside it is read against. Where the template was read from a picture, that picture stands first as the reference, and the picture beside it is the first step, with no setting on it. One image model runs, so what parts two pictures is the setting. Resting on a picture's name — holding it — shows what was set and what the model wrote from it." "The properties come from the human labelling guidelines of VisionReward, where each of them carries one ordered list of words with one of those words marked as the neutral one. Those guidelines give one position on such a list, which is why there is one handle here. The lists are of different lengths and reach different distances to either side, so each property is set on its own rather than by one axis over all of them, and a setting is free to stand at the good end of one property and at the bad end of the next. Every row is written by the same model from the same template, so what stands between two rows is the setting, and the pictures show what the checklist does to a template." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Chose the example prompt. Pressed two chips to see what they do: “best” put all ten bars at their left end (coordinated, very rich, beautiful, very clear, bright, beautiful colors, very distinct, realistic, very refined, very positive); “worst” put all ten at their right end (uncoordinated, empty, no background, completely blurry, dark, ugly colors, no lighting, greatly unrealistic, fragmented, very negative). Back to “neutral” (all "ordinary", Detail realism "neutral").
3. Moved two bars notably: Clarity to the left end ("very clear") and Emotion to the right end ("very negative"). Image model SD 3.5 Large. "Run the series" (play triangle) at 22:41.
4. Server log: the properties were turned into prompt text by a language model twice (Claude Opus 5.5 over OpenRouter, about 1850 characters each): "A plain color photograph, taken with an ordinary digital camera or a phone at eye level from the edg…" and "A large-format color photograph, shot on an 8x10 view camera at f/45, renders a single farmhouse wit…". The Help text says that resting on a picture's name shows what was set and what the model wrote from it; I did not use that and read the texts in the server log. Two pictures, "Reference image" and "Run 1", arrived, with "Interpretation help" at the top right.

Runs: 1 series, 2 pictures, 2 rewrites.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Property chips: set all ten bars to one pole at once; “neutral” resets to "ordinary".
- Bars: each is a scale with named steps; the word at the right end names the current step; the number of steps differs per property (3 to 7).
- Image model chips: the model that draws both pictures.
- Run the series: writes a prompt from the bar settings, draws the reference (the "ordinary" setting) and the run; the written prompt is shown by resting on the picture's name (Help text), which I did not do.
- Interpretation help, Hide column: not used. Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Reference image: a white two-storey house with a slate roof at the end of a gravel track under a flat grey sky, a woman in a grey coat with a green bucket and a small child in a red jacket on the track, two chickens, two cows in a stubble field, a satellite dish; a plain snapshot, as the rewrite's "ordinary digital camera or a phone" says.
- Run 1 ("very clear", "very negative"): a wide harvested field in hard sunlight filling three quarters of the frame, a run-down farmhouse with a patched roof far back, an old man and a child with a green basket, two brown cows, and, dumped in the field, a cardboard box, a blue tarpaulin and a white sack. Everything sharp to the horizon; the scene reads as bleak. The rewrite's "8x10 view camera at f/45" is the clarity; the rubbish and the ruin are the emotion.
- The pair shows what two words did: the clarity setting changed the camera, the emotion setting changed what is in the picture (rubbish, decay, distance between the people). The Help text says that a model writes the prompt from the checklist and the template; what it wrote for "very negative" is shown by resting on the picture's name.
- The note's point that the scale carries a norm is visible in the labels: the left end of every bar is the VisionReward "good" end.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The chips look like a rating of the picture; the Help text says they set the whole checklist at once.
- The bar words only appear at the right end; the other positions are unnamed until the bar is moved.
- The prompt written from the bars is shown only by resting on the picture's name, as the Help text says; a user who has not read that cannot see why "very negative" became rubbish in a field.
- No counter while the pictures compute; the box stays empty.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that the checklist is set property by property, that a property left at its neutral word stays out of the prompt, that the chips set the whole checklist at once, that one setting is one prompt, that the first row stays at the neutral word as what every picture is read against, that resting on a picture's name shows what was set and what the model wrote, and where the properties come from. It should add: a bar shows only its current word, at the right end; no counter shows while the pictures compute; the left end of every bar is the end the framework's raters were told to prefer, and the surface lets you draw the other end.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Set everything to “best” and then to “worst” and compare the two pictures with the reference: what does the model think a bad picture is?
- Move one bar at a time to its far end and keep the rest ordinary; collect ten pictures, one per property.
- Set "very clear" and "very negative" (or the reverse) and discuss whether a sharp picture can be sad.
- Run the same bar settings on SD 3.5 Large and Flux 3 Klein and see whether both models have the same idea of "ugly colors".

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — What is a good picture?** (formal, art, grades 8–11, 90 min). Pairs run “best”, “neutral” and “worst” on one prompt and write down what changed in each picture; then they read the note and discuss who decided which end is "best". Sequence: 10 min; 20 min runs; 30 min description; 30 min reading the note and discussion. Subject link: taste, norm, judgement.

**S2 — One property at a time** (formal, media or computer science, grades 10–13, 2 × 45 min). Groups each take one property, run its two ends, and present the pair; the class builds a table of what each scale changed (camera, light, objects, people). Subject link: operationalisation of aesthetic terms.

**S3 — The sentence in between** (non-formal, media workshop, 90 min). Participants guess from a picture which bars were moved, then rest on the picture's name and compare their guess with the setting and with the prompt the language model wrote from it. Subject link: chains of models. Uncertainty: I did not rest on a picture's name; the Help text says the setting and the written prompt are shown that way.

**S4 — Who lives at the worst end?** (formal, ethics or art, grades 9–12, 90 min). Pairs write a prompt that names people and a place ("a family in front of their house", "people at a bus stop") and run it at “best” and at “worst” with the same model; for the two pictures they fill a table: who is shown (age, clothing, posture), where (the state of the house, the street, the ground), what lies about. Then they read in the note where the properties come from and discuss which people and places the scale's “good” end keeps out of the picture and which it puts at the “worst” end. In my run two bars alone (“very clear”, “very negative”) turned the ordinary house into a run-down farmhouse with rubbish in the field and the woman with the bucket into an old man. Sequence: 10 min prompts; 20 min two runs; 30 min table; 30 min note and discussion. Subject link: norm, representation, who is pictured as “bad”. instruments.name: Denoising Archaeology

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/denoising-archaeology` (sidebar "Denoising Archaeology", Diffusion Lab). Left: Example prompts select with 14 entries (the house-in-a-landscape sentence; the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal; a person in typical clothing; a walk in the forest, in the afternoon; a walk in the forest, seen through the eyes of a child; friendship; loneliness; a family at dinner; a street in the evening; a nurse at work; a plumber at work; a crowded place, completely empty; a house), the prompt field with its five buttons; "DENOISING — Backbone (the net that removes the noise)" with two chips, SDXL (2023) U-Net and SD 3.5 (2024) MMDiT (selected); "Advanced settings", collapsed (it holds a negative-prompt field, Denoising steps 25 (10–50), CFG 4.5 (1–20), Seed 123456789 and a checkbox); a note "Denoising Archaeology": "An image generator builds a picture up out of noise, in steps. Choi et al. (2022) derive from their measurements that coarse features are settled at high noise, the content in the middle, details below the threshold of perception at the end. They measured it by noise level. As a place in the run, this division is a rough orientation." and two sentences on U-Net cross-attention versus MMDiT joint attention (Esser et al. 2024); three references (Choi 2022, Ho 2020, Esser 2024). Header: the play triangle ("Generate") and an "Outputs" button. Bottom: a "RUNS" strip. The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "An image generator starts from pure random noise, a flicker with no object in it, and removes that noise step by step, preset at 25, until a scene is left. The platform holds every single one of those steps; the slider in the left column picks which of them fills the view. Two nets stand at the Backbone to choose from, SDXL (2023) and SD 3.5 (2024), and every run stays under "Runs"." "The model works on the whole picture at once, step by step. Go back and forth along the slider and watch for the step from which the scene is recognisable. That point shifts with the prompt and with the model; for that, compare two runs with the same prompt." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Chose the example prompt, kept SD 3.5 MMDiT and 25 steps, pressed Generate. Server log: backbone sd35, checkpoint sd3.5_large, sampler euler/normal, steps 25, seed 123456789. I could not watch the 25 steps build up: when I first looked, all steps were there and the picture area showed "Step 1 / 25" with a slider "Denoising steps" marked 1, 6, 11, 16, 21 and three labels under it, Composition, Semantics, Detail. The RUNS strip got one entry, a thumbnail of the finished picture labelled "SD 3.5 (2024) · Steps 25 · CFG 4…" with an ×.
3. Scrubbed the slider back and forth: to the end (the caption disappears and the finished picture shows), to step 13, step 4, step 21, step 2, step 7, and stopped at step 4 (an early step).
4. Pressed "Outputs": a drawer opened over the lower half with the RUNS strip and the thumbnail; pressed again to close.

Runs: 1 generation, 25 steps.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Prompt select and field as elsewhere; the Translate button is disabled while the field is empty.
- Backbone chips: U-Net (SDXL) or MMDiT (SD 3.5); only MMDiT used.
- Advanced settings: steps, CFG, seed, negative prompt; left at defaults.
- Generate: one run; the picture area then shows one step at a time.
- Slider: picks the step shown; the caption "Step n / 25" sits on the picture; at the right end the caption goes and the final picture shows.
- Outputs: a drawer with the run list; × on a run removes it (not pressed).
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Steps 2, 4, 7 and 13: a field of coloured speckle with no structure the eye can read; step 13 is slightly greener and smoother than step 2, nothing more. Step 21: the house, the big tree, the cows and two people are there in rough blocks under a heavy grain. Final: a clean, photograph-like picture: a cream house with blue shutters and a chimney, a large tree against it, five or six cows, a child in pink and a man in blue in a green meadow under a rising green field.
- On this run the first structure visible to the eye appeared between step 13 and step 21, i.e. under the slider's "Detail" label; under "Composition" (steps 1–8) and "Semantics" (9–16) the previews show noise. The surface does not say what the frame is. The platform's own node code does: each frame is the working latent at that step, still noisy, decoded to a picture; the net's prediction of the finished picture at that step, which the ComfyUI live preview shows, is not shown here. So the note's "coarse features settled at high noise" is about what the net predicts, and not what the eye sees in these frames.
- The slider is the instrument, the generation is not.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The picture area shows "Step 1 / 25" after the run, i.e. noise; a user may think the run failed.
- Twenty of the 25 steps look alike (noise); the three labels promise composition and content where nothing can be seen.
- The caption disappears at the last position; "Step 25" is never written.
- The run list is at the bottom and in a drawer; the Help text says every run stays under "Runs", and the Outputs button carries no label apart from its title.
- Advanced settings are collapsed with no hint of what is inside; the seed is fixed, so two runs with the same prompt give the same picture.
- A single step can be enlarged by clicking the picture, and the enlarged frame carries "Step n / 25" and "Download Image"; nothing on the picture says so (from the page's code; not clicked).

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that the generator starts from noise and removes it step by step, preset at 25, that the platform holds every step and the slider picks the one in view, that two nets stand at the Backbone, that every run stays under "Runs", and to watch for the step from which the scene is recognisable and to compare two runs with the same prompt. It should say what the instrument is for: understanding what denoising is, as something the eye does and as something painters have done, and taking the mystery out of image generation by showing the whole run. It should say what the frame is: the noisy state of the run at that step, and not what the net at that step predicts the finished picture to be. The platform's code records the working latent; the live preview of ComfyUI, the engine underneath, shows the prediction instead, and the platform's own source check of 2026-08-13 names the difference as a didactic one that the surface leaves out. A frame that is noise to the eye is a frame from which the net already computes a whole picture; the first readable shape comes later for the eye than the three labels suggest, and the labels are the orientation from Choi et al. (2022) by noise level. It should say that a step can be enlarged by clicking the picture and saved with "Download Image", which makes one step a sheet to draw on. It should say that the surface shows one frame and no strip of thumbnails on purpose; the platform's decision of 2026-08-19 reads "Thumbnails take away the experience of imagining the next denoising step." And it should add: the view starts at step 1, which is noise; the seed is fixed in the advanced settings, so the same prompt gives the same run until the seed is changed, and two prompts under the same seed start from the same noise.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Understanding what "denoising" means, persceptively and aesthetically. De-mystifying Denoising genAI.
- Generate once and find the first step at which you can name an object; write the step number down and compare with a neighbour's prompt.
- Click the picture at step 21, save it with "Download Image", print it, and draw the scene the prompt names along the noise pattern; then put the drawing next to the net's final picture: two readings of the same noise, one by an eye and a hand, one by a net that predicts a whole picture at every step.
- Do the painters' exercise with the model's material: Leonardo advised looking at stained walls to find landscapes and figures in them, and Alexander Cozens published in 1785 a method of composing landscapes from ink blots. A step-7 frame is such a blot; draw from it, then scrub forward and see what the net made of the same frame.
- Run two prompts under the same seed and scrub both from step 1: find the first step at which the eye can tell the two runs apart, and the step at which each becomes a scene.
- Change the seed in the advanced settings, keep the prompt, and see what the noise decides: where the house stands, where the tree.
- Run the same prompt on U-Net and MMDiT and compare at which step each shows structure.
- Change the step count to 10 and to 50 and compare the final pictures and the step at which the house appears.
- Use the slider as a slow reveal: show step 21 and ask what the picture will be.
- Take the words on the surface one by one, Denoising, Backbone, U-Net, MMDiT, cross-attention, joint attention, Steps, CFG, Seed, Negative Prompt, Composition, Semantics, Detail, and for each move the control that carries it and watch what changes; write what each word names in your own sentence.
- Collect how the room talks about image AI before the run ("it paints", "it searches for pictures and puts them together", "it knows what a house looks like"), scrub one run together, and rewrite every phrase in words that name what was seen.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument shows one generation as 25 frames, each the noisy state of the run at that step, one at a time, so that the next step has to be imagined. It is for understanding what denoising is, with the eye and the hand as much as with the slider, and for taking the mystery out of the generator: no picture is fetched, nothing is painted stroke by stroke, the whole frame changes at every step, and the picture is not there until the end.

**S1 — When does the house appear?** (formal, computer science or art, grades 8–11, 45 min). Pairs generate one prompt each, scrub, and note the first step with a readable shape; the class collects the numbers on the board and compares with the slider's three labels. Sequence: 5 min prompt; 5 min run; 15 min scrubbing; 20 min collection on the board, one sentence per pair on what the slider did between step 0 and their number, and reading of the note. Subject link: iterative processes, noise.

**S2 — Two nets, and the words on the surface** (formal, computer science, grades 11–13, 90 min). Groups run the same prompt on both backbones, read the note's two sentences on cross-attention and joint attention, and present the step at which each net shows structure, in sentences that name steps, noise and the net, and not seeing, knowing or wanting. Then the class reads the surface's own words, "Watch the model work", "Backbone (the net that removes the noise)", "Archaeology", and the three labels Composition, Semantics, Detail, and says of each whether it names a process or makes the net sound like someone at work, and what each does to the trust a newcomer puts in the picture. Sequence: 15 min two runs; 25 min reading the note and scrubbing; 25 min presentations; 25 min the words on the surface. Subject link: architecture, attention; language about machines.

**S3 — The reveal** (non-formal, family workshop, 30 min). The facilitator shows step 21 of a run and the group guesses the prompt; then the final picture. Subject link: perception, how little is needed to recognise a scene.

**S4 — The Human Denoiser** (non-formal, family workshop, 30 min). The facilitator shows step 21 of a run and makes a printout. The print is used as a template to draw a picture according to the prompt along the noise pattern. Subject link: perception, imagination.

**S5 — Blot, wall, step** (formal, art, grades 7–10, 90 min). First the painters: the teacher reads Leonardo's advice to look at stained walls for landscapes and figures, and shows one of Alexander Cozens's blots (1785) with the landscape he drew from it. Pupils make an ink blot and draw a landscape from it. Then the model's material: a printed step-7 frame of a run whose prompt they know, and the task of S4, the prompt's scene drawn along the noise. Then the comparison: the drawing next to step 21 and the final picture of the same run. Where did the pupil put the house, where did the net; what in the noise did each take for a shape; what did the net settle first (the big masses, the division of the frame) and what last. Closing talk: the eye finds figures in noise, painters have used this on purpose for five hundred years, and the net does something else with the same noise: it computes, at every step, a prediction of the whole picture, in numbers, without an eye. Sequence: 15 min Leonardo and Cozens; 20 min blots; 25 min step-7 drawings; 20 min comparison; 10 min closing talk. Subject link: perception, imagination, chance as a method in art (Leonardo, Cozens, Max Ernst's frottage of 1925). Uncertainty: I did not try saving a frame; the enlarged frame's bar carries "Download Image" in the page's strings.

**S6 — Same noise, two prompts** (formal, computer science or art, grades 8–11, 45 min). The seed stays as it is. Pairs run two prompts, say a house in a landscape and a street in the evening, scrub both from step 1 side by side, and find the first step at which the eye can tell the two runs apart, and then the step at which each becomes its scene. One sentence per pair on what the prompt did to the same noise. Sequence: 5 min prompts; 10 min two runs; 20 min scrubbing in parallel; 10 min sentences on the board. Subject link: randomness and instruction, what a prompt does. Uncertainty: not run; that two prompts under one seed start from the same noise is how the platform's generator works and was not compared frame by frame here.

**S7 — How we talk about it** (formal, any subject, grades 7–10, 90 min). Before the run the teacher collects on the board how the class talks about image AI: "it paints", "it searches for pictures and puts them together", "it knows what a house looks like", "it sees the picture before it is finished". One run, scrubbed together on the projector from step 1 to the end. Each phrase is held against the 25 frames: which ones are misleading, and why; each is rewritten in words that name what was seen (noise, steps, the whole frame changing at once, a picture that was not there until late). Then pairs save the frames of steps 1, 7, 13 and 21 and the final picture, print them, and make a poster for the corridor: five frames, one rewritten sentence each, and the title of the myth it answers. Sequence: 10 min phrases; 25 min run and scrubbing with the phrases; 20 min rewriting; 35 min posters. Subject link: language about machines, description. Uncertainty: I did not try saving a frame.

**S8 — The words on the surface** (formal, computer science or art, grades 9–12, 90 min). The surface is full of terms, and each one stands next to the control that carries it. The class lists them: Denoising, Backbone, U-Net, MMDiT, cross-attention and joint attention (in the note), Steps, CFG, Seed, Negative Prompt, Random variation, and the three labels Composition, Semantics, Detail. Pairs take two terms each, move the control (Steps 10 and 50, CFG 1 and 20, a changed seed, a negative prompt, the other backbone), scrub the run, and write one sentence per term that names what the control did to the run, in their own words and without a human trait; for U-Net and MMDiT the sentence comes from the note's two sentences and from the two runs. The sentences are read aloud and tested by another pair against the surface; a sentence that cannot be checked there is rewritten. Then the class reads what the platform says the Latent Lab is for, in the Help's description of the lab, and writes the first line of the glossary: what this instrument does, for whom, and what it cannot do (one picture per run, 10 to 50 steps, two nets). Sequence: 10 min list; 30 min controls and runs; 20 min sentences; 15 min testing; 15 min the first line. Subject link: the vocabulary of generative AI, learned from the control that carries each word; description. Uncertainty: I did not change CFG and the negative prompt, and the Help's description of the lab was not opened on this surface.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S8)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." S7: the phrases on the board ("it paints", "it knows what a house looks like"), the judgement which are misleading and why, and the rewriting after the scrub, as the framework's classroom example has it; S2: the same judgement on the surface's own words.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S7: the myth "it searches for pictures and puts them together" answered with a poster of five frames and five sentences, the framework's classroom example's artefact; S1: the pairs' one sentence on what the slider did between step 0 and their number; S8: the glossary, one checked sentence per term on the surface.
- Engage 2 Advanced — "Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding." S2: two nets on the same prompt, the step at which each shows structure explained in sentences that name process and not seeing or knowing, and the surface's own words ("Watch the model work", the three labels) read as design features that shape what a newcomer takes the net to be and trusts it with; the framework's classroom example has learners compare design choices that make systems appear human-like and reflect on trust; S8: U-Net against MMDiT and cross-attention against joint attention in the pupils' own sentences, tested against the surface.
- Shape 1 Intermediate — "Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool." S8: the glossary's first line names what the instrument does, for whom (read from the platform's description of the Latent Lab in the Help) and what it cannot do, and the sentences per term name the inputs (prompt, negative prompt, seed, steps, CFG, backbone) and how the output comes about; the framework's classroom example has learners identify a tool's primary task and explain what input it uses and how the outputs execute the task.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

--

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's knowledge statement 1.3 says generative AI "uses probabilities to generate advanced outputs", and its Engage 2 has learners explain the process in words and on posters. Here the process itself is the material: the run stands as 25 frames, one at a time, and the platform's decision of 2026-08-19 reads "Thumbnails take away the experience of imagining the next denoising step." S4 and S5 put the learner's own perception next to the net's prediction on the same noise, a printed frame drawn over by hand, and read denoising as something the eye does and as a method painters have used since Leonardo. The framework has no competence for perception or for the history of art; this instrument is built for both.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 2, 3, 4, Create 1–4.

scenarios.sequence: 15 min two runs; 25 min reading the note and scrubbing; 25 min presentations; 25 min the words on the surface.
scenarios.subject_link: architecture, attention; language about machines.

scenarios.title: The reveal
scenarios.setting: non-formal, family workshop, 30 min
scenarios.text: The facilitator shows step 21 of a run and the group guesses the prompt; then the final picture.
scenarios.subject_link: perception, how little is needed to recognise a scene.

scenarios.title: The Human Denoiser
scenarios.setting: non-formal, family workshop, 30 min
scenarios.text: The facilitator shows step 21 of a run and makes a printout. The print is used as a template to draw a picture according to the prompt along the noise pattern.
scenarios.subject_link: perception, imagination.

scenarios.title: Blot, wall, step
scenarios.setting: formal, art, grades 7–10, 90 min
scenarios.text: First the painters: the teacher reads Leonardo's advice to look at stained walls for landscapes and figures, and shows one of Alexander Cozens's blots (1785) with the landscape he drew from it. Pupils make an ink blot and draw a landscape from it. Then the model's material: a printed step-7 frame of a run whose prompt they know, and the task of S4, the prompt's scene drawn along the noise. Then the comparison: the drawing next to step 21 and the final picture of the same run. Where did the pupil put the house, where did the net; what in the noise did each take for a shape; what did the net settle first (the big masses, the division of the frame) and what last. Closing talk: the eye finds figures in noise, painters have used this on purpose for five hundred years, and the net does something else with the same noise: it computes, at every step, a prediction of the whole picture, in numbers, without an eye.
scenarios.sequence: 15 min Leonardo and Cozens; 20 min blots; 25 min step-7 drawings; 20 min comparison; 10 min closing talk.
scenarios.subject_link: perception, imagination, chance as a method in art (Leonardo, Cozens, Max Ernst's frottage of 1925).
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not try saving a frame; the enlarged frame's bar carries "Download Image" in the page's strings.

scenarios.title: Same noise, two prompts
scenarios.setting: formal, computer science or art, grades 8–11, 45 min
scenarios.text: The seed stays as it is. Pairs run two prompts, say a house in a landscape and a street in the evening, scrub both from step 1 side by side, and find the first step at which the eye can tell the two runs apart, and then the step at which each becomes its scene. One sentence per pair on what the prompt did to the same noise.
scenarios.sequence: 5 min prompts; 10 min two runs; 20 min scrubbing in parallel; 10 min sentences on the board.
scenarios.subject_link: randomness and instruction, what a prompt does.
scenarios.uncertainty: not run; that two prompts under one seed start from the same noise is how the platform's generator works and was not compared frame by frame here.

scenarios.title: How we talk about it
scenarios.setting: formal, any subject, grades 7–10, 90 min
scenarios.text: Before the run the teacher collects on the board how the class talks about image AI: "it paints", "it searches for pictures and puts them together", "it knows what a house looks like", "it sees the picture before it is finished". One run, scrubbed together on the projector from step 1 to the end. Each phrase is held against the 25 frames: which ones are misleading, and why; each is rewritten in words that name what was seen (noise, steps, the whole frame changing at once, a picture that was not there until late). Then pairs save the frames of steps 1, 7, 13 and 21 and the final picture, print them, and make a poster for the corridor: five frames, one rewritten sentence each, and the title of the myth it answers.
scenarios.sequence: 10 min phrases; 25 min run and scrubbing with the phrases; 20 min rewriting; 35 min posters.
scenarios.subject_link: language about machines, description.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not try saving a frame.

scenarios.title: The words on the surface
scenarios.setting: formal, computer science or art, grades 9–12, 90 min
scenarios.text: The surface is full of terms, and each one stands next to the control that carries it. The class lists them: Denoising, Backbone, U-Net, MMDiT, cross-attention and joint attention (in the note), Steps, CFG, Seed, Negative Prompt, Random variation, and the three labels Composition, Semantics, Detail. Pairs take two terms each, move the control (Steps 10 and 50, CFG 1 and 20, a changed seed, a negative prompt, the other backbone), scrub the run, and write one sentence per term that names what the control did to the run, in their own words and without a human trait; for U-Net and MMDiT the sentence comes from the note's two sentences and from the two runs. The sentences are read aloud and tested by another pair against the surface; a sentence that cannot be checked there is rewritten. Then the class reads what the platform says the Latent Lab is for, in the Help's description of the lab, and writes the first line of the glossary: what this instrument does, for whom, and what it cannot do (one picture per run, 10 to 50 steps, two nets).
scenarios.sequence: 10 min list; 30 min controls and runs; 20 min sentences; 15 min testing; 15 min the first line.
scenarios.subject_link: the vocabulary of generative AI, learned from the control that carries each word; description.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not change CFG and the negative prompt, and the Help's description of the lab was not opened on this surface.

a.expectation: Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding.
a.text: S7: the phrases on the board ("it paints", "it knows what a house looks like"), the judgement which are misleading and why, and the rewriting after the scrub, as the framework's classroom example has it; S2: the same judgement on the surface's own words.

a.expectation: Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works.
a.text: S7: the myth "it searches for pictures and puts them together" answered with a poster of five frames and five sentences, the framework's classroom example's artefact; S1: the pairs' one sentence on what the slider did between step 0 and their number; S8: the glossary, one checked sentence per term on the surface.

a.expectation: Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding.
a.text: S2: two nets on the same prompt, the step at which each shows structure explained in sentences that name process and not seeing or knowing, and the surface's own words ("Watch the model work", the three labels) read as design features that shape what a newcomer takes the net to be and trusts it with; the framework's classroom example has learners compare design choices that make systems appear human-like and reflect on trust; S8: U-Net against MMDiT and cross-attention against joint attention in the pupils' own sentences, tested against the surface.

a.expectation: Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool.
a.text: S8: the glossary's first line names what the instrument does, for whom (read from the platform's description of the Latent Lab in the Help) and what it cannot do, and the sentences per term name the inputs (prompt, negative prompt, seed, steps, CFG, backbone) and how the output comes about; the framework's classroom example has learners identify a tool's primary task and explain what input it uses and how the outputs execute the task.

mapping.beyond: the framework's knowledge statement 1.3 says generative AI "uses probabilities to generate advanced outputs", and its Engage 2 has learners explain the process in words and on posters. Here the process itself is the material: the run stands as 25 frames, one at a time, and the platform's decision of 2026-08-19 reads "Thumbnails take away the experience of imagining the next denoising step." S4 and S5 put the learner's own perception next to the net's prediction on the same noise, a printed frame drawn over by hand, and read denoising as something the eye does and as a method painters have used since Leonardo. The framework has no competence for perception or for the history of art; this instrument is built for both.

instruments.name: Mean Images

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/mean-images`. Preparing column: an Example prompts select (two entries: the house in a landscape; "the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal"), the prompt field with its five small buttons, "Images per cell" with a slider at 5 (range 2–50, marks 2/10/20/30/40/50), "Rows · models" chips (SD 3.5 Large Turbo preselected; CommonCanvas XL C, Flux 3 Klein, SD 3.5 Large, Flux 2), "View" chips Contact sheet / Mean (preselected) / Relief, "Advanced settings" (Seed 424242, "Random variation"), and a note "Mean Images" quoting Hito Steyerl (2025, Medium Hot, pp. 72 and 78): the pictures an AI model generates are ‘mean images’, ‘a rendition of correlated averages’; ‘“Mean” may refer to minor or shabby origins, to the norm, to the stingy or to nastiness’; ‘statistics are integrated directly into an object’s likeness, through determinations of likelinesses’; then "On this page, you apply the mean method back on (or against) generative AI models…". Right: one row "SD 3.5 Large Turbo" with two empty cells headed "Seed fixed · 5 prompt variants" and "Prompt fixed · 5 random seeds". The run button is the play triangle. The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "The instrument generates many images from one prompt and averages them into one mean image, per AI model. Two means are computed per model. The first is the mean of the images generated from English variants of the prompt, which a language model writes with the same content in other words, as many as the setting ‘Images per cell’ says. The second is the mean of the images generated from the prompt as entered on randomly varied starting seeds. The models are selectable, one row each; both columns always stand. A switch in the left column shows the single images as a contact sheet, or a relief of the mean, instead. For the two SD 3.5 models the mean is taken before the decoder: the latents of the pictures are averaged and decoded once. The other models are averaged pixel by pixel, and each row says which." "This page applies the artist Hito Steyerl’s ‘mean images’ as a method against generative AI models. The mean of many images, generated from rewordings of one prompt or from one prompt on different seeds, can be compared across AI models. The comparison serves the exploration of visual clichés, prejudices and other forms of the statistical production of ‘normality’." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Chose the example prompt "A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen.", left 5 per cell, pressed run at 22:52:58. The header counted "Image n / 9" and named the weight file "sd3.5_large_turbo.safetensors · local". The cells went from "waiting" to a percentage to "done · latent mean". Server log: a language model was asked for four rewordings of the prompt and returned four distinct ones. While the row was still running, the finished Seed-fixed cell showed a purple/green/yellow noise picture with a faint house under a "100 %" bar; when the row finished, the decoded mean replaced it.
3. Looked at the three views of both cells (Contact sheet, Mean, Relief) and opened the lightbox of a cell in each view by clicking the cell.
4. Expanded "Generated prompt variants" and "Advanced settings".

Runs: 1 series: 9 pictures, 2 latent means.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Example prompts, prompt field, Copy / Paste / Choose Perspective / Translate to English / Delete: as on the other picture surfaces.
- Images per cell: sets n for both cells.
- Rows · models: multi-select; each selected model is one row with the two cells.
- View chips: switch all cells at once. Contact sheet shows the n pictures as 259 × 173 thumbnails; Mean shows one 259 × 259 picture ("The latents of these pictures were averaged and decoded once."); Relief shows a 259 × 259 grey relief rendering of the mean. The Help text names the relief and says no more about how it is computed.
- Click on a cell: a lightbox with five icons (favourite, add, download, print, zoom), PROMPT, AI MARKING "AI-generated (marked in the file)", the config id and model, the cell type, n, the seed ("Seed 982146524" for the Seed-fixed cell; "5 random seeds" for the other), the sentence on the averaged latents, the variants (Seed-fixed cell), the time, and a caption "SD 3.5 Large Turbo · Seed fixed · Relief". × or Escape closes it.
- Generated prompt variants: a collapsible that appears after the run with the five prompts.
- Advanced settings: Seed 424242 and a "Random variation" checkbox. The run used seed 982146524 (lightbox); I did not check whether the box was ticked.
- "Interpretation help" button on the last cell: not opened.
- Header during the run: image counter and weight file.
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- The four rewordings: "Surrounded by farmland, nature and animals, a house stands in a landscape. Some people can be seen." / "A dwelling sits in a terrain, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen." / "A house stands in a landscape, encircled by fields, nature and wildlife. Some individuals can be observed." / "Some persons may be viewed. In a vista, encircled by acreage, nature and creatures, rests a home." The first is the original; the fifth replaces every noun.
- Contact sheet, Seed fixed (one seed, five prompts): four of five pictures share one composition, a farmhouse centre-left, a path, cows on a meadow, wooded hills; the fifth (the "rests a home" variant) is a different picture, a house seen through a tree-framed opening with a path leading in. Prompt fixed (one prompt, five seeds): five different farmhouses in the same kind of composition, none standing out.
- Mean, Seed fixed: a ghosted multiple exposure in which the house, its chimney, the fence posts and the cows remain legible, because the same seed put them in the same places. Mean, Prompt fixed: a blurred house with doubled roofs and chimneys, cows as smears, a path at the bottom; what remains is what all five pictures had: a house in the centre, meadow below, tree line and hills above, a path to the house. The people of the prompt are in none of the means.
- Relief: a grey emboss of the mean in which the roof tiles, window frames, fence and cow outlines appear as lines; the recurring structures of the five pictures become visible as a drawing.
- The counter ran to 9 for ten thumbnails; the first thumbnail of both cells looks identical, so the original prompt with the fixed seed appears to be computed once and shown in both cells.
- The note's claim level: it quotes Steyerl and says what the page applies; the run shows an average of five pictures of one model, nothing about the training data.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- "Mean" is the preselected view, so the first thing after the run is a blur; the contact sheet behind it has to be found through the View chips.
- The noise picture with the "100 %" bar during the run looks like a result; it is replaced only when the whole row is done.
- The Help text says that a language model writes the rewordings; which one is not named anywhere; the variants appear in a collapsible below the fold.
- The counter says 9, the cells show 10 thumbnails.
- The seed in Advanced settings (424242) is not the seed the run used (982146524, in the lightbox).
- "Relief" is named in the Help text; no sentence says what it computes.
- The slider goes to 50 with no estimate of what a run of that size means.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says that the instrument generates many images from one prompt and averages them per model, which two means are computed (prompt variants written by a language model on one seed; the prompt as entered on random seeds), that the models are selectable one row each, what the view switch shows, that the SD 3.5 means are taken before the decoder and the other models' pixel by pixel, and what the method is applied for. It should add: the Mean view is preselected, so the contact sheet stands behind it; the noise picture with the 100 % bar during the run is replaced when the whole row is done; the counter said 9 for ten thumbnails, which fits one picture shared by both cells; the seed the run used stands in the lightbox, not in Advanced settings; click a cell to see the prompt, the seed and the variants. What survives the average is what the model drew in every picture; what vanishes is what it placed differently each time. The help should also say what the mean is as a picture: with the seed fixed a ghosted multiple exposure in which house, chimney, fence posts and cows stay legible; with the prompt fixed a blur that keeps only what every picture had; and the relief a grey drawing of the lines that recur. It is a picture to be looked at and judged, and the note says what it is called: ‘a rendition of correlated averages’. The heart in the lightbox keeps the run in the favourites bar, from where it opens again in this instrument.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Run one prompt with five per cell and look at the mean as a picture before reading it: what sharpens, what blurs, where the ghosting is; then the relief as a drawing of what the model draws every time.
- Draw the sentence by hand first, overlay the class's drawings on tracing paper, and put the class's mean beside the model's.
- Match the five thumbnails of the Seed-fixed cell to the five variants and find the rewording that changed the composition.
- Run the surface's second example, "the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal", with ten per cell on two models and hold the two means against your own street.
- Run a word with no picture in it ("friendship", "loneliness") and read the mean as the one cliché the model falls into for it.
- Run a profession ("a nurse at work") with ten per cell and read the mean as the model's average person for that word.
- Keep a run with the heart and come back to it; a mean is a picture of a model at a date, and a second run months later is a comparison.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument applies an artist's method back on the model: Hito Steyerl's ‘mean images’, quoted in the note, the pictures a model makes read as ‘a rendition of correlated averages’. The mean of many pictures to one sentence is itself a picture, and it is looked at before it is read: a ghost image, a blur, a relief of recurring lines. What survives the average is the model's convention for the sentence, and the judgement whether that convention is also ours, or anyone's, needs eyes that know pictures: the picture formula of a house, the way a street is usually photographed, what a nurse looks like in pictures and in life. The instrument is at its strongest where the class has a mean of its own to put beside the model's.

**S1 — The class's mean image** (formal, art, grades 7–10, 90 min). Every pupil draws the sentence "A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen." by hand on thin paper, same format, ten minutes. The drawings are stacked on a window or a light table, and the class traces what shows through in most of them onto one sheet: the class's mean image. Then the sentence runs here with ten per cell on one model; the class's sheet is pinned beside the Prompt-fixed mean and the relief. Two lists: what the class draws every time (the pointed roof, the chimney, the sun, the path), what the model draws every time, and where the two conventions meet and where they part. The phrases "the model imagines a house" and "the model knows what a house looks like" are put on the board and rewritten after the comparison as what the mean shows: what recurs in the pictures, not what anyone imagines. Sequence: 10 min drawing; 15 min overlay; 15 min run (used for the overlay); 30 min lists; 20 min phrases and plenary. Subject link: the picture formula (schema), convention in children's drawing and in a model's output. Uncertainty: I did not run ten per cell; five per cell gave means in which the house and the path were legible.

**S2 — What survives the average** (formal, art, grades 9–12, 90 min). Pairs run one prompt with five per cell, look at the contact sheet, then at the two means and the two reliefs as pictures: what sharpened, what blurred, what the ghosting did to the figures; they write a description of each mean as of a picture (composition, light, what is legible) before they write what survived. The class compares Seed-fixed and Prompt-fixed and names the model's convention for the sentence; the question whether the mean is a picture, and whose, closes the lesson with the note's quotations. Sequence: 10 min prompt; 20 min run (used for reading the note); 30 min descriptions and lists; 30 min plenary. Subject link: composition, convention; the multiple exposure and the blur as pictorial forms.

**S3 — Five ways to say it** (formal, language teaching, grades 8–10, 45 min after a run prepared by the teacher). The class reads the five variants, matches each thumbnail of the Seed-fixed cell to its text, and finds the one variant that changed the picture; then they write a sixth variant and predict whether it would change the composition, and write under the contact sheet the one sentence that explains it: the same seed fixed the composition, and only the wording that changed every noun moved it. Subject link: paraphrase, synonymy, what a word does to a picture.

**S4 — Whose street is normal?** (formal, art or geography, grades 8–12, 90 min, plus a homework photograph). Every pupil photographs their own street in the morning, without people, and brings the picture. The surface's own example "the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal" runs with ten per cell on two models. The two means and the pupils' photographs are hung together: what the model's mean street has (which houses, which road, which light, which animal) and what theirs have; whose street is in the mean and whose is not; whether the two models agree. The class writes what the word "normal" means in a mean image: what occurred most often in whatever the model was trained on. Sequence: 10 min hanging; 20 min runs; 30 min comparison in groups; 30 min plenary. Subject link: the local and the default; representation of place. Uncertainty: not run; the models' means of a street are not known to me.

**S5 — Steyerl's method** (non-formal, art-education workshop, adults or age 16+, 3 h). Participants read the note's quotations and the passage they come from, then make a mean series of their own as a work: one word or sentence of their choosing, twenty per cell on two models, contact sheet, mean and relief hung as a triptych per model; the platform's own knowledge names "friendship", "loneliness", "a nurse at work" as words whose mean shows the one cliché a model falls into. The round discusses the means as ‘mean images’ in Steyerl's double sense, the average and the shabby, and what it means to apply an artist's method against the machine that produced the pictures; a kept run is the work's record. Sequence: 30 min reading; 60 min runs and hanging; 60 min round; 30 min records. Subject link: artistic research; the mean as method; the series as work. Uncertainty: twenty per cell on two models is eighty pictures and a long wait on a shared server.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S5)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." S1: the phrases "the model imagines a house" and "the model knows what a house looks like" are judged against the mean and rewritten as what recurs in the pictures; the framework's classroom example has learners identify misleading phrases and develop better descriptions.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S3: same seed, five wordings, four pictures alike and one different, explained in one sentence under the contact sheet as what the seed fixed and what the words moved; the sentence is the artefact against the idea that the picture comes from the words alone.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S4 and S5: the model's mean street against the pupils' own streets, and the mean nurse, read for whose street and whose person is in the mean and whose is not; the framework's classroom example explores how and why a system's output differs across groups and discusses the impacts.
- Create 2 Intermediate — "Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs." S4 and S5: one sentence on two models, the means compared for what each model made of it; the framework's classroom example compares how different tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

--

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Engage 6 examples have learners explore reported differences; here the class computes the mean of a model's pictures and puts its own mean, drawn by hand, beside it (S1), and its own streets beside the model's (S4). The mean is a picture before it is a measurement, and the judgement whether its convention is ours needs eyes that know pictures. The method is an artist's, named in the note, and applied back against the machine. The framework has no competence for a statistical reading of a model's output, none for the picture formula as a thing to be known, and none for artistic research.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 1–4, Create 1, 3, 4.

scenarios.setting: formal, language teaching, grades 8–10, 45 min after a run prepared by the teacher
scenarios.duration: 45 min after a run prepared by the teacher
scenarios.text: The class reads the five variants, matches each thumbnail of the Seed-fixed cell to its text, and finds the one variant that changed the picture; then they write a sixth variant and predict whether it would change the composition, and write under the contact sheet the one sentence that explains it: the same seed fixed the composition, and only the wording that changed every noun moved it.
scenarios.subject_link: paraphrase, synonymy, what a word does to a picture.

scenarios.title: Whose street is normal?
scenarios.setting: formal, art or geography, grades 8–12, 90 min, plus a homework photograph
scenarios.subjects: art or geography, plus a homework photograph
scenarios.text: Every pupil photographs their own street in the morning, without people, and brings the picture. The surface's own example "the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal" runs with ten per cell on two models. The two means and the pupils' photographs are hung together: what the model's mean street has (which houses, which road, which light, which animal) and what theirs have; whose street is in the mean and whose is not; whether the two models agree. The class writes what the word "normal" means in a mean image: what occurred most often in whatever the model was trained on.
scenarios.sequence: 10 min hanging; 20 min runs; 30 min comparison in groups; 30 min plenary.
scenarios.subject_link: the local and the default; representation of place.
scenarios.uncertainty: not run; the models' means of a street are not known to me.

scenarios.title: Steyerl's method
scenarios.setting: non-formal, art-education workshop, adults or age 16+, 3 h
scenarios.text: Participants read the note's quotations and the passage they come from, then make a mean series of their own as a work: one word or sentence of their choosing, twenty per cell on two models, contact sheet, mean and relief hung as a triptych per model; the platform's own knowledge names "friendship", "loneliness", "a nurse at work" as words whose mean shows the one cliché a model falls into. The round discusses the means as ‘mean images’ in Steyerl's double sense, the average and the shabby, and what it means to apply an artist's method against the machine that produced the pictures; a kept run is the work's record.
scenarios.sequence: 30 min reading; 60 min runs and hanging; 60 min round; 30 min records.
scenarios.subject_link: artistic research; the mean as method; the series as work.
scenarios.uncertainty: twenty per cell on two models is eighty pictures and a long wait on a shared server.

a.expectation: Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding.
a.text: S1: the phrases "the model imagines a house" and "the model knows what a house looks like" are judged against the mean and rewritten as what recurs in the pictures; the framework's classroom example has learners identify misleading phrases and develop better descriptions.

a.expectation: Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works.
a.text: S3: same seed, five wordings, four pictures alike and one different, explained in one sentence under the contact sheet as what the seed fixed and what the words moved; the sentence is the artefact against the idea that the picture comes from the words alone.

a.expectation: Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups.
a.text: S4 and S5: the model's mean street against the pupils' own streets, and the mean nurse, read for whose street and whose person is in the mean and whose is not; the framework's classroom example explores how and why a system's output differs across groups and discusses the impacts.

a.expectation: Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs.
a.text: S4 and S5: one sentence on two models, the means compared for what each model made of it; the framework's classroom example compares how different tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.

mapping.beyond: the framework's Engage 6 examples have learners explore reported differences; here the class computes the mean of a model's pictures and puts its own mean, drawn by hand, beside it (S1), and its own streets beside the model's (S4). The mean is a picture before it is a measurement, and the judgement whether its convention is ours needs eyes that know pictures. The method is an artist's, named in the note, and applied back against the machine. The framework has no competence for a statistical reading of a model's output, none for the picture formula as a thing to be known, and none for artistic research.

instruments.name: Attention Cartography

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/attention-cartography`. Preparing column: Example prompts select, prompt field with the five small buttons, "Advanced settings" (Negative Prompt, Steps 25 (10–50), CFG 4.5, Seed 123456789 with "Random variation"), and a note "Attention Cartography" with two references (Hertz et al. 2022, "Prompt-to-Prompt"; Tang et al. 2022, DAAM). Right: an empty picture area. The run button is the play triangle ("Generate + Analyze"); an "Outputs" drawer button sits in the header. The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "Enter a prompt and click "Generate + Analyze"; the image model generates an image for it. Below, the same prompt stands once more, split into single words: click one, and the page draws a colour patch over the image exactly where this word had the most influence in the computation; several words carry several colours. Three controls change the view: the slider picks one of the computation steps, the network depth the layer within it (shallow, middle, deep), and the text-encoder control switches between the two decompositions of the same prompt that the model uses side by side." "The influence of a word spreads over areas, softly bounded and often somewhere other than expected: a word that mattered in the prompt sometimes gets only a small area, a passing one an area over half the picture. Compare an early computing step with a late one. And where a word begins and ends the model sets itself: the one decomposition has 77 tokens for the prompt, the other up to 512, and a long word falls into pieces that only together make the word again." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Typed "a lighthouse and a violin", pressed Generate + Analyze. Done. Server log: SD 3.5 Large, 25 steps, 1024 × 1024, seed 123456789, layers 3, 9 and 17 captured, 25 timesteps, 5 tokens, attention grid 64 × 64.
3. After the run the preparing column gained: "Text Encoder" with two buttons CLIP-L + G (77 Tokens) and T5-XXL (512 Tokens), both active; "TOKENS" chips a, lighthouse, and, a, violin, each with a small number; "Denoising step" slider 0–24 at Step 17 / 25; "Network depth" buttons Shallow (Composition), Middle (Semantics), Deep (Detail), All layers; "Heatmap" slider at 100 %; "Base image" buttons Color, B/W, Off (Off preselected). Two tokens were preselected, lighthouse and violin, each with a colour. The picture area showed the attention map: two coloured regions on black.
4. The script's "switch the text-encoder control if offered": toggled CLIP-L + G off (T5 alone), then T5 off (CLIP alone), then both on. Compared Shallow, Middle, Deep and All layers at step 17. Switched Base image to Color and moved the step slider to 0 and to 24. Toggled the token chips off and on.
5. Opened Advanced settings and the Outputs drawer (RUNS: one entry, "a lighthouse and a · Steps 25 · CFG 4.5").

Runs: 1 generation with analysis; all other changes are instant re-renderings of the captured maps.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Generate + Analyze: generates the picture with SD 3.5 Large and records the cross-attention of every token at three layers and every step.
- Text Encoder: toggles which encoder's tokens are mapped; the chips' small numbers change with it. CLIP alone: no numbers (one token per word). T5 alone: a (2), lighthouse (2), a (2). Both: a (3), lighthouse (3), and (2), a (3), violin (2); the number is the sum of the sub-tokens over the active encoders.
- Token chips: toggle; a selected chip gets a colour (the first selected red, the second blue, in the order of selection); the map draws one coloured region per selected token. With no chip selected the map is empty.
- Denoising step: re-renders the map for that step, 0 to 24.
- Network depth: Shallow, Middle, Deep or All layers.
- Heatmap: opacity of the overlay.
- Base image: the generated picture under the map in colour, in grey, or none.
- Advanced settings, RUNS strip, Outputs drawer: as listed above.
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- The picture: a white lighthouse with a red lantern on a rocky coast at sunset, and a violin with its bow leaning upright in the foreground right, as tall as a person.
- All layers, step 17, base off: a red lighthouse-shaped region left of centre and a blue violin-shaped region right, clearly separated, with faint red speckle over the sky. The map draws the two things where the picture has them.
- CLIP alone and T5 alone, same step: nearly the same two shapes; T5's lighthouse region is a little taller and narrower. Deep (Detail) alone: the same sharp shapes. Middle (Semantics): a diffuse wash, red and blue blotches mixed over the whole square, no shape. Shallow (Composition): a near-uniform magenta wash. The shapes come from the deep layer; the two shallower layers show no object.
- With the colour base: at step 17 the red lies on the lighthouse tower and lantern and the blue on the violin's body, with blue specks on the rocks beside it. At step 0 the red spreads over the lighthouse and the sky around it and the blue blotches lie loosely over the rocks; at step 24 both are tight on the objects. The regions settle during the denoising.
- The chips' numbers show that "lighthouse" is three sub-tokens for the two encoders together; "a" is three as well.
- The server log recorded, before the run, that a ComfyUI chunk file for this instrument was not found and that the diffusers backend was "unavailable, no fallback"; the run nevertheless succeeded. Nothing of this reached the surface.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The map's colours are assigned in the order of selection, so deselecting and reselecting swaps red and blue; nothing says so.
- Deselecting both chips leaves an empty black square.
- Step 17 and "All layers" are the defaults; the Shallow and Middle maps look broken (a wash) to someone who has not read that the shapes live in the deep layer.
- The chips' numbers have no legend; the Help text says that a long word falls into pieces, and the numbers count them.
- The Advanced settings are above the analysis controls and collapse the column; the step slider and the depth buttons appear only after a run.
- The references name two papers; what the map shows stands in the Help text, and the note box on the page has no sentence on it.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says to enter a prompt and click "Generate + Analyze", that clicking a word draws a colour patch where that word had the most influence, what the three controls change, that the influence spreads over areas and often lies somewhere other than expected, to compare an early step with a late one, and that the two decompositions have 77 and up to 512 tokens. It should add: the picture is generated by SD 3.5 Large; the colours are assigned in the order of selection; the shapes of the named things appear in the deep layer and settle in the later steps, and the shallow and middle layers show diffuse maps; the step slider and the depth buttons appear only after a run; with the base image on, the coloured regions lie over the picture.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Prompt two things, generate, and read at which step each thing's region first takes its shape.
- Select a function word ("and", "a") and see where its attention lies compared with a noun.
- Compare CLIP and T5 for a long sentence or a rare word and read the sub-token counts on the chips.
- Change one word of the prompt, generate again with the same seed, and compare the two maps of the unchanged word.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Where the word lands** (formal, art or computer science, grades 9–12, 90 min). Pairs write a prompt with two things, generate, select the two chips, and move the step slider from 0 to 24 in steps of four, noting at which step each thing's region appears; then they switch the depth and describe the difference in one sentence each. Sequence: 10 min prompt; 5 min generation; 30 min slider protocol; 20 min depth comparison; 25 min plenary on what "attention" is on this surface. Subject link: how a text becomes a picture, step by step.

**S2 — Shallow, middle, deep** (formal, computer science, grades 11–13, 90 min). After a generation the class compares the four depth settings at three steps, records which show shapes, and reads the abstract of one of the two references to find the term "cross-attention"; groups explain to each other what the map is a map of. Subject link: neural network layers, attention. Uncertainty: the references are papers in English; the teacher selects the passages.

**S3 — Two encoders** (non-formal, media workshop, age 14+, 2 h). Participants generate with a long prompt and with a prompt containing a rare or foreign word, switch between CLIP and T5, read the sub-token counts on the chips and compare the two encoders' maps for the same word. Subject link: tokenisation, text encoders. Uncertainty: the difference between the encoders' maps was small for "lighthouse" and "violin"; a rare word may show more or nothing.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: the step protocol describes how the model places the named things over 25 steps.
- Engage 2 Advanced — "Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding." S2: "attention" is the surface's own word, and the groups must explain it as a weighting of regions, not as looking.
- Shape 1 Intermediate — "Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool." S2: the constraints are on the surface: one model, three captured layers, 25 steps, 64 × 64 grid.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." Modification: the misleading phrase met here is that the model "looks at" the prompt; S1 at the lower grades replaces it with "the word steers a region", read off the map. The framework's classroom example has learners replace misleading phrases about AI with accurate ones; here one phrase is replaced from the map.

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's knowledge statement 1.1 names "weights"; the map shows them, per word and per step, on the picture they produce. S1's step protocol records what the framework states.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 2, 3, 4, Create 1–4.
