instruments.name: Encoder Fusion

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/encoder-fusion` (sidebar tooltip "Surrealistic blending"). Preparing column: Example prompts select, a prompt field with the placeholder "Choose an example prompt, write your own prompt, or drag a picture onto this area (it is converted into a verbal image description).", then "CONDITIONING TABLE" with six preset chips (Standard, CLIP only, T5 only, Surrealization 5, Surrealization 15, Surrealization 35), a diagram of the conditioning tensor (columns 0–2047 and 2048–4095, "pool → modulation", a CLIP block of rows 0–76 labelled "a·CLIP + b·T5" and "0 + b·T5", a T5 block of rows 0–511 labelled "c·T5", and a dashed box "T5 rows 0–76" with an arrow labelled b pointing into the CLIP block), and three sliders: a "CLIP block" (1.00, with chips "pool CLIP" / "pool 0"), b "T5 rows 0–76 into the CLIP block" (0.00), c "T5 block" (1.00, with chips "rows 0–511" / "rows 77–511"). Under them "Advanced settings". Right: an empty picture area. The run button is the play triangle ("Execute"); an "Outputs" drawer button sits in the header. The surface has no note box; the chip tooltips carry the only explanations ("a 1.00 · b 0.00 · c 1.00"; "CLIP-L's and CLIP-G's pooled vector, 768 and 1280 numbers joined"; "Zeros of the same shape in the pooled vector's place"; "T5 block with all 512 rows under the CLIP block"; "T5 block with rows 77–511 alone, rows 0–76 only as the b-fold addend inside the CLIP block"; the Surrealization chips "a −4.00 · b 5.00 · c 1.00 · T5 77–511", "a −14.00 · b 15.00 …", "a −34.00 · b 35.00 …").
2. Chose the example prompt "A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen." A token table "Row | CLIP | T5" appeared under the sliders: CLIP cuts the sentence into 22 tokens between <|startoftext|> and <|endoftext|> (row 22), padding 23–76; T5 into 25 tokens with "▁" tokens at rows 4 and 8 (the spaces before "a" and "surrounded"), "farmland" as "farm", "l", "and" (rows 11–13), </s> at row 25, padding 26–76 and 77–511.
3. Standard preset (a 1.00 · b 0.00 · c 1.00), Execute. The picture arrived.
4. Moved the b slider strongly: the raw slider went to 801 of 1000 and the display read 22.00 (the scale is non-linear: 300 shows as 1.00, the ends as ±75). The preset chips all deselected. Execute at 23:28:44; the second picture arrived between 23:32:44 and 23:36:56 (my polling missed the moment).
5. Opened the Outputs drawer: RUNS 2, entries "a 1.00 · b 0.00 · c 1.00" and "a 1.00 · b 22.00 · c 1.00", each with ×. Opened Advanced settings: Negative Prompt (empty), CFG Scale 5.5 (1–15, step 0.1), Seed 123456789, "Random variation" unticked.

Runs: 2 pictures, 1024 × 1024, same seed.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Preset chips: set a, b, c and the pool/rows chips at once; the tooltip states the values. Moving any slider deselects all presets.
- a: factor on the CLIP block; "pool CLIP" / "pool 0" chooses whether the pooled CLIP vector or zeros go to the modulation.
- b: factor with which T5's rows 0–76 are added into the CLIP block (the dashed box in the diagram).
- c: factor on the T5 block; "rows 0–511" / "rows 77–511" chooses whether all T5 rows or only rows 77–511 stand under the CLIP block.
- Token table: shows how the two encoders cut the prompt; it changes with the prompt and needs no run.
- Execute: one picture with the current table and seed. Outputs drawer: list of runs by their a/b/c.
- Prompt field buttons, Hide column, Help: as elsewhere. Drag-a-picture onto the field (not used): converted into a description.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Standard: a photographic farm scene; a stone house with a tiled roof on a meadow, forest behind, cows, sheep and goats, four people walking in the foreground, telephoto look.
- b = 22, everything else as Standard, same seed: a naive painting. A white house seen frontally with a thick mossy roof and an orange-tiled gable; objects stuck on the facade like reliefs (a fish, a bird, jugs, shells, a nest); people in old-fashioned dress (a woman in white, one in yellow); goats, cows and sheep in a fenced meadow; yellow flower fields; painted clouds. The prompt's content is still there (house, farmland, animals, people), but the style, the composition and the objects on the wall are not in the prompt.
- The same seed gave two different compositions, so the seed does not pin the layout when the conditioning changes this much.
- The token table shows two tokenisations of one sentence: 22 against 25 tokens, "farmland" whole in CLIP and in three pieces in T5.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The sliders' scale: the display jumps from 1.00 to 22.00 over half the slider's travel and the marks read −75 / 0 / 1 / 75; nothing says the scale is non-linear.
- "a", "b", "c", "pool", "rows 0–76", "modulation": the diagram names them, nothing explains them; the tooltips are the only prose, and they are hidden until hovered.
- Moving a slider silently deselects the preset; the chips go dark without a message.
- No note box: the surface does not say what "surrealization" is or why T5 rows added into the CLIP block produce it.
- No progress display; the picture simply appears.
- The Outputs drawer names the runs by their numbers only.
- The page's strings carry a note on what the instrument does (the table of 589 rows, Esser et al. 2024, the sentence that a row holding both encodings lies outside the trained states), and the surface does not show it; the chip tooltips are all there is.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The page has no Help text of its own and no note on the surface. It should first say what the pictures are: pictures from a conditioning that no prompt produces. SD 3.5 reads a prompt through three encoders into a table of 589 rows, a CLIP block of 77 rows above a T5 block of 512; the model was trained on that table and on tables with one encoder set to zero, never on a row that holds both encodings at once. The b slider writes T5's first 77 rows into the CLIP block, and the page's own note, which the surface does not show, says of such a row that it "lies outside those trained states. What the model computes from such a table is the question of this instrument." The help should say what that means for the one who uses it: the naive painting with the reliefs on the facade that came out of b = 22 is a picture nobody could have written a prompt for, on this model or any other; writing a prompt reaches only what the training made sayable, and this slider reaches past it. The platform's concept says this is the point of the Surrealizer, insights into the model's latent spaces that conventional prompting does not reach, and the Latent Lab's purpose text says what to do with them: "to carry the estrangements and intermediate products on into artistic work". The help should say that the work is in the choosing: along b the picture stays a picture for a while and then falls apart, and the place where it is still a picture and no longer the prompt's picture is where the series is worth keeping. Then the mechanics: Standard first (a 1, b 0, c 1), then a preset or own values with the same seed; the token table shows how each encoder cut the prompt; a picture is kept with the heart and goes on to Flow.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Make a picture no prompt can make: one prompt, Standard, then Surrealization 15 with the same seed; then try to write a prompt that gives the second picture on Standard, run it, and put the three side by side.
- Find the edge: move b upward in steps from 0 and keep every picture; mark the last one that is still a picture and the first that is no longer the prompt's.
- Run Standard, CLIP only and T5 only with one prompt and the same seed; list which named things each picture keeps.
- Draw the objects the model put where the prompt had none; then run the drawing's description through Standard and see whether the model gives them back.
- Take the kept picture onto the Flow board and carry it on: a video, a sound, a perspective.
- Write a prompt with a compound word ("farmland", "lighthouse") and read how CLIP and T5 cut it in the table.
- Drag a photograph onto the prompt field and run its description at Surrealization 5 and 35.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument makes pictures that no prompt can make. Everything a prompt can reach lies inside what the model was trained to read; the b slider writes one encoder's reading into the other's rows, a state the model never saw in training, and what it computes from that is a picture nobody wrote. The work with it is artistic before it is technical: to find, along the slider, the place where the picture is still a picture and no longer the prompt's, to keep the series, to choose, and to carry the chosen picture on. The questions that come with it are the platform's own: whether this is still my picture, and what the model gives when it is asked something unsayable.

**S1 — The picture no prompt can make** (formal, art, grades 9–13, 2 × 45 min). The class writes one prompt and runs it on Standard, then on Surrealization 5, 15 and 35, same seed, all four kept. Then the attempt: pairs describe the Surrealization-15 picture as precisely as they can (a naive painting, a white house seen frontally, objects stuck on the facade like reliefs, people in old-fashioned dress) and run that description on Standard. The two pictures side by side: the written one is a picture in a style, the fused one is something else, and the pairs say what. Reading of the note's sentence that such a row lies outside the trained states. Closing: one sentence per pair on what a prompt can reach and what it cannot. Sequence: 10 min prompt and four runs; 20 min description and run; 30 min side by side; 20 min note and sentences; 10 min plenary. Subject link: the sayable and the picturable; style against state. Uncertainty: not run as a sequence; Standard and b = 22 were run, the presets were not.

**S2 — Finding the edge** (non-formal, art workshop, age 16+, 3 h). Participants write a prompt of their own and move b up in steps (2, 5, 10, 15, 22, 35), same seed, every picture kept with the heart. Along the series they mark two places: the last picture that is still a picture, and the first that is no longer the prompt's picture. Between the two lies the stretch where the work is; each participant chooses one picture from it and says why. The chosen picture goes to the Flow board and is carried on: a video from it, a sound, a perspective. At the end the series and the continued work hang together, and the round asks what the model gave that nobody asked for, and whether it belongs to anyone. Sequence: 20 min prompts; 60 min series; 30 min marking and choosing; 50 min continuation on Flow; 20 min round. Subject link: the series as a form of work; the choice as the artistic act; the Latent Lab's purpose of carrying the estrangements on into artistic work. Uncertainty: a strong b can give noise instead of a painting, and the stretch between the two marks may be short; I did not try the Flow path from this surface.

**S3 — Is this still my picture?** (formal, art or ethics, grades 10–13, 45 min). sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S5)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Create 1 Basic — "Learners explore how different AI tools can expand their thinking or spark new ideas." S5: the objects the model placed where the prompt had none, drawn and taken as the start of own work; S2: the picture chosen from the series carried on into a video or a sound; the framework's classroom example has learners write new stories inspired by unexpected results.
- Create 2 Intermediate — "Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs." S1 and S2: one prompt under Standard and three or six settings of b, the series kept and compared for what each setting made of the same prompt; the framework's classroom example compares how different prompts and tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.
- Create 4 Advanced — "Learners assess the ethical implications of AI-generated outputs for creative work, distinguish inspiration from replication in their outputs, and justify how their use of AI maintains authenticity and respects other creators." S3: the prompt's picture, the fused picture and the continued one side by side, and for each who made which choice, which the pair would sign and what the model's share is; the framework's classroom example puts human-made, AI-generated and human-with-AI work side by side and asks what choices a human did or did not make and who should be credited.

S4: the two encoders explained from the token table and the tensor diagram as rows and factors, the three sentences about the model rewritten without reading, understanding or seeing.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

--

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Create competences have learners prompt, vary and combine; every one of its examples stays inside what a prompt can reach. This instrument reaches past it: a conditioning the model never saw in training, and pictures that no prompt on any model produces. The platform's concept names these pictures as insights into the model's latent spaces that conventional prompting does not reach, and its Latent Lab purpose as carrying the estrangements on into artistic work. The framework has no competence for the unsayable, and none for the choice along a series as an artistic act; this instrument is built on both.

SD 3.5 reads a prompt through three encoders into a table of 589 rows, a CLIP block of 77 rows above a T5 block of 512; the model was trained on that table and on tables with one encoder set to zero, never on a row that holds both encodings at once. The b slider writes T5's first 77 rows into the CLIP block, and the page's own note, which the surface does not show, says of such a row that it "lies outside those trained states. What the model computes from such a table is the question of this instrument." The help should say what that means for the one who uses it: the naive painting with the reliefs on the facade that came out of b = 22 is a picture nobody could have written a prompt for, on this model or any other; writing a prompt reaches only what the training made sayable, and this slider reaches past it. instruments.scenarios_intro: The instrument makes pictures that no prompt can make. Everything a prompt can reach lies inside what the model was trained to read; the b slider writes one encoder's reading into the other's rows, a state the model never saw in training, and what it computes from that is a picture nobody wrote. The work with it is artistic before it is technical: to find, along the slider, the place where the picture is still a picture and no longer the prompt's, to keep the series, to choose, and to carry the chosen picture on. The questions that come with it are the platform's own: whether this is still my picture, and what the model gives when it is asked something unsayable.

instruments.name: Dimension Explorer

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/dimension-explorer` (sidebar tooltip "Dimension-level analysis"). Preparing column: Example prompts select with three pairs ("A red house by the lake / A blue house by the lake"; the street where I live as a pencil drawing / as an oil painting; "a meadow at noon / a meadow at midnight"), "Prompt A (Original)" and "Prompt B (Comparison)" fields with placeholders, "Encoder" chips All (recommended), CLIP-L (768d), CLIP-G (1280d), T5-XXL (4096d), "Advanced settings" (Negative Prompt, Steps 25, CFG 4.5, Seed 123456789, "Random variation" unticked), and "Select dimensions from Prompt B": a two-handle range slider, two number fields (from – to), buttons "+", "All", "None", "Descending", the line "0 dimensions from Prompt B selected (rank – of 0)" and "The 0 dimensions from Prompt B with the largest difference to Prompt A". Right: three empty columns "Original (Prompt A)", "Modified (Transfer from Prompt B)" (with the sentence "Select a rank range below and click ▶ 2 — this will show prompt A with the transferred dimensions from B (same seed).") and "Original (Prompt B)". The header has two run buttons, ▶1 "Analyze" and ▶2 "Transfer selected vector dimensions from Prompt B into the generated image". No note box and no references on this surface.
2. Typed "a calm lake" and "a stormy lake", pressed Analyze. The ranking appeared and the picture for A; the picture for B arrived later while I was elsewhere.
3. The ranking: "The 4096 dimensions from Prompt B with the largest difference to Prompt A", one row per dimension with a checkbox, a rank, a name, a bar and a value: 1 d1478 1.182; 2 d806 0.667; 3 d1828 0.643; 4 d1544 0.465; 5 d1567 0.453; 6 d1619 0.427; 7 d1092 0.426; 8 d1164 0.424; 9 d1742 0.422; 10 d1760 0.421; 11 d1266 0.421; 12 d892 0.414 … The bars are proportional (100 %, 56 %, 54 %, 39 % …). The default selection after the analysis read "1144 dimensions from Prompt B selected (rank 13–1156 of 4096)".
4. Set the range to 1–10 ("10 dimensions from Prompt B selected (rank 1–10 of 4096)", the first ten checkboxes ticked), pressed ▶2; the modified picture arrived.
5. Set the range to 1–100, pressed ▶2; done. RUNS showed 4.

Runs: 1 analysis (two pictures), 2 transfers (one picture each).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Prompt A / B, Example prompts, the five field buttons: as elsewhere.
- Encoder chips: which encoder's embedding is compared; I used "All (recommended)", which ranked "of 4096".
- ▶1 Analyze: generates A and B with the same seed and ranks the dimensions of B's embedding by their difference to A's.
- Range slider, from/to fields, +, All, None, Descending: choose a rank range; the checkboxes in the list follow; the line above the list states the count and the range.
- ▶2: regenerates A with the selected dimensions replaced by B's values, same seed, into the middle column.
- Advanced settings as on the other diffusion surfaces. RUNS strip counts every picture.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- A, "a calm lake": a flat turquoise lake to the horizon, hazy blue hills, a thin cloud, clear sky.
- B, "a stormy lake": dark storm clouds with rain streaks hanging over a green lake, wooded shores left and right.
- Modified, ranks 1–10: indistinguishable from A to my eye.
- Modified, ranks 1–100: still a calm lake under a clear sky, but a different picture: hills on both sides, wooded shores left and right, stronger haze. The composition moved towards B's, the weather did not.
- Ten of 4096 dimensions carried nothing visible; a hundred carried the shores and hills but not the storm. The word "stormy" is not in the first hundred ranked dimensions of this embedding.
- The number 4096 under "All (recommended)" equals T5-XXL's width; CLIP-L has 768 and CLIP-G 1280. Nothing on the surface says how "All" is counted.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Two run buttons, numbered, with the second one explained only in the empty middle column.
- After the analysis the selection defaults to ranks 13–1156; nothing says why these numbers.
- "d1478", "1.182": the names and values have no legend.
- A arrives first and B later with no status; the right column stays empty without a word.
- Transferring the top ten changes nothing visible; the surface does not say that small ranges rarely show.
- "rank – of 0" and "The 0 dimensions …" before the analysis read like an error.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The page has no Help text of its own. It should first say what there is to experience here, and that it is not what the surface's wording promises. The list is called "The 4096 dimensions from Prompt B with the largest difference to Prompt A", and the second button "Transfer selected vector dimensions from Prompt B into the generated image"; both read as if a word sat in some of these numbers and could be carried over. The Latent Lab's own description in the Help says what the lab is for: "to explore the in-between spaces of an AI that are never shown", "to understand that it is made, and to open the black box a little". Here the box opens and stays dark: every one of the 4096 numbers is on the table, with its rank and its bar, and none of them is a trait. The help should say so: a dimension is not "colour" or "weather"; ten of them carried nothing visible, a hundred moved the shores and the haze and left the storm where it was; the word is spread over the whole table in a way that has no name in our language. It should say that working through the ranges and failing to find the word is the use of the instrument, and that the protocol of the attempts is what is taken away. Then the mechanics: two prompts that differ in one point; Analyze generates both with the same seed and ranks the dimensions by the size of their difference; a range of ranks and the second button generate A again with those dimensions from B; the encoder chips choose whose table is compared; the count depends on the encoder.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Learn how Dimensions are everything but human-understandable, identifiable traits of things, experience how a non-human intelligence work deeply opaquely.
- Set out to find the storm: a one-word pair ("calm" / "stormy"), then 10, 100, 1000 ranks, then the top three alone, then the smallest with "Descending", then each encoder on its own; write down after every attempt what changed and what did not. The storm does not arrive; the shores do.
- Try to name a dimension: take the first-ranked one, transfer it alone, and say what it did; then test the name with a second pair. The name does not hold.
- Keep the series of modified pictures from one pair as a sequence: A, ten ranks, a hundred, a thousand, B. Read it as a drift towards B that never passes through the word.
- Compare the three example pairs, colour, drawing style, time of day, and say which of them the table gives up first and which it holds longest.
- Run one pair with CLIP-L, CLIP-G and T5 separately: three tables, three orders, none of them readable.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument is defined by working through and failing. Two prompts that differ in one word go in, 4096 numbers come out with their differences ranked, and the task that suggests itself, find the numbers that hold the word, cannot be done. What there is to experience is that a model's order is not made of traits a person can name, and that it works all the same. The failure is the finding, and it is productive: the protocol of attempts, the series of pictures that drift without arriving, and the sentences the class writes afterwards.

**S1 — Where is the storm?** (formal, art, mathematics or computer science, grades 9–12, 90 min). Pairs choose a one-word pair and set out to find the word's dimensions. They work through: the ten largest, the hundred largest, a thousand, the first one alone, the smallest ones with "Descending", one encoder at a time; after every attempt one line in a protocol: what changed in the middle picture, what did not. The plenary collects the protocols: nobody found the word; what moved were shores, hills, haze, a horizon, things nobody asked for; and the picture did move towards B. Closing sentence per pair on what a dimension is, and is not. Sequence: 10 min pair; 10 min analysis; 40 min attempts and protocol; 20 min plenary; 10 min sentences. Subject link: vector, dimension, representation; the limit of naming. Uncertainty: ten ranks changed nothing visible and a hundred moved the composition and not the weather; a thousand and the encoder chips were not run.

**S2 — A name for d1478** (formal, language teaching or philosophy, grades 11–13, 90 min). The class tries to do with the model's dimensions what we do with traits: name them. Groups take the three highest-ranked dimensions of one pair, transfer each alone and in twos, and write a label for each as one would for a trait ("weather", "colour", "mood"). Every label is then tested on a second pair: does the same dimension do the same there? The labels fall; the discussion is about why: our words cut the world into things with traits, the model's table cuts it into 4096 numbers that each hold a little of everything, and the two cuts do not meet. Sequence: 15 min analysis of two pairs; 30 min transfers and labels; 20 min tests; 25 min discussion. Subject link: category, trait, concept; what a word is to us and what it is to the model. Uncertainty: not run; whether a single dimension changes anything visible is doubtful (ten together did not), which is the point of the exercise and is said beforehand.

**S3 — The series of attempts** (non-formal, art workshop, age 15+, 3 h). Participants work on one pair of their own and keep every modified picture: a series from A over 10, 100, 1000 ranks to B, and the protocol beside it. The series is hung as a work: a drift from one picture to another that never passes through the word that separates the two prompts. The round at the end asks what the series shows about the model, and what the protocol of failing shows about the one who tried. One picture of the series is carried on in Flow (favourite, then a perspective or a sound). Sequence: 20 min prompts and analysis; 70 min attempts; 40 min hanging and protocol; 30 min round; 20 min continuation. Subject link: the series as a form of work; failure as material; artistic research. Uncertainty: I did not try the favourite path from this surface.

**S4 — Encoder by encoder** (non-formal, maker space, age 15+, 2 h). Participants run one pair with each encoder chip, compare the three rankings (which dimension names come first, how long the lists are: 768, 1280, 4096) and the modified pictures at the same range, and write what the three tables have in common: nothing a person can read. Subject link: text encoders of a diffusion model; three orders of the same sentence.

sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." S1 and S2: the sentences "the model knows what stormy means" and "the storm sits somewhere in the model" are held against the protocol and rewritten; the framework's classroom example has learners identify misleading phrases and develop accurate descriptions, and the accurate description here is that the word is a difference spread over 4096 numbers that carry no trait.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: the protocol and the closing sentences describe what the second button does, a transfer of ranked numbers between two tables at one seed, against the idea that a word is stored somewhere in the model and can be moved.
- Engage 2 Advanced — "Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding." S4: three encoders, three tables of different length and order, explained from what each did to the picture at the same range, in sentences without seeing or knowing; the framework's classroom example has learners explain how different systems produce outputs as programmed processes.
- Shape 2 Basic — "Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task." S1: what counts as "the word shows" is defined by each pair before the attempts and applied to every range; the framework's classroom example has learners define what would make the system successful before judging it.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

--

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's expectations assume that how an AI system works can be described, and its Engage 2 examples have learners describe it. The Latent Lab's own purpose in the Help names it: "to explore the in-between spaces of an AI that are never shown", "to open the black box a little". The framework has no competence for the experience of opacity and none for failure as a form of knowledge; this instrument is built on both.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 1, 3, 4, Create 1–4.

scenarios.setting: formal, art, mathematics or computer science, grades 9–12, 90 min
scenarios.text: Pairs choose a one-word pair and set out to find the word's dimensions. They work through: the ten largest, the hundred largest, a thousand, the first one alone, the smallest ones with "Descending", one encoder at a time; after every attempt one line in a protocol: what changed in the middle picture, what did not. The plenary collects the protocols: nobody found the word; what moved were shores, hills, haze, a horizon, things nobody asked for; and the picture did move towards B. Closing sentence per pair on what a dimension is, and is not.
scenarios.sequence: 10 min pair; 10 min analysis; 40 min attempts and protocol; 20 min plenary; 10 min sentences.
scenarios.subject_link: vector, dimension, representation; the limit of naming.
scenarios.uncertainty: ten ranks changed nothing visible and a hundred moved the composition and not the weather; a thousand and the encoder chips were not run.

scenarios.title: A name for d1478
scenarios.setting: formal, language teaching or philosophy, grades 11–13, 90 min
scenarios.text: The class tries to do with the model's dimensions what we do with traits: name them. Groups take the three highest-ranked dimensions of one pair, transfer each alone and in twos, and write a label for each as one would for a trait ("weather", "colour", "mood"). Every label is then tested on a second pair: does the same dimension do the same there? The labels fall; the discussion is about why: our words cut the world into things with traits, the model's table cuts it into 4096 numbers that each hold a little of everything, and the two cuts do not meet.
scenarios.sequence: 15 min analysis of two pairs; 30 min transfers and labels; 20 min tests; 25 min discussion.
scenarios.subject_link: category, trait, concept; what a word is to us and what it is to the model.
scenarios.uncertainty: not run; whether a single dimension changes anything visible is doubtful (ten together did not), which is the point of the exercise and is said beforehand.

scenarios.title: The series of attempts
scenarios.setting: non-formal, art workshop, age 15+, 3 h
scenarios.text: Participants work on one pair of their own and keep every modified picture: a series from A over 10, 100, 1000 ranks to B, and the protocol beside it. The series is hung as a work: a drift from one picture to another that never passes through the word that separates the two prompts. The round at the end asks what the series shows about the model, and what the protocol of failing shows about the one who tried. One picture of the series is carried on in Flow (favourite, then a perspective or a sound).
scenarios.sequence: 20 min prompts and analysis; 70 min attempts; 40 min hanging and protocol; 30 min round; 20 min continuation.
scenarios.subject_link: the series as a form of work; failure as material; artistic research.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not try the favourite path from this surface.

scenarios.title: Encoder by encoder
scenarios.setting: non-formal, maker space, age 15+, 2 h
scenarios.text: Participants run one pair with each encoder chip, compare the three rankings (which dimension names come first, how long the lists are: 768, 1280, 4096) and the modified pictures at the same range, and write what the three tables have in common: nothing a person can read.
scenarios.subject_link: text encoders of a diffusion model; three orders of the same sentence.

a.expectation: Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding.
a.text: S1 and S2: the sentences "the model knows what stormy means" and "the storm sits somewhere in the model" are held against the protocol and rewritten; the framework's classroom example has learners identify misleading phrases and develop accurate descriptions, and the accurate description here is that the word is a difference spread over 4096 numbers that carry no trait.

a.expectation: Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works.
a.text: S1: the protocol and the closing sentences describe what the second button does, a transfer of ranked numbers between two tables at one seed, against the idea that a word is stored somewhere in the model and can be moved.

a.expectation: Learners explain how different AI systems work using language that does not attribute human traits or abilities, knowing that their phrasing shapes understanding.
a.text: S4: three encoders, three tables of different length and order, explained from what each did to the picture at the same range, in sentences without seeing or knowing; the framework's classroom example has learners explain how different systems produce outputs as programmed processes.

a.expectation: Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task.
a.text: S1: what counts as "the word shows" is defined by each pair before the attempts and applied to every range; the framework's classroom example has learners define what would make the system successful before judging it.

mapping.beyond: the framework's expectations assume that how an AI system works can be described, and its Engage 2 examples have learners describe it. Here the description is attempted and fails at the level of the dimension, on purpose, with the whole table on screen; what remains is the experience of a way of working that functions and has no names in it, and the protocol of having tried. The Latent Lab's own purpose in the Help names it: "to explore the in-between spaces of an AI that are never shown", "to open the black box a little". The framework has no competence for the experience of opacity and none for failure as a form of knowledge; this instrument is built on both.

instruments.name: Concept Algebra

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/concept-algebra` (sidebar tooltip "Vector arithmetic"). Preparing column: Example prompts select with three triples ("the street where I live, in the morning, with an animal − the street where I live, in the morning + a river"; the street seen through the eyes of a child − the street + the street seen through the eyes of an adult; "a street in the evening, with people − a street in the evening + loneliness"), the fields "Prompt A (Base)", "Prompt B (Subtract)", "Prompt C (Add)" under the line "A − B + C = ?", "Encoder" chips (All (recommended), CLIP-L (768d), CLIP-G (1280d), T5-XXL (4096d)), "Advanced settings" (Negative Prompt, Steps 25, CFG 4.5, Subtraction scale 1 (0–3, step 0.1), Addition scale 1 (0–3, step 0.1), Seed 123456789, "Random variation"), and "Research References" (Mikolov et al. 2013, "Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality", NeurIPS 2013; Liu et al. 2022, "Compositional Visual Generation with Composable Diffusion Models", ECCV 2022, both with DOI). Right: two columns "Reference (Prompt A)" and "Result (A − B + C)" with "Enter three prompts and click Compute — the result of the vector arithmetic will appear here." The run button is the play triangle ("Compute").
2. Typed A "king", B "man", C "woman"; both scales at 1. Compute; both pictures arrived.
3. Set the Addition scale to 2, Compute; the result arrived. RUNS 2.

Runs: 2 computations, 3 pictures (the reference is kept).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Three prompt fields with the five small buttons each; Example prompts fills all three.
- Encoder chips: whose embedding the arithmetic is done on.
- Subtraction scale / Addition scale: factors on B and C in A − s·B + t·C.
- Compute: generates the reference from A alone and the result from the combined embedding, same seed.
- RUNS strip, Hide column, Help: as elsewhere.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Reference "king": a painted portrait of an old bearded king, gold crown with a cross, red robe with ermine, on a yellow ground, frontal.
- Result "king − man + woman", scales 1 and 1: a young woman with long black hair, a gold-and-red crown with a cross, a red, black and gold robe with gold borders, on a gold ground, in a flat illustration style, frontal. The crown, the cross, the colours and the pose stayed; the beard and the age went; the style changed from painterly to flat.
- Result with Addition scale 2: a photographic portrait of a young woman with a jewelled crown, a white veil, two braids, long earrings and an embroidered robe on a muted brown ground. More jewellery, more fabric, and a style that no longer shares anything with the reference.
- The classic analogy holds on this surface: the result reads as "queen" in both runs; the scale decides how far the result moves from the reference's style.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- "A − B + C = ?" is the only explanation; the references are papers.
- Nothing says that the reference is A alone and that the result shares its seed.
- The scales sit in Advanced settings; their effect (style drift at 2) is not described.
- The example triples are long sentences; the classic word triple is not among them.
- No progress display while a computation runs.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: Three prompts: the model's text embedding of B is subtracted from that of A and C's is added, and the picture of that sum stands next to the picture of A alone, both with the same seed. The two scales in Advanced settings weight the subtraction and the addition; at 1 and 1 the result keeps much of A's style, at larger values it moves further away. Short prompts of one or two words make the arithmetic readable; sentences mix many things at once. The references name the word-vector arithmetic (2013) and the diffusion composition (2022) the surface builds on.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Run the classic "king − man + woman" and then your own triples ("doctor − man + woman", "Paris − France + Japan").
- Run one triple at Addition scale 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 and pin the results in a row.
- Subtract a word from an occupation ("a nurse − woman") and look at what is left.
- Run the same triple with CLIP-L only and with T5 only and compare.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — king − man + woman** (formal, computer science or mathematics, grades 10–13, 90 min). Pairs run the classic, then two triples of their own, and write for each what stayed from A and what came from C; the teacher shows the 2013 paper's famous example. Sequence: 10 min intro; 30 min three computations; 30 min written comparison; 20 min plenary on vectors as meaning. Subject link: vectors, analogy.

**S2 — What is left of a nurse** (formal, language teaching or ethics, grades 9–12, 90 min). Groups run "a nurse − a woman + a man", "a boss − a man + a woman" and similar; they record what the result keeps (uniform, setting, age) and discuss what the model holds in the word. Subject link: stereotype, connotation. Uncertainty: results can be unexpected; the teacher previews.

**S3 — The scale** (non-formal, art workshop, age 16+, 2 h). One triple, four addition scales (0.5, 1, 2, 3); participants pin the four results in a row and mark where the style breaks away from the reference. Subject link: gradation, style.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S3)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: the written comparison per triple (what stayed from A, what came from C) and the plenary on vectors as meaning, against the idea that the model understands the word.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S2: what the word "nurse" carries after the subtraction.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

- Engage 6 Basic — "Learners understand that biases can exist in the data used to train AI and can be perpetuated when humans design, develop and use AI systems." Modification: what S2 sees is the bias as it arrived in the embedding from the training data; the data themselves are not on the surface, their trace in the word is. The framework's classroom example asks what the data about a person capture and leave out; S2 asks what the word "nurse" still carries once "woman" is subtracted.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 1–4, Create 1–4.

instruments.name: Composable Diffusion

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/composable-diffusion` (sidebar tooltip "Each concept scored separately"). Preparing column: Example prompts select with four pairs ("a red house on a hill + a blue ship on the ocean"; the street seen through the eyes of a child + of an adult; "a tree + a house"; "an apple tree + apples"), "Concept 1" and "Concept 2" fields (placeholder "e.g. a red house on a hill"), each with "Weight 1.00", a slider from −2 to 2 (step 0.05) and a green badge "AND"; a button "+ Add concept"; "Combination" chips "In the embedding" / "In the denoiser" (preselected) with the sentence "In the embedding the run interpolates between the concepts once, at the start. In the denoiser it puts every concept through the model at each step and weights the predictions into one."; "Advanced settings" (Negative Prompt, Steps 25, CFG 4.5, Seed 123456789, "Random variation" unticked, "Normalize weights (sum to 1.0)" ticked); "Research References" (Liu et al. 2022, "Compositional Visual Generation with Composable Diffusion Models", ECCV 2022, DOI). Right: an empty picture area. The run button is the play triangle ("Generate").
2. Pressed "+ Add concept": a third field appeared, and each concept gained a × button. Typed Concept 1 "a cat on a sofa" (1.00), Concept 2 "a sunny living room" (1.00), Concept 3 "a window" and moved its slider to −1.00: the badge turned from "AND" to "NOT". Denoiser selected, normalization ticked. Generate. Under the references the line "Composable generation in progress..." appeared; then the picture.
3. Switched the Combination chip to "In the embedding", same concepts and weights, Generate; the picture arrived. RUNS 2.

Runs: 2 pictures.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Concept fields with the five small buttons; "+ Add concept" adds a field; × removes one.
- Weight slider: −2 to 2; a positive weight shows "AND", a negative one "NOT".
- Combination chips: where the concepts are combined, as the sentence under them says.
- Normalize weights: divides the weights by their sum; with 1, 1 and −1 the sum is already 1.
- Generate: one picture; a status line "Composable generation in progress..." while it runs.
- Advanced settings, RUNS strip, Hide column, Help: as elsewhere.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- In the denoiser (cat on a sofa AND sunny living room NOT window): a tabby cat lying on a beige sofa in warm side light, an orange wall behind, no window in the frame. All three instructions are met.
- In the embedding, same concepts and weights: a noise picture, black, white and dark-green pixel blocks over the whole square, no object. The one-time mix of the three embeddings with a negative weight produced a vector the model could not turn into a picture.
- The same three concepts and weights gave a usable picture at one site and noise at the other; the sentence under the chips names the difference, the surface does not warn.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Nothing says that a negative weight at the embedding site can give noise, or that the noise is the result and not an error.
- "Normalize weights (sum to 1.0)" is ticked by default and does nothing visible for 1, 1, −1.
- The slider's AND / NOT badge is the only explanation of the weights' meaning.
- The example prompts are pairs; the third concept and the NOT have no example.
- "Composable generation in progress..." stands under the references, far from the run button.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The page has no Help text of its own. It should first say what the instrument is for: composing a picture out of several concepts, each with its own weight, and watching what the weights do, which is a question of composition before it is a question of the model. Positive weight: the concept pulls the picture its way (AND); negative weight: it pushes the picture away from it (NOT). Then the two places of combination, because the difference between them is the content of this surface: "In the denoiser" every concept keeps its own pull at every step, and the picture holds them together as a montage holds its parts; "In the embedding" the concepts are mixed once into one before the run, as a double exposure melts two pictures into one, which works for close concepts and gives noise for a subtraction. It should say that the noise is the result and not an error. It should say that the weight the slider sets is not the weight the eye reads, and that the picture is where the two meet: size, place, colour and sharpness are what the model made of the number. It should say that the heart on the picture keeps it in the favourites, from where a picture goes on to the Flow board as material, so a series made here can be continued there. And it should say that the seed is fixed, so the same concepts and weights give the same picture, which is what makes a series comparable, and that Normalize divides the weights by their sum.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Compose by hand first: two motifs from the own sketchbook as cut-outs on paper, one dominant; then the same two as concepts at three weight pairs (2 / 0.5, 1 / 1, 0.5 / 2) in the denoiser, same seed; keep the three with the heart, put them next to the paper, and read where the model's weight shows: in size, place, colour, sharpness.
- The same two concepts at both sites: montage in the denoiser, blend in the embedding; keep the noise picture as the record of what a blend cannot do.
- A third concept with a negative weight: a thing, then a colour, then a mood; write down what left the picture and what filled the gap.
- The example pair "the street where I live, in the morning, seen through the eyes of a child" / "… of an adult" at 1.5 / 0.5 and 0.5 / 1.5: what the model uses for "child" (colour, scale, viewpoint, objects), and whether that is a child's seeing or a cliché of it.
- A series over one weight: one concept held at 1, the other from −2 to 2 in steps of 0.5; keep every picture; read the series as one work.
- Four concepts: watch how much each one gets, and which one the picture drops first.
- Constellations that no plain prompt reaches: weights above 1 and below 0 together, a NOT on something the AND needs; compare with the same concepts written as one plain prompt on the same model, and keep what the plain prompt cannot give.
- Take one picture from the favourites onto the Flow board and continue it: a perspective, a sound, a video.
- Compare the montage with a photomontage from art history (Hannah Höch, 1919; Max Ernst's collage novels, 1929) and the blend with a double exposure: where the seam is visible, and whether a seam is wanted.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument is a composition instrument. Two or more concepts go in, each with its own weight, and one picture comes out; the judgement the picture asks for is the one art lessons train: what dominates, what recedes, what is left out, how the parts are joined, and whether the result is one the maker stands behind. The two places of combination make two ways of joining visible that art has used for a century, montage and blend, and the difference between them is what there is to see. And the weights reach constellations that a written prompt does not, which is material for the own work.

**S1 — Weight by hand, weight by number** (formal, art, grades 7–10, 90 min). Pupils bring two motifs from their current work, a thing and a place. First by hand: a quick paper composition of the two, cut-outs or a drawing, in which one of them is to dominate; the choice is written under it in one line. Then the same two motifs as concepts, in the denoiser, same seed, at three weight pairs: 2 / 0.5, 1 / 1, 0.5 / 2. The three pictures are kept with the heart and printed or shown next to the paper. Reading: where does the model's weight show, in size, in place, in colour, in sharpness, in what is in front; does the 2 / 0.5 picture dominate the way the paper does; which of the four compositions does the pupil stand behind, and did seeing the model's three change the judgement of the own one. Sequence: 20 min paper composition; 10 min concepts and first run; 20 min two more runs and the hearts; 25 min reading in pairs; 15 min plenary on weight as a number and weight as a thing the eye reads. Subject link: composition, dominance, visual weight; the own decision next to the model's. Uncertainty: I did not run the weight series; only one run per site was made, with three concepts.

**S2 — Montage or blend** (formal, art, grades 9–13, 2 × 45 min). The class looks at a photomontage (Hannah Höch, "Cut with the Kitchen Knife", 1919) and at a double exposure, and names the difference: in the montage every part keeps its edge and its own light, in the blend two pictures become one surface. Pairs then make both by hand with the same two motifs, a collage of cut-outs and a tracing-paper overlay. Then the model: the same two concepts at 1 / 1, once "In the denoiser" and once "In the embedding", same seed, both kept. Four pictures on the wall per pair. Reading: which of the model's two is the montage and which the blend, and by what in the picture they can tell; where the seam is, and whether they want it. Then the question the framework's classroom example asks of the three kinds of work: for the collage, the overlay, the model's montage and the model's blend, which choices did the pupil make (what, where, how big, which weight, which place) and which did the model make (everything the seed decided), which of the four they would sign, and whose the model's pictures are. Sequence: 15 min Höch and the double exposure; 30 min collage and overlay; 20 min two runs; 25 min reading on the wall. Subject link: montage and blend as two ways of putting two things into one picture; authorship. Uncertainty: the embedding site gave a usable picture for close concepts in the page's own examples and noise for the subtraction; for two plain motifs at 1 / 1 the result was not seen.

**S3 — Leaving out** (formal, art or language teaching, grades 8–11, 45 min). Two concepts at 1 / 1 and a third at −1, in the denoiser: first a thing (a window), then a colour (red), then a mood (cheerful). After each run two notes: what left the picture, and what filled the place where it was. The class compares with the oldest means of composition, the omission: what a picture does not show and how the empty place carries the rest. Then the criterion is written on the board, "the thing is gone and the rest of the picture stayed", and each of the three runs is held against it; the model pushes a thing out and does not remove a property bound to an object or a whole register. Sequence: 10 min concepts; 15 min three runs; 10 min notes; 10 min criterion and comparison. Subject link: omission and the empty place; what an instruction can and cannot take out. Uncertainty: the window left the picture; a colour and a mood were not tried.

**S4 - Unlikely Constellations**. (non-formal, art workshop, age 10+, 2 h). Class experiments with combinations in order to achieve images that could not be prompted conventionally. They compare these images to traditionally prompted images using the same model. They use the results for art creation (-> flow) and/or reflect upon how a model achieves order between different elements in the prompt.

**S5 — Two readings of one street** (formal, art or ethics, grades 7–10, 45 min). The example pair, the street where I live, in the morning, seen through the eyes of a child and seen through the eyes of an adult, at 1.5 / 0.5 and then 0.5 / 1.5, same seed. Pupils list what the model used for "child": colour, scale, viewpoint, the objects it put in; then they say whether that is how a child sees a street or how pictures of children's seeing look. The sentence "the model saw it as a child would" is held against that list and rewritten: the model has no eyes and no childhood, it turned the words into the patterns that go with them in its data. Then each pupil writes two readings of their own street in one line each, and one pair is run. Sequence: 10 min two runs; 15 min lists and the rewritten sentence; 20 min own readings and one run. Subject link: perspective as a decision in the prompt (the platform's separation of what from how); cliché. Uncertainty: I did not run the child/adult pair.

**S6 — The series as a work** (non-formal, art workshop, age 14+, 2 h). Participants choose two concepts of their own and build a series over one weight: the first held at 1, the second from −2 to 2 in steps of 0.5, nine pictures, same seed, every one kept with the heart. The series is read as one work, left to right: where the second concept enters, where it takes over, where the picture breaks. Each participant chooses the one picture of the nine they would continue, takes it from the favourites onto the Flow board and gives it a perspective or a sound; the series and the continued picture are shown together at the end. Sequence: 15 min concepts; 45 min nine runs; 30 min reading the series; 30 min continuation on Flow and the showing. Subject link: the series as a form of work and of knowledge; the result as material. Uncertainty: I did not try taking a favourite from this surface onto the Flow board; the Flow report (01) describes the favourites bar.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S6)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Create 2 Basic — "Learners use AI to generate an image, story or model to represent an idea." S1: two motifs from the own work as concepts, one picture per weight pair, and the written line under each on what the weight did to the picture and whether it dominates the way the paper composition does; the framework's classroom example has learners generate one image and write how specific elements of their prompt shaped the result and how well it matches the idea they had in mind.
- Create 2 Intermediate — "Learners experiment with AI tools (e.g., text, image or music generators) to develop diverse ideas and produce varied outputs." S2, S4 and S6: the same concepts at two sites, constellations that no plain prompt reaches next to plainly prompted pictures from the same model, and a series of nine over one weight, compared for what each combination made of the same idea; the framework's classroom example compares how different prompts and tools produce varied interpretations of the same idea.
- Create 1 Basic — "Learners explore how different AI tools can expand their thinking or spark new ideas." S4: combinations that could not be prompted conventionally, taken as material for art creation on Flow; the framework's classroom example has learners write new stories inspired by unexpected results.
- Create 1 Intermediate — "Learners compare AI-generated suggestions to their own ideas during a brainstorming process." S1: the paper composition is made before the model's three pictures are seen, and the pair discusses which of the four they stand behind and whether seeing the model's versions changed the judgement of their own; the framework's classroom example has learners brainstorm independently before reviewing AI-generated ideas and discuss how exposure to them shapes originality and confidence.
- Create 4 Advanced — "Learners assess the ethical implications of AI-generated outputs for creative work, distinguish inspiration from replication in their outputs, and justify how their use of AI maintains authenticity and respects other creators." S2: collage, overlay, model montage and model blend on one wall, and for each the choices the pupil made and the choices the model made, which they would sign, and whose the model's pictures are; the framework's classroom example puts human-made, AI-generated and human-with-AI work side by side and asks which choices a human did or did not make and who should be credited.
- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S3: a NOT is a negative weight on a prediction at every step, which pushes a thing out and does not take a property or a register out, held against the idea that the model understood an instruction not to show something.
- Engage 2 Basic — "Learners know AI is a non-human tool that produces outputs based on patterns of data and lacks authentic context or understanding." S5: the sentence "the model saw it as a child would" held against the list of what the model used for "child" and rewritten, as the framework's classroom example has learners identify misleading phrases and develop better descriptions.
- Shape 2 Basic — "Learners define criteria for whether an AI system has accomplished a task." S3: the criterion "the thing is gone and the rest of the picture stayed", written by the class and applied to a thing, a colour and a mood; the framework's classroom example has learners define what would make the system successful and compare it across different cases.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

--

**Beyond the framework**: the framework's Create competences have learners generate, vary and combine; the judgement they ask for is whether the result matches the idea. Here the judgement is a compositional one, dominance, omission, the seam between two parts, and it needs what art lessons train and what a hand composition next to the model's makes visible. The two places of combination put montage and blend side by side, two ways of joining that art has used since the photomontage of 1919, and the difference between them is the subject of the surface. The framework has no competence for aesthetic judgement and none for the history of composition; this platform places its Latent Lab under the paradigm of aesthetic and artistic research, and this instrument is one of its instruments.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 1, 3, 4, Create 3.

instruments.help_should_say: The page has no Help text of its own. It should first say what the instrument is for: composing a picture out of several concepts, each with its own weight, and watching what the weights do, which is a question of composition before it is a question of the model. Positive weight: the concept pulls the picture its way (AND); negative weight: it pushes the picture away from it (NOT). Then the two places of combination, because the difference between them is the content of this surface: "In the denoiser" every concept keeps its own pull at every step, and the picture holds them together as a montage holds its parts; "In the embedding" the concepts are mixed once into one before the run, as a double exposure melts two pictures into one, which works for close concepts and gives noise for a subtraction. It should say that the noise is the result and not an error. It should say that the weight the slider sets is not the weight the eye reads, and that the picture is where the two meet: size, place, colour and sharpness are what the model made of the number. It should say that the heart on the picture keeps it in the favourites, from where a picture goes on to the Flow board as material, so a series made here can be continued there. And it should say that the seed is fixed, so the same concepts and weights give the same picture, which is what makes a series comparable, and that Normalize divides the weights by their sum.
possibilities: Compose by hand first: two motifs from the own sketchbook as cut-outs on paper, one dominant; then the same two as concepts at three weight pairs (2 / 0.5, 1 / 1, 0.5 / 2) in the denoiser, same seed; keep the three with the heart, put them next to the paper, and read where the model's weight shows: in size, place, colour, sharpness.
The same two concepts at both sites: montage in the denoiser, blend in the embedding; keep the noise picture as the record of what a blend cannot do.
A third concept with a negative weight: a thing, then a colour, then a mood; write down what left the picture and what filled the gap.

The example pair "the street where I live, in the morning, seen through the eyes of a child" / "… of an adult" at 1.5 / 0.5 and 0.5 / 1.5: what the model uses for "child" (colour, scale, viewpoint, objects), and whether that is a child's seeing or a cliché of it.
A series over one weight: one concept held at 1, the other from −2 to 2 in steps of 0.5; keep every picture; read the series as one work.
Four concepts: watch how much each one gets, and which one the picture drops first.

Constellations that no plain prompt reaches: weights above 1 and below 0 together, a NOT on something the AND needs; compare with the same concepts written as one plain prompt on the same model, and keep what the plain prompt cannot give.
Take one picture from the favourites onto the Flow board and continue it: a perspective, a sound, a video.

Compare the montage with a photomontage from art history (Hannah Höch, 1919; Max Ernst's collage novels, 1929) and the blend with a double exposure: where the seam is visible, and whether a seam is wanted.
instruments.scenarios_intro: The instrument is a composition instrument. Two or more concepts go in, each with its own weight, and one picture comes out; the judgement the picture asks for is the one art lessons train: what dominates, what recedes, what is left out, how the parts are joined, and whether the result is one the maker stands behind. The two places of combination make two ways of joining visible that art has used for a century, montage and blend, and the difference between them is what there is to see. And the weights reach constellations that a written prompt does not, which is material for the own work.

scenarios.title: Weight by hand, weight by number
scenarios.setting: formal, art, grades 7–10, 90 min
scenarios.text: Pupils bring two motifs from their current work, a thing and a place. First by hand: a quick paper composition of the two, cut-outs or a drawing, in which one of them is to dominate; the choice is written under it in one line. Then the same two motifs as concepts, in the denoiser, same seed, at three weight pairs: 2 / 0.5, 1 / 1, 0.5 / 2. The three pictures are kept with the heart and printed or shown next to the paper. Reading: where does the model's weight show, in size, in place, in colour, in sharpness, in what is in front; does the 2 / 0.5 picture dominate the way the paper does; which of the four compositions does the pupil stand behind, and did seeing the model's three change the judgement of the own one.
scenarios.sequence: 20 min paper composition; 10 min concepts and first run; 20 min two more runs and the hearts; 25 min reading in pairs; 15 min plenary on weight as a number and weight as a thing the eye reads.
scenarios.subject_link: composition, dominance, visual weight; the own decision next to the model's.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not run the weight series; only one run per site was made, with three concepts.

scenarios.title: Montage or blend
scenarios.setting: formal, art, grades 9–13, 2 × 45 min
scenarios.text: The class looks at a photomontage (Hannah Höch, "Cut with the Kitchen Knife", 1919) and at a double exposure, and names the difference: in the montage every part keeps its edge and its own light, in the blend two pictures become one surface. Pairs then make both by hand with the same two motifs, a collage of cut-outs and a tracing-paper overlay. Then the model: the same two concepts at 1 / 1, once "In the denoiser" and once "In the embedding", same seed, both kept. Four pictures on the wall per pair. Reading: which of the model's two is the montage and which the blend, and by what in the picture they can tell; where the seam is, and whether they want it. Then the question the framework's classroom example asks of the three kinds of work: for the collage, the overlay, the model's montage and the model's blend, which choices did the pupil make (what, where, how big, which weight, which place) and which did the model make (everything the seed decided), which of the four they would sign, and whose the model's pictures are.
scenarios.sequence: 15 min Höch and the double exposure; 30 min collage and overlay; 20 min two runs; 25 min reading on the wall.
scenarios.subject_link: montage and blend as two ways of putting two things into one picture; authorship.
scenarios.uncertainty: the embedding site gave a usable picture for close concepts in the page's own examples and noise for the subtraction; for two plain motifs at 1 / 1 the result was not seen.

scenarios.title: Leaving out
scenarios.setting: formal, art or language teaching, grades 8–11, 45 min
scenarios.text: Two concepts at 1 / 1 and a third at −1, in the denoiser: first a thing (a window), then a colour (red), then a mood (cheerful). After each run two notes: what left the picture, and what filled the place where it was. The class compares with the oldest means of composition, the omission: what a picture does not show and how the empty place carries the rest. Then the criterion is written on the board, "the thing is gone and the rest of the picture stayed", and each of the three runs is held against it; the model pushes a thing out and does not remove a property bound to an object or a whole register.
scenarios.sequence: 10 min concepts; 15 min three runs; 10 min notes; 10 min criterion and comparison.
scenarios.subject_link: omission and the empty place; what an instruction can and cannot take out.
scenarios.uncertainty: the window left the picture; a colour and a mood were not tried.

scenarios.title: Unlikely Constellations
scenarios.setting: non-formal, art workshop, age 10+, 2 h
scenarios.text: Class experiments with combinations in order to achieve images that could not be prompted conventionally. They compare these images to traditionally prompted images using the same model. They use the results for art creation (-> flow) and/or reflect upon how a model achieves order between different elements in the prompt.

scenarios.title: Two readings of one street
scenarios.setting: formal, art or ethics, grades 7–10, 45 min
scenarios.text: The example pair, the street where I live, in the morning, seen through the eyes of a child and seen through the eyes of an adult, at 1.5 / 0.5 and then 0.5 / 1.5, same seed. Pupils list what the model used for "child": colour, scale, viewpoint, the objects it put in; then they say whether that is how a child sees a street or how pictures of children's seeing look. The sentence "the model saw it as a child would" is held against that list and rewritten: the model has no eyes and no childhood, it turned the words into the patterns that go with them in its data. Then each pupil writes two readings of their own street in one line each, and one pair is run.
scenarios.sequence: 10 min two runs; 15 min lists and the rewritten sentence; 20 min own readings and one run.
scenarios.subject_link: perspective as a decision in the prompt (the platform's separation of what from how); cliché.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not run the child/adult pair.

scenarios.title: The series as a work
scenarios.setting: non-formal, art workshop, age 14+, 2 h
scenarios.text: Participants choose two concepts of their own and build a series over one weight: the first held at 1, the second from −2 to 2 in steps of 0.5, nine pictures, same seed, every one kept with the heart. The series is read as one work, left to right: where the second concept enters, where it takes over, where the picture breaks. Each participant chooses the one picture of the nine they would continue, takes it from the favourites onto the Flow board and gives it a perspective or a sound; the series and the continued picture are shown together at the end.
scenarios.sequence: 15 min concepts; 45 min nine runs; 30 min reading the series; 30 min continuation on Flow and the showing.
scenarios.subject_link: the series as a form of work and of knowledge; the result as material.
scenarios.uncertainty: I did not try taking a favourite from this surface onto the Flow board; the Flow report (01) describes the favourites bar.

instruments.name: Encoder Fusion Workbench

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/fusion-workbench` (sidebar "Enc. Fus. Workbench", tooltip "3-axis comparison"). Preparing column: the prompt field prefilled with the house sentence ("A house stands in a landscape, surrounded by farmland, nature and animals. Some people can be seen."); under it the hint "Short text: T5 reads in barely more here than CLIP does. The perspectives in the field make a text out of a sentence — 'Your Story' is written for that."; a button "T5 expand" that opens a textarea "Optional T5 enrichment — added to the T5 encoder only, held constant across the sweep"; "X · columns" with a select set to "Fusion strategy" and five chips (Centered Fade, Legacy, Dual Alpha, Slerp, Normalized), all preselected; "Y · rows" with a select set to "Denoising window" and three ranges, "composition" Steps 1–8, "semantics" Steps 9–17, "detail" Steps 18–25, each with a two-handle slider and two number fields, and the sentence "The fusion is injected only in the steps the window covers, of 25 in the run."; "Z · slider" set to "No third axis" ("Two axes then carry the sweep, and this axis shows no slider."); a block "Fusion formula (active)" that prints the formula of the selected strategies (Centered Fade: core = w_C·CLIP + w_T5·T5, tail = T5 ×1, h=1; α≤0: w_C=max(1,−α), w_T5=1+α; α>0: w_C=1−α, w_T5=max(1,α); Legacy: core=(1−α)·CLIP+α·T5; Dual Alpha: tail=0.15·α·T5; Slerp: the spherical interpolation formula; Normalized: tail = T5·‖core‖/‖T5‖; and the key "core = the first 77 token positions (CLIP-L+CLIP-G, padded to 4096d) blended with T5; tail = the T5-only remainder (positions 78–512). α is the fusion strength value."); Advanced settings with α 20, CFG 5.5, entry block 0, seed 42, negative prompt, steps 25; the sentence "Assign the axes, then run a sweep. Each cell is recorded to the research store (purpose: workbench)." Right: an empty grid headed "Denoising window \ Fusion strategy", three rows, five columns.
2. Pressed "T5 expand" and wrote into the T5 field a second scene that is not in the prompt: "A lighthouse stands on a rocky coast at night. A storm is coming in from the sea, and a small boat is heading for the harbour." Kept the house prompt.
3. Clicked four strategy chips off, so that only Centered Fade remained; the run button's title changed from "Run sweep · 15 cells" to "Run sweep · 3 cells". Ran at 23:56:50. The header counted "Image 0 / 3 … 3 / 3" and named the weight file ("sd3.5_large.safetensors · local", at other moments "stable-diffusion-3.5-large · local").
4. Clicked Centered Fade off and Slerp on ("Run sweep · 3 cells"), ran again; three pictures.
5. Read the six pictures (3 below).

Runs: 2 sweeps, 6 pictures.

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Prompt field: as on the other picture surfaces (Copy, Paste, Choose Perspective, Translate, Delete).
- T5 expand: shows the second field; its text goes to the T5 encoder only and stays the same in every cell.
- X / Y / Z selects: assign what varies along columns, rows and a third axis; with "No third axis" the slider is hidden.
- Strategy chips: toggle; the run button's title counts the cells (strategies × windows).
- Window sliders and number fields: set the step range of each row; the three defaults cover 1–8, 9–17, 18–25.
- Fusion formula block: changes with the selected strategies; it is a display, not a control.
- Advanced settings: α, CFG, entry block, seed, negative prompt, steps.
- Run sweep: one picture per cell, same seed, the header counts; cells fill as they arrive.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- Centered Fade, Steps 1–8 (composition): two pictures stacked. At the top a black gabled house on a green hill under a grey sky, with a figure at its wall; below, as if hung on a wall, a darker scene with a pond, two cows drinking and a longhorn walking in at the lower left.
- Centered Fade, Steps 9–17 (semantics): a wall-like block of straw-yellow texture across the whole middle of the picture, with a pig and a person perched on its top edge and a lawn and trees behind; the house is reduced to a roof silhouette on the block. The scene is dismembered.
- Centered Fade, Steps 18–25 (detail): a white farmhouse with a brown roof, sheep and cows in front, trees, a sunlit field with fine vertical streaks over it. Close to what the plain prompt gives.
- Slerp, Steps 1–8: a house with lit windows and people inside, standing on a floating block of clipped hedge, the block mirrored upside down beneath it, two goats in the sky below. A surreal composition.
- Slerp, Steps 9–17: a white house with a dark roof, cows, a truck and a jeep in front, trees. Ordinary.
- Slerp, Steps 18–25: a white house with sheep, cows and hedges, vertical rain-like streaks over the field. Ordinary with a texture artefact.
- Across the grid: the row changes the picture far more than the column. Fusion in the first eight steps produces a composition of two pictures in both strategies; in the middle steps it damages the scene (Centered Fade) or leaves it ordinary (Slerp); in the last steps it adds a streak texture and nothing else. The lighthouse, the storm and the boat given to T5 alone appear in none of the six pictures as objects; the dark pond and the rain streaks are the most that could be read as traces of "storm" and "sea".
- The grid shows row and column headers only; α, seed and the active formula stand in the preparing column, not at the cell.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Five strategies preselected: the first press would compute 15 pictures; the number stands only in the button's tooltip.
- X, Y, Z and the formula block are the language of a parameter sweep; nothing says what one would look for in a row or a column.
- α stands in Advanced settings as a number (20); with the formula on the screen a user can compute that Centered Fade with α=20 sets w_C to −19 and w_T5 to 20, but nothing says what α means here or how it relates to the slider of the Encoder Fusion surface.
- The T5 field is hidden behind "T5 expand", and the hint under the prompt speaks of "Your Story", a perspective that is on another surface.
- "Each cell is recorded to the research store (purpose: workbench)": a user does not know what the store is or who reads it.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: Choose which fusion strategies form the columns and which denoising windows form the rows; each cell is one picture from the same prompt and seed, with the fusion applied only in the steps its row covers. The optional text behind "T5 expand" goes to the T5 encoder alone and is the same in every cell, so a difference between cells never comes from it. The sweep computes one picture per cell; the header counts them. Read along a row to see what the strategy changes and down a column to see what the window changes; the formula block states what the active strategy computes, and the pictures are recorded for research.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- One strategy, the three windows: see at which stage of the denoising the fusion acts on composition, on objects, or on texture only.
- Two strategies, one window: see whether the strategy matters where the window is held constant.
- The same sweep with and without a T5 enrichment, and look for the enrichment in the pictures.
- Change the seed in Advanced settings and run the same sweep again to separate what the seed does from what the window does.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — Where in the process does the mixture act?** (formal, art or computer science, grades 11–13, 90 min). Pairs keep one strategy and the three default windows, run the sweep, and write for each of the three pictures what changed against the plain picture: the arrangement, the objects, or the surface. Then they switch to a second strategy and compare the two rows. Sequence: 10 min setting the axes; 30 min first sweep (used for reading the formula block); 30 min second sweep and the table of changes; 20 min plenary on the stages of denoising. Subject link: process of image generation, early and late steps.

**S2 — The hidden sentence** (non-formal, media workshop, 2 h, age 15+). Groups write a second scene into the T5 field that the prompt does not contain, run one strategy over the three windows, and search the pictures for any trace of the second scene; then they discuss what it means that a text given to one encoder can leave no object in the picture. Sequence: 15 min writing the two texts; 45 min sweep; 30 min searching and comparing; 30 min discussion. Subject link: how a prompt reaches a model through several encoders.

**S3 — Reading a formula against a picture** (formal, mathematics or computer science, grades 12–13, 45 min). The class reads the formula of the active strategy, computes the weights for the α in Advanced settings (for Centered Fade with α=20: w_C = 1−α = −19, w_T5 = max(1,α) = 20) and for α=0, then runs one cell each and describes what a negative weight on CLIP does to the picture. Subject link: weighted sums, interpolation.
