instruments.name: LoRA Training

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/lora-sd35` (sidebar "LoRA Training", tooltip "Training takes 1-3 hours and blocks image generation"). Preparing column: "Project Name" (placeholder "e.g. Our School Building"); "Trigger Words" (placeholder "e.g. our_school_building, schoolyard, classroom") with the hint "Comma-separated tags. First = primary trigger, rest = additional tags per image."; "Training Images (10–50 recommended)" with a drop zone "Click or drop images here"; a note "LoRA Training" with "Training setup" (Repeats × epochs 40 × 10; Rank (dim / alpha) 32 / 16; Learning rate 0.0004, cosine; Optimizer AdamW8bit; Resolution, buckets 1024×1024, 512–2048; Text encoder trained along; Batch size 1; Intermediate states every 2 epochs) and "Cost per run": "1–3 hours of the GPU. At this GPU's 600 W limit that is roughly 0.6–1.8 kWh and 240–720 g CO₂ (400 g/kWh, German grid). A single tree would need 4–12 days to take up that amount. (Ask yourselves how many trees it takes to absorb the CO₂ that training a whole model produces!) An estimate." Right: a monospace panel "Waiting for training to start...". Run button "Start Training". The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "This is about extending the image model Stable Diffusion 3.5. The model itself cannot be changed, but a LoRA model can be added to it: what is learned is not the model again but a small number of additional values, which shift the output towards your images as soon as your trigger word stands in the prompt. Before training, a captioning model looks at every uploaded image and writes down what it recognises — so what a machine recognised takes part in deciding what is learned." "Three things can be learned here: to curate — to assemble a series from your own material and to give aesthetic reasons for the selection as well as for the exclusions, under conditions of scarcity. To sound out the dimensions of responsibility in that selection. First towards the image material: it is processed into something that is no longer an image. Everything depicted is taken out of its context and processed into a small piece of a large statistical collection of numbers. Second towards the training energy: the reason we train a LoRA should be able to justify the energy it consumes. And to understand in practice what is fixed in a large image model and what can be attached to it: does the model learn style or content, and does it learn what was defined beforehand, or something else?" I overlooked it on first use.
2. Project Name "Atelier house series", Trigger Words "atelierhaus, farmhouse, landscape". Uploaded a small series of eight pictures generated earlier on the picture surfaces (farmhouses, a king, a cat on a sofa, a lake). The zone showed "8 images selected" and, at once, "Describing your images … 0 of 8" with a strip of eight cards, each a thumbnail and a text field "waiting to be described", and a button "Describe all again". The descriptions are written by a vision model on the server's queue; they arrived one by one.
3. Pressed "Start Training" at 11:22:09. A modal "GPU VRAM Check" opened: a bar "87 GB / 95.6 GB used · 7.9 GB free", the line "Not enough free VRAM for training (need 50 GB). Clear VRAM to continue?", the estimate "This run: ~0.6–1.8 kWh, ~240–720 g CO₂. A single tree would need ~4–12 days to take up that amount.", and two buttons "Clear ComfyUI + LLM VRAM" and "Cancel". The server log recorded "Detected GPU VRAM: 95.6 GB" and an auto-configuration for 95 GB (batch size 1, no gradient checkpointing, latents cached to disk, 16 workers).
4. Pressed "Cancel" at 11:24:25. Clearing the VRAM would have unloaded the models that the other running jobs (Bias Research 2, the Re-enactment's song, other users) were using; that is outside "VRAM check and preparation stage". The panel on the right stayed at "Waiting for training to start..."; the descriptions kept arriving.
5. Read the descriptions (3 below) and stopped there.

Runs: none (no training).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Project Name, Trigger Words: text; the hint explains the comma list.
- Drop zone: takes several pictures; the count appears; the description strip appears and starts filling by itself.
- Caption cards: each description is an editable text field; "Describe all again" redoes them.
- Start Training: first the VRAM check; with enough free memory it would start the run and log into the right panel; with too little it offers to clear the server's VRAM or to cancel.
- The note: the fixed training setup and the cost estimate, which the modal repeats for the run.
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
- The VRAM check refused: 7.9 GB free of 95.6, 50 GB needed. The memory was held by the image model, the language models and the audio models of the other instruments in use at that moment (the card is shared by everyone on the server).
- Five of eight descriptions by 11:32, each one long sentence from the vision model, for example for the farmhouse with sheep: "This photograph captures a serene pastoral scene featuring a solitary cream-colored farmhouse nestled on a sun-drenched, rolling green hillside, framed by a dense, shadowed forested backdrop, with scattered livestock and several human figures dispersed across the foreground meadow, rendered in warm, natural daylight with soft, diffused lighting …"; for the second farmhouse: "This AI-generated pastoral scene features a whimsical, storybook-style farmhouse with a white facade, wooden shutters, and a tiled roof …" (the describer called the generated picture AI-generated); for the lake: "This photograph captures a serene, expansive body of water in the foreground with subtle, rhythmic ripples …"; for the king: "A regal, weathered king with a thick gray beard and intense gaze is captured in a dramatic, painterly portrait, crowned with an ornate golden crown …". The trigger words were not yet in the texts; the hint says the first word becomes the primary trigger and the rest additional tags per image, which presumably happens when the captions are assembled for training.
- Once all eight descriptions had arrived, the strip's heading read: "A model wrote these. What stands here is what the training reads — correct it if it got your images wrong."
- Where it stands at the stop: eight pictures uploaded and described, the trigger words set, no training started, the right panel at "Waiting for training to start...".

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- The descriptions start by themselves on upload; the Help text says that a captioning model writes down what it recognises before training, and the strip says so only once all eight are there.
- "Not enough free VRAM … Clear VRAM to continue?" with a button that clears the whole server's models: a user cannot know who else is using them.
- The recommended 10–50 pictures and the 1–3 hours are in the labels; the "blocks image generation" of the tooltip is only in the sidebar.
- The right panel says "Waiting for training to start..." both before and after a cancelled check.
- "Rank (dim / alpha) 32 / 16", "AdamW8bit", "buckets": the setup is named for someone who trains; nothing says what the user should change (nothing, apparently; it is fixed).
- The cost estimate is the most readable text in the form and, apart from the Help text, the only one that addresses the user directly.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says what a LoRA adds to Stable Diffusion 3.5, that the output shifts towards your images once the trigger word stands in the prompt, that a captioning model describes every uploaded image before training, and what is learned about curating, responsibility and energy. It should add the handling: write the trigger word first and tags after it, and drop ten to fifty pictures; the descriptions are editable, and the trigger word is put in front of every description for training; "Start Training" first checks the card's free memory, and if other models hold the 50 GB it offers to unload them, which interrupts whatever else is running on the server; a run takes one to three hours, blocks picture generation meanwhile, and costs what the note estimates; intermediate adapters are saved every two epochs and the finished adapter appears in the LoRA Explorer. It should say where the result is read, in the Explorer's own words: "The third row against the second is the reach: what the training added on top of what the words already carried. The fourth row against the first is the limit: whether the adapter also answers when it is not called, which is how it shows that it has overwritten what the model knew rather than added to it." And it should say what is trained: the adapters attach to the denoiser and to the two CLIP text encoders, T5 stays frozen, and SD 3.5 Large is the only trainable model (the platform's own overview). The Help's last question is the instrument's: does the model learn style or content, and does it learn what was defined beforehand, or something else.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- Try to put your own place into the model: twenty to forty pictures of your street, your school, your region (buildings, objects, landscapes, no people), a trigger word, a training, and the next day the Explorer with motifs from the series and from outside it; read the reach and the limit.
- Try to correct a default: find something the base model gets wrong about what you know (the storybook farmhouse, the person at work), gather pictures that show it as it is, train, and see whether thirty pictures and a card correct it or lay a varnish over the model's own.
- Decide the series together: what goes in, what stays out, one reason per exclusion; the Help names this as what there is to learn, aesthetic reasons under scarcity.
- Read the captions as what the machine saw of your pictures and correct where it saw something else; then see in the Explorer whether the correction was learned.
- Two adapters, one on a narrow series and one on a mixed one, or one on eight pictures and one on thirty (two sessions): compare in the Explorer what size and mixture did.
- Weigh the energy: the note's estimate against the reason for the training, decided by the group that trains.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
The instrument is the one place on the platform where a group changes a model instead of a prompt, with means a school has: thirty pictures, a word, one card for one to three hours. What it teaches is how far such means reach into a model trained at the cost of millions, and where they stop: the Explorer's third row against its second is the reach, its fourth against its first the limit, and a motif the series never showed asks whether a manner carried over or the subjects came along. The decisions are the group's: what the model is to learn, which pictures stand for it, what the caption says, whether the reason justifies the energy. The question underneath is cultural: whether a local form, a group's manner, a place as its people know it, can be made to hold in a model, and what of the model's own order survives the attempt.

**S1 — Our place in the model** (formal, art, geography or local history, grades 9–13, two sessions of 90 min and a training in between). The class collects thirty pictures of its own place, buildings, objects, landscapes, no people, and decides together which go in and which stay out, with a reason written for every exclusion; the trigger word is the place's name. The captions are read and corrected where the describer saw something else than the class knows to be there. The training runs between the sessions. In the second session the LoRA Explorer runs with motifs from the series ("a house", "a street in the morning") and one the series never showed; the class reads the third row against the second for what the training added, the fourth against the first for whether the adapter answers uncalled, and the outside motif for whether the place came along as subjects or as a manner. The closing question is whether the model took the place in, or put a varnish of it over its own houses. Sequence (session 1): 20 min selection and reasons; 15 min captions; 10 min start and the VRAM check; (session 2): 30 min Explorer; 40 min reading; 20 min plenary. Subject link: the local and the default; representation of place; dataset, caption, trigger word. Uncertainty: the training needs 50 GB free and one to three hours; the shared server did not have the memory.

**S2 — Correcting a default** (formal, art or ethics, grades 10–13, two sessions). The class first finds a default in the base model that it knows to be wrong or narrow (the describer called a generated farmhouse "storybook-style"; the Explorer's base rows for "a person at work" are another), then assembles twenty to forty pictures that show the thing as the class knows it, trains, and reads in the Explorer whether the correction holds with the trigger word, without it, and on motifs the series never showed. The finding is the limit: what thirty pictures can correct in a model and what the model keeps, and the class writes it down as such. Subject link: the default as a claim about the world; correction with one's own material; the limit of correctability. Uncertainty: not run; the outcome is not known to me.

**S3 — What the machine saw** (formal, language teaching or art, grades 9–12, 45 min, no training). Pupils upload a series of their own pictures (objects, not faces), wait for the descriptions, and correct each one by hand: what is wrong, what is missing, what the describer added; each description is checked against the picture it describes. Then they discuss that what is learned is decided by whoever writes the sentence, and that the sentence is theirs now. Sequence: 10 min upload; 20 min reading; 15 min corrections and discussion. Subject link: description, caption, dataset; the author of the training text.

**S4 — What it costs, and for what** (formal, ethics or physics, grades 10–13, 45 min). The class reads the note's estimate (0.6–1.8 kWh, 240–720 g CO₂, 4–12 tree-days) and the VRAM check's numbers, and the Help's sentence that the reason for training should be able to justify the energy; it writes a one-page sheet that puts the run's kWh beside the classroom's devices and beside a published figure for training a large model, and then decides, with reasons given, whether its own reason for a training carries the run. Subject link: energy, units, scale; a decision taken together. Uncertainty: the figures on the surface are stated as an estimate; the class treats them as such.

**S5 — A manner of our own** (non-formal, art workshop, age 14+, two days). The group agrees on a manner before drawing (a palette, a line, a way of framing) and makes twenty to forty drawings in it, together; the adapter is trained on them. Day 2 in the Explorer: motifs from the drawings and from outside; the group marks in the adapter's pictures what of its manner is recognisable, whether the adapter brings the group's subjects along, and whether it answers uncalled. Then three things side by side: their drawings, the adapter's pictures, and pictures made with the adapter by them; for each, who made which choice and who would sign. The round asks whether a manner made together can be taken into a model, what that does to the group that made it, and whether they would find it fair on a stranger's adapter trained on their drawings. Sequence: day 1: 60 min manner and drawing; 30 min selection and captions; training; day 2: 40 min Explorer; 40 min marking; 40 min the three side by side; 30 min round. Subject link: style as a collective decision; authorship; what a model takes from a series. Uncertainty: a reserved card for the training.

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S5)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Shape 3 Basic — "Learners identify examples of data that might be used to train AI systems." S1 and S5: the group decides which pictures stand for the thing it wants learned, and which aspects of them count, with a reason per exclusion, before training; the framework's classroom example has small groups decide what data to collect to train a tool and which aspects of the data matter most.
- Shape 3 Advanced — "Learners evaluate how specific properties of a dataset (e.g. size, features, biases) affect the performance and impact of an AI model." S1 with the two-adapter variant of 7: one adapter on a narrow series and one on a mixed one, or eight pictures against thirty, read in the Explorer on the same motifs; the framework's classroom example has learners see how the size and diversity of a dataset change the outcome.
- Shape 4 Intermediate — "Learners propose specific design changes to improve an AI system for themselves and others." S2: the class analyses a default of the model, plans the series that is to change it and carries the change out, then reads whether it held; the framework's classroom example has learners analyse how data sources shape what a system represents and plan concrete changes.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S2: the base model's narrow default for a farmhouse or a person at work, where it comes from and whom it leaves out, held against the adapter trained on the class's own pictures; the framework's classroom example explores how and why a system's output differs across groups and discusses the impacts.
- Engage 7 Basic — "Learners recognise that ethical AI use depends on a number of factors that include AI system design, development and a user’s own intentions." S5: the group marks what of its own manner is recognisable in the adapter's pictures and discusses whether that would be fair on a stranger's adapter trained on its drawings; the framework's classroom example has learners identify recognisable aspects of artists' work in AI examples and discuss fair use and the implications for the artists.
- Create 4 Advanced — "Learners assess the ethical implications of AI-generated outputs for creative work, distinguish inspiration from replication in their outputs, and justify how their use of AI maintains authenticity and respects other creators." S5: the group's drawings, the adapter's pictures and pictures made with the adapter by the group side by side, and for each who made which choice and who would sign; the framework's classroom example puts human-made, AI-generated and human-with-AI work side by side and asks the same.
- Engage 3 Intermediate — "Learners verify AI-generated outputs for accuracy and relevance by consulting trusted sources and considering task-specific expectations." S3: each description is checked against the picture it describes, the primary source for a caption, and corrected by hand before anything is trained on it.
- Engage 5 Basic — "Learners recognise that computers and AI systems require resources to function." S4: the kWh, CO₂ and VRAM numbers are on the surface and are read.
- Engage 5 Intermediate — "Learners describe different ways that AI impacts the environment (e.g. hardware production, data centre development, water use, energy intensity)." S4: the one-page sheet puts the run's kWh beside the classroom's devices and a published figure for a large model; the framework's classroom example has learners make an informational artefact comparing the training of large models with household energy use.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**

--

**Beyond the framework**: the framework reasons about training data and system design in examples: a class pet survey, a recycling sorter, a library predictor. Here the training is run, by a group, on its own place or its own manner, and the result is read in rows for reach and limit. What the group finds out is how far a large model yields to thirty pictures and a card, and what of its own order survives, which is a question about a model's resilience against local knowledge, and about the resilience of that knowledge in a model. The decisions what is to be learned, which pictures stand for it, what the caption says and whether the reason carries the energy are the group's. The framework has no competence for changing a model with one's own material, none for a collective decision about what a model is to learn, and none for reading the limit of that change.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 2, 4, Manage 1–4, Shape 1, 2, Create 1, 2, 3.

instruments.name: LoRA Explorer

sections.title: What I did
sections.text:
1. Opened `/latent-lab/lora-explorer`. Preparing column: "Adapter" with three chips (19th_century_photography_landscape [preselected], destroyednegative, solarization); "Trigger word" with an Example prompts select (19th_century_photography, landscape, historic photograph; destroyed negative; solarization) and a field prefilled with "19th_century_photography, landscape, historic photograph"; "Motifs, one per line" with an Example prompts select (a landscape; a busy street; a room with a window; a person; a person at work; first meal of the day; a bowl of fruit; a machine) and a field prefilled with "a landscape / a person / a bowl of fruit"; "Adapter strength" slider 50–100 % at 100 %; a note "LoRA Explorer": "This platform trains a LoRA adapter on captions that all begin with the same trigger word. Whether it also acts on something else is a question about the model that took it on: personalisation can drift, so that the ordinary meaning of a word that stood in the captions changes as well (Ruiz et al. 2023)." with three references (Hu et al. 2022, LoRA, ICLR 2022; Ruiz et al. 2023, DreamBooth, CVPR 2023; Kim et al. 2025, Preserve and Personalize). Right: a grid, columns "a landscape / a person / a bowl of fruit", rows "Model · no trigger / Model · trigger / Adapter · trigger / Adapter · no trigger", twelve empty cells. Run button "Run the comparison". The Help panel opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text: "You choose an adapter that was trained here, the word its images were captioned under, and a few motifs — one motif per line, and each becomes a column. Every column is then generated four times over: the plain model on the motif alone, the plain model with the word in front of it, the adapter with the word, and the adapter without it. All sixteen pictures come from one model with one starting number, so what separates two of them is the prompt and the adapter alone." "The third row against the second is the reach: what the training added on top of what the words already carried. The fourth row against the first is the limit: whether the adapter also answers when it is not called, which is how it shows that it has overwritten what the model knew rather than added to it. A motif the adapter was never shown asks the same question from the other side — whether a trained manner carries over, or whether the adapter brings the subjects of its training set along with it." I overlooked it on first use.
2. Kept the defaults (the first adapter, its trigger words, the three motifs, 100 %). Ran at 10:17:48. The header counted "Image 0 / 12 … 12 / 12" and named "sd3.5_large.safetensors · local".
3. Read the four states of the "a person" column and the other two columns (3 below).

Runs: 1 (12 pictures, 11 arrived).

sections.title: What the controls did
sections.text:
- Adapter chips: one trained adapter at a time; the trigger field follows the Example prompts select, not the chip.
- Trigger word field: the words that were in front of every training caption; used in the "trigger" rows.
- Motifs field: one motif per line, one column each.
- Adapter strength: 50–100 % in steps of 10.
- Run the comparison: four pictures per motif with one seed: the base model with and without the trigger words, the model with the adapter with and without them. The header counts.
- "Interpretation help" button on the last picture: not opened.
- Help: opens by itself on the first arrival with the page's text quoted in 1; every later click shows that text again.

sections.title: What came out
sections.text:
The "a person" column, read top to bottom:

- Model · no trigger: a colour photograph, soft and faded, of a woman with a dark bob in a sheer grey top and a black skirt against a beige wall, the face without features. The base model's "a person".
- Model · trigger ("19th_century_photography, landscape, historic photograph, a person"): a sepia photograph of a man in a tall hat and a dark suit standing on a field path by a stream, trees and hills behind, the paper tone and softness of an old print. The trigger words alone, which are plain English, make the base model draw a 19th-century photograph; no adapter was involved.
- Adapter · trigger: a dark sepia picture of a person waist-deep in water seen from behind, mist above, a few blossoms at the lower left. The adapter's look: darker, more vignetted and blurred than the base model's "19th-century" picture.
- Adapter · no trigger: nearly the same picture (the person in the water, the mist, the blossoms), slightly different in the head and the water. The adapter acts without its trigger word, and acts on "a person", a motif that is not in its name.

The other columns: "a landscape" with trigger, base model: a sepia valley with fields, trees and a white house, and a printed caption-like scrawl at the lower left; with the adapter, with and without trigger: two figures in a boat on a grey sea, sepia, the same scene twice. "a bowl of fruit": base model, no trigger, a bright colour photograph of a bowl of apples, oranges, grapes and a pear; with trigger, a warmer still life with grapes and apples on a cloth; with the adapter, with and without trigger, a dark bowl of dull apples on a dark table, nearly identical to each other.

Reading across all three columns: the row that changes the picture is the adapter, not the trigger. The two adapter rows are near-duplicates in every column; the trigger changes the base model strongly (sepia, old print) and the adapter rows barely. This is what the note calls drift: the adapter has taken over the model's "a person" and "a bowl of fruit" even when its word is absent.

The cell "Model · no trigger / a landscape" shows "Service not reachable." instead of a picture; the eleven others arrived. The line names the cause as the surface sees it; the server log shows the other eleven jobs admitted one by one.

sections.title: Where a newcomer stumbles
sections.text:
- Four pictures per motif, as the Help text says; the total stands in the header only after pressing.
- The trigger field does not change when the adapter chip changes; a user who picks "solarization" keeps the 19th-century trigger words unless they also use the select.
- The four row names ("Model · no trigger …") are explained row by row in the Help text; the note on the page explains the trigger, not the rows.
- One cell failed with "Service not reachable." and the run was reported complete; nothing offers to recompute the cell.
- The near-identical adapter rows look like a mistake until the Help text's sentence on the fourth row, or the note's sentence about drift, is read.

sections.title: What the help text should tell a user
sections.text: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says what is chosen, that every motif becomes a column generated four times over, which four states the rows are, that all pictures come from one model with one starting number, and how the third row against the second and the fourth against the first are read. It should add: the trigger field follows the Example prompts select, not the adapter chip; the count stands in the header during the run; the note's word for what the fourth row shows is drift; a cell that shows a sentence instead of a picture did not arrive, and running again fills it.

sections.title: Use possibilities, action-oriented
sections.text:
- One motif that has nothing to do with the adapter's subject (a bowl of fruit for a landscape adapter): see whether the adapter still takes over.
- Adapter strength 50 % against 100 % for the same motifs.
- The three adapters in turn with the same three motifs; compare how much each one drifts.
- Write the trigger words as plain English into a base-model prompt elsewhere and compare with the "Model · trigger" row.

sections.title: Teaching scenarios
sections.text:
**S1 — What did the adapter learn?** (formal, art or computer science, grades 10–13, 90 min, the run started before the lesson). The class reads one column's four pictures and writes what changed between rows 1→2 (the words), 2→3 (the adapter) and 3→4 (the missing word); then a second column; then they read the note and the term drift. Sequence: 10 min rows explained; 30 min two columns in pairs; 20 min comparison; 30 min the note and the question what "learning a style" did to "a person". Subject link: fine-tuning, style, generalisation.

**S2 — Words against weights** (formal, language teaching, grades 11–13, 45 min). Pupils compare the "Model · trigger" row (plain English words that already produce a 19th-century look) with the "Adapter" rows and discuss what a word can do that an adapter cannot, and the reverse. Subject link: description vs. training.

**S3 — Train, then explore** (non-formal, two-day workshop, age 16+). Day 1 the group trains an adapter on its own pictures (LoRA Training); day 2 they explore it here with motifs from outside their series and look for drift. Subject link: dataset, caption, trigger word. Uncertainty: training needs 50 GB of free VRAM and one to three hours (per the training surface), which the shared server did not have on the day.

**S4 — Who is "a person at work"?** (formal, ethics or art, grades 9–12, 45 min, the run started before the lesson). Motifs "a person", "a person at work" and "first meal of the day", all from the surface's own Example prompts, with one adapter; the class fills a table per row: who is shown (age, gender, clothing), doing what, where. Then they compare the base model's two rows with the adapter's two rows and sort the differences: which come from the adapter's series, which the base model brought along. In my run the base model's "a person" was a woman against a wall, the trigger words alone made it a man in a tall hat, and the adapter made it a figure waist-deep in water. Sequence: 10 min rows explained; 20 min table; 15 min sorting and discussion. Subject link: representation, dataset, who is pictured. Uncertainty: I did not run "a person at work" and "first meal of the day".

sections.title: AI-Lit mapping (built from S1–S4)
sections.text:
**(a) 100 % hits**

- Engage 2 Intermediate — "Learners accurately describe how a specific AI tool carries out a task in order to address commonly-held misconceptions about how AI works." S1: the four-row description of what the words do and what the adapter does.
- Shape 3 Advanced — "Learners evaluate how specific properties of a dataset (e.g. size, features, biases) affect the performance and impact of an AI model." S3: the group's own pictures and captions as the dataset, and the drift seen on motifs outside it.
- Engage 6 Intermediate — "Learners explain how biased data or design choices (e.g. stereotyped content, misclassification, unequal recommendations) can lead AI systems to generate unfair or skewed outcomes for certain groups." S4: two sources of skew in whom the pictures show, the base model's data and the adapter's series, separated by the four rows.
- Shape 1 Intermediate — "Learners describe the purpose, intended users and basic constraints of a specific AI tool." S1 and S3: an adapter made for one look, its trigger word, and the constraint that it acts without the word.
- Create 4 Basic — "Learners know that AI-generated content may reuse or copy work protected by intellectual property or copyright laws and recognise implications for the humans who created the original work." S3: an adapter trained on a series of pictures reproduces their look; whose pictures go in is the question the group has to answer before day 1.

**(b) Mutatis mutandis**


**Beyond the framework**: S4 separates two sources of skew in whom a picture shows, the base model's data and the adapter's series, by four rows of the same motif; the framework's Engage 6 examples have one system and one reported difference.

**Non-fits**: Engage 1, 3, 4, 5, 7, Manage 1–4, Shape 2, 4, Create 1, 2, 3.

instruments.help_should_say: The Help panel's own text, which opens on arrival, is quoted in 1: it says what is chosen, that every motif becomes a column generated four times over, which four states the rows are, that all pictures come from one model with one starting number, and how the third row against the second and the fourth against the first are read. It should add: the trigger field follows the Example prompts select, not the adapter chip; the count stands in the header during the run; the note's word for what the fourth row shows is drift; a cell that shows a sentence instead of a picture did not arrive, and running again fills it.
possibilities: One motif that has nothing to do with the adapter's subject (a bowl of fruit for a landscape adapter): see whether the adapter still takes over.
Adapter strength 50 % against 100 % for the same motifs.
The three adapters in turn with the same three motifs; compare how much each one drifts.
Write the trigger words as plain English into a base-model prompt elsewhere and compare with the "Model · trigger" row.
